docs.title: Convolutional Tsetlin Machines
docs.text:
TL;DR

A standard Tsetlin machine ties every literal to one fixed pixel, so a pattern seen in one place means nothing in another. A convolutional Tsetlin machine fixes this by looking at the image through a small window that slides over every position. Each rule is checked against every patch the window sees, and the rule's output for the whole image is the OR of those checks: it fires if the pattern is there anywhere. Learning is the same Recognize, Erase and Reject Feedback as before, with one new choice: when several patches match, the rule learns from one of them, picked at random. To let rules also say where a pattern may appear, each patch gets its window position as extra features, thermometer-coded so a rule can express a range like "in the upper half". The idea is the same sliding filter as a convolutional neural network, but each filter is a small picture you can read.

Level: intermediate · Prerequisites: Classification by voting (rules voting for and against a class, the vote sum \(v\), the Voting Margin \(T\), and how feedback is allocated). The math needs nothing beyond AND, OR and counting.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
Many interesting patterns can turn up anywhere:

  • Heart disease in an ECG. A recording holds many heartbeats. One abnormal waveform may reveal disease, but you don't know which beat it is (Granmo, An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines, Ch. 4, §4.1). The model must find the waveform and learn what it looks like at the same time.
  • Objects in images. A flower, a lesion on a skin photo, a nodule on an X-ray: the same thing can sit in the corner or the centre.
  • Two problems in one. To learn what the pattern looks like you need to know where it is, and to find it you need to know what it looks like. Convolution solves both together.

A standard Tsetlin machine (the previous lessons) would have to learn one rule for every place the pattern can appear. A convolutional one learns the pattern once and recognises it everywhere. And unlike the filters of a convolutional neural network, every learned filter is a small black-and-white picture that you can read and check.

docs.title: Step 1 — One pattern, many places
docs.text:
The chapter's running example is tiny on purpose: eight black-and-white images of \(4 \times 4\) pixels, from two classes, Circle (four black pixels around a white centre) and Cross (the same four plus a black centre). Each shape appears in four different places (Granmo, Ch. 4, §4.2, Table 4.1).

As in lesson 1, each pixel becomes one Boolean feature: True for black, False for white. Name them \(x_{i,j}\), with \(i\) the row and \(j\) the column, so a \(4 \times 4\) image has 16 features (32 literals with their negations).

A standard Tsetlin machine needs a separate rule for each position, because "the pixel at row 2, column 1 is black" is a different literal from "the pixel at row 3, column 2 is black". The chapter's rule for a Circle in the top-left corner is

\[ R_1: \quad \text{if } x_{1,2} \wedge x_{2,1} \wedge \lnot x_{2,2} \wedge x_{2,3} \wedge x_{3,2} \text{ then Circle,} \]

and a Circle one pixel to the right needs a different rule, \(R_2\), with every index shifted. Four positions times two shapes gives eight rules, and a bigger image would need even more.

Try it: switch between the two views.

🔍 Interactive: eight position-specific rules, or two window rules

What to notice

  • Without a window, the eight rule pictures are the same shape moved around. The machine would have to discover the same pattern four times, from a quarter of the examples each time.
  • With a 3×3 window, two rules cover all eight images. The window is placed wherever the shape is, and the rule only describes what is inside the window.
  • The window rules use the same five literals as \(R_1\) (\(R_5\) for Circle), with \(x_{i,j}\) now meaning "row \(i\), column \(j\) of the window", not of the image.

docs.title: Step 2 — Looking through a window: patches and patch features
docs.text:
The fix is to give the Tsetlin machine a local view. Put a rectangular convolution window on the image, say \(3 \times 3\) pixels, and use only the pixels inside it as features. The pixels the window covers form an image patch, and their truth values are the patch features \(x_{1,1}, \dots, x_{3,3}\) (Granmo, Ch. 4, §4.2).

Now slide the window to every position where it fits. Name each position by the column \(x\) and row \(y\) of the window's top-left corner, counting from 0. A \(4 \times 4\) image has room for a \(3 \times 3\) window at four positions: \((0,0)\), \((1,0)\), \((0,1)\) and \((1,1)\). In general, a window of \(w \times w\) on an image of \(W \times H\) pixels has

\[ (W - w + 1) \times (H - w + 1) \]

positions, so a \(6 \times 6\) image gives 16 patches.

The key property: every patch has the same nine features, whatever its position. Patch feature \(x_{2,2}\) always means "the centre of the window", whether the window is in the top-left corner or the bottom-right. So a rule written in patch features is automatically position-free, and the chapter's two rules

\[ \begin{aligned} R_5 &: \text{ if } x_{1,2} \wedge x_{2,1} \wedge \lnot x_{2,2} \wedge x_{2,3} \wedge x_{3,2} \text{ then Circle} \\ R_6 &: \text{ if } x_{1,2} \wedge x_{2,1} \wedge x_{2,2} \wedge x_{2,3} \wedge x_{3,2} \text{ then Cross} \end{aligned} \]

replace all eight. Making the image bigger only adds window positions; the rules stay the same.

Time series: 1-D convolution

An ECG is a sequence, not an image. Describe each moment in time by a few features (one column per time step), and slide the window only along time. That is 1-D convolution: the same idea, with the window moving in one direction (Granmo, Ch. 4, §4.2). The next widget has a "1-D sequence" image of 3 features × 8 time steps, where the window can only move sideways.

What to notice

  • The window gives the machine a way to direct its attention: it looks at one piece of the image at a time.
  • A \(3 \times 3\) window has 9 patch features, so every rule chooses from 18 literals, however large the image is. A standard Tsetlin machine on a \(6 \times 6\) image would have 72 literals per rule.

docs.title: Step 3 — Evaluating a rule: match every patch, then OR
docs.text:
With several patches per image, a rule no longer gives one truth value directly. The chapter's procedure (Granmo, Ch. 4, §4.3, Figure 4.3) is:

Write \(I_j\) for the set of literals that rule \(C_j\) has memorized, and \(l_k^{(p)}\) for the truth value of literal \(l_k\) in patch \(p\). Then the rule's output for the image is

\[ C_j(\text{image}) \;=\; \bigvee_{p=1}^{P} \;\bigwedge_{k \in I_j} l_k^{(p)} , \]

an AND inside each patch (as before) and an OR across the \(P\) patches (new). An empty rule (nothing memorized) matches every patch, so it is True, just as an empty rule was always True in a standard Tsetlin machine.

Try it: the widget starts with the chapter's example image and rule \(R_5\). Step the window through the four positions, then paint your own images and rules.

🪟 Interactive: slide the window, match the rule, OR the results

What to notice

  • The chapter's example. \(R_5\) fails at \((0,0)\), \((1,0)\) and \((1,1)\) and matches at \((0,1)\), where the window sits exactly on the Circle. So the rule is False OR False OR True OR False = True for the image (we checked this in Python too).
  • Many matches still give one vote. Load the bigger image: \(R_5\) matches once and \(R_6\) matches once. Paint a second Circle somewhere: the match map shows two Ts, but the rule's output is still a single True. A rule says "the pattern is present", not "how many times".
  • The match map is a feature map. The grid of Ts and Fs, one cell per window position, is exactly what a convolutional neural network calls a feature map. The OR squeezes it into one bit.
  • 1-D sequence: the window can only move sideways, and the Circle (left) and Cross (right) are found at different time steps by the same rules.

docs.title: Step 4 — Learning: which patch does the rule learn from?
docs.text:
Learning uses the same three kinds of feedback as before (Recognize, Erase & Reject feedback), and the same rule for how often: with vote sum \(v\) for the image's true class, clipped to \([-T, T]\), each rule is selected for feedback with probability

\[ \frac{T - v}{2T}. \]

What changes is one detail. Recognize and Reject Feedback update the memory using the truth values of the literals: memorize the True ones, forget (or, for Reject, memorize) the False ones. With convolution, the rule saw many patches, and their literals disagree. Which patch's literals should it use?

The chapter's answer (Granmo, Ch. 4, §4.4, Figure 4.5) is random selection among the patches the rule matched:

Rule's output on this image Rule belongs to the image's class Rule belongs to the other class True (matches at least one patch) Recognize Feedback, using the literals of one matching patch picked at random Reject Feedback, using one matching patch picked at random False (matches no patch) Erase Feedback: forget literals at random; no patch needed no feedback

Why a matching patch? Recognize Feedback should make the rule more like what it already recognised, so it must learn from a patch where it fired. Reject Feedback should stop the rule firing on the wrong class, so it must learn from a patch where it fired wrongly. Why random? Every matching patch is equally good evidence, and picking at random lets the rule, over many images, drift towards what all its matches have in common. Erase Feedback never looks at truth values, so it needs no patch at all.

How a pattern gets found from nothing

At the very start every rule is empty, so it matches every patch, including empty background. Recognize Feedback then learns from a random patch, often background. But Erase and Reject Feedback keep knocking out literals that don't help, and only patches that contain the shape show up again and again in images of one class. In the next widget, the first step of seed 1 shows it: all 8 rules fire on the first image, so \(v = 4 - 4 = 0\), each rule is selected with probability \(\tfrac{4 - 0}{8} = 0.5\), and the selected rules each learn from 1 of the 16 patches, picked at random.

What to notice

  • The only new ingredient in learning is "pick one matching patch at random". Everything else (the vote sum, the Voting Margin, the selection probability, the three feedback types) is unchanged.
  • Because rules can now specialise in different kinds of patches, it helps to let more rules work together on each image. The chapter does this with a Voting Margin \(T\) larger than 2: the vote sum must reach \(T\), so more rules are recruited (Granmo, Ch. 4, §4.4, Remark).

docs.title: Step 5 — Training a convolutional Tsetlin machine
docs.text:
Let's make the chapter's task harder. Each image is now \(6 \times 6\) with one Circle or Cross anywhere (16 possible places) plus two random black noise pixels outside the shape. There are 300 training images and 300 test images. The machine has 4 rules per class, Voting Margin \(T = 4\), Forget Value 0.7 (so Memorize Value 0.3), and the book's memory depth of 10 positions per literal (Memorized = positions 6 to 10). Everything is seeded, and the widget runs exactly the same code as our Python check, so it shows the numbers below.

Try it: press Train to 20 epochs, then click the rule pictures. Use Step: one image (after Reset) to watch individual updates.

🧠 Interactive: train a convolutional Tsetlin machine on Circle vs Cross

What to notice

  • It learns fast. With seed 1, test accuracy is 90.7% after one epoch and 100% after two. It wobbles slightly on the way (98.7% at epoch 10) and ends at 100%. Seeds 1 to 10 all end at 100% test accuracy.
  • The rules are readable. All four Circle rules learned the same picture: the four black pixels of a Circle, a white centre, and white corners. That is the chapter's \(R_5\) plus four extra "must be white" literals. Two Cross rules learned \(R_6\) plus white corners. Each of these fires on all 147 test Circles (or all 153 test Crosses) and on none of the other class.
  • Not every rule is useful. One Cross rule ended up as a single black pixel: it fires on all 300 test images, so it adds the same vote to every image and changes nothing. Another, "two black pixels side by side", fires on 117 of the 153 Crosses but also on 13 Circles (where a noise pixel lands next to the shape). The clean rules outvote it.
  • Switch to a 6×6 window. A 6×6 window on a 6×6 image has one position, so this is a standard Tsetlin machine with 72 literals per rule. With the same settings it reaches only 54.7% test accuracy (seed 1), and 51.8% on average over seeds 1 to 10: barely better than guessing. Even with 32 rules per class, \(T = 16\), Forget Value 0.1 and 30 epochs, our Python runs only reached 62.7% to 65.7% (seeds 1 to 3). It would need a rule per shape and per position, and about 9 training images per shape and place is too few to learn them.
  • Train on the left half only. Now training shapes appear only in the left half, and the test shapes only in the right half, in places the machine has never seen a shape. The convolutional machine still scores 100% (all 10 seeds): its rules never mention where. The standard one drops to 49.0% (seed 1; 48.6% on average), a coin flip.

In the chapter's example of a truck photo (Granmo, Ch. 4, Figure 4.4), six different rules match different parts of the image: one captures the dark parts of the truck, another the ground beneath it. That is the same effect at a larger scale: each rule specialises in one kind of patch, and the vote combines them.

docs.title: Step 6 — Position encoding: letting a rule say where
docs.text:
Sometimes position does matter. In a handwritten 7, a horizontal stroke at the top is a strong clue, while the same stroke at the bottom belongs to a 2 (Granmo, Ch. 4, §4.5, Figure 4.6). A pure convolutional rule can't tell them apart: it fires wherever the stroke is. We want rules that may restrict a pattern to a region, without being forced to.

The fix: add the window's position to each patch's features. The chapter uses thermometer encoding. An integer from 0 to 3 is written with 3 Boolean features, by switching on features from the bottom up, like the mercury in a thermometer:

value \(X_{\ge 1}\) \(X_{\ge 2}\) \(X_{\ge 3}\) 0 F F F 1 T F F 2 T T F 3 T T T

Feature \(X_{\ge t}\) simply means "the value is at least \(t\)". That makes ranges easy to write with literals:

  • \(X_{\ge 1}\) alone means "1 or more".
  • \(\lnot X_{\ge 3}\) means "less than 3".
  • \(X_{\ge 1} \wedge \lnot X_{\ge 3}\) means "1 or 2": a range, in a single rule.

Ordinary binary encoding would need only 2 bits for 4 values, and could say things like "even" in one literal. But a range like "1 to 2" would no longer be a single AND, and ranges are what you need to describe a rectangular region of an image (Granmo, Ch. 4, §4.5).

Each patch now gets two thermometers, one for its window column \(x\) and one for its row \(y\) (Granmo, Ch. 4, Figure 4.8). On a \(6 \times 6\) image with a \(3 \times 3\) window, \(x\) and \(y\) run from 0 to 3, so that is 3 + 3 = 6 position features, and each patch has 9 + 6 = 15 features, or 30 literals. A rule that forgets all position literals is still position-free; a rule that memorizes some of them only matches patches in a rectangle of window positions.

Try it: set the allowed region, then click pixels to move the Circle in and out of it. Then press Learn to train a machine on a task where position is the whole point.

🌡️ Interactive: thermometer-coded positions make a rule location-sensitive

What to notice

  • Same pattern, different answer. With Upper half (\(\lnot Y_{\ge 2}\), so window row 0 or 1), the rule fires for a Circle in the top rows and stays False when you move the same Circle down. The pattern part matched both times (✓ or ✗ in the grid); only the position literals changed.
  • The learning task. "Is the Circle in the upper or the lower half?" (6×6 images, 2 noise pixels, same settings as Step 5). Without position literals, the machine can only reach 73.3% test accuracy (seed 1; 61.0% on average over seeds 1 to 10). It does a little better than a coin flip only through quirks of the data, such as where the noise pixels can fall. With position literals it reaches 100% (seed 1; 98.9% on average).
  • The learned rules say exactly what we'd hope. With seed 1, two "upper" rules learned the full Circle picture plus \(\lnot Y_{\ge 2} \wedge \lnot Y_{\ge 3}\), i.e. "a Circle with its window in row 0 or 1". Each fires on all 152 upper-half test images and on none of the 148 lower-half ones. Some other rules learned partial Circles with looser regions, which also work.

docs.title: Step 7 — The link to convolutional neural networks
docs.text:
If you have met convolutional neural networks (CNNs), all of this should look familiar. The two share the sliding-window idea; they differ in what slides.

Convolutional neural network Convolutional Tsetlin machine What slides over the image a filter: a small grid of real-valued weights a rule: an AND of literals on the patch features Result at one position a weighted sum, then a non-linearity (a number) match or no match (one bit) Result over all positions a feature map a match map (Step 3 widget) Squeezing the map to one value (global) max pooling OR, which is exactly the max of a map of 0s and 1s Learning signal goes to the position that won the max (back-propagation through max pooling) one matching patch, picked at random Reading the learned filter a grid of numbers; needs visualisation tools a picture of must-be-black, must-be-white and don't-care pixels Position mostly discarded by pooling; can be added (e.g. extra coordinate channels) thermometer-coded position literals the rule may use or ignore

So a convolutional Tsetlin machine is roughly "one convolutional layer plus global max pooling, with logic rules as filters". A CNN stacks many layers, so it can build large patterns from small ones; the chapter's Tsetlin machine has one layer of rules over the patches. What you gain is that every filter is a statement you can check by eye: "a Circle is four black pixels around a white centre, with white corners".

What to notice

  • OR is max pooling for Booleans. Both throw away where the pattern was found and keep whether it was found. That is what makes both of them position-free.
  • Both also send the learning signal through one position. A CNN chooses the position with the highest response; the Tsetlin machine picks at random among the positions that matched, because all matches are equally "high" (they are all True).

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
The complete learning loop (Granmo, Ch. 4, §4.4) is the standard Tsetlin machine loop from the previous lesson with two convolution steps added.

Here is a complete convolutional Tsetlin machine in numpy, on the Step 5 task. It is shorter than the widget's code, and uses numpy's random numbers, so its exact numbers differ from the widget's.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
CIRCLE = [(-1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1), (1, 0)]          # the chapter's two shapes (offsets from the centre)
CROSS = CIRCLE + [(0, 0)]


def make_image(cls):
    """A 6x6 image: a Circle (0) or Cross (1) at a random place, plus 2 random noise pixels."""
    img = np.zeros((6, 6), bool)
    r, c = rng.integers(1, 5, size=2)
    for dr, dc in (CIRCLE, CROSS)[cls]:
        img[r + dr, c + dc] = True
    while img.sum() < len((CIRCLE, CROSS)[cls]) + 2:
        rr, cc = rng.integers(0, 6, size=2)
        if max(abs(rr - r), abs(cc - c)) > 1:
            img[rr, cc] = True
    return img


def patches(img, w=3):
    """Slide a w x w window over the image; each patch -> its literals [x_1..x_9, NOT x_1..NOT x_9]."""
    P = np.array([img[y:y + w, x:x + w].ravel()
                  for y in range(img.shape[0] - w + 1) for x in range(img.shape[1] - w + 1)])
    return np.hstack([P, ~P])


class ConvTM:
    def __init__(self, n_literals, rules_per_class=4, T=4, forget=0.7, depth=10):
        self.half = depth // 2                                            # memory positions 1 .. depth;
        self.state = np.full((2 * rules_per_class, n_literals), self.half)  # start just below Memorized
        self.cls = np.repeat([0, 1], rules_per_class)                     # which class each rule votes for
        self.T, self.F, self.depth = T, forget, depth

    def match(self, P):
        """(rules x patches): a rule matches a patch if none of its memorized literals is False there."""
        memorized = self.state > self.half
        return ~(memorized[:, None, :] & ~P[None, :, :]).any(axis=2)

    def predict(self, P):
        fires = self.match(P).any(axis=1)                                 # OR over all patches
        return 0 if fires[self.cls == 0].sum() >= fires[self.cls == 1].sum() else 1

    def update(self, P, y):
        m = self.match(P)
        fires = m.any(axis=1)
        v = np.clip(fires[self.cls == y].sum() - fires[self.cls != y].sum(), -self.T, self.T)
        for j in np.flatnonzero(rng.random(len(self.cls)) <= (self.T - v) / (2 * self.T)):
            s = self.state[j]
            if fires[j]:
                p = P[rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(m[j]))]                  # ONE matching patch, at random
                if self.cls[j] == y:                                      # Recognize Feedback
                    up = p & (rng.random(len(s)) <= 1 - self.F)
                    down = ~p & (rng.random(len(s)) <= self.F)
                    s += up & (s < self.depth)
                    s -= down & (s > 1)
                else:                                                     # Reject Feedback
                    s += ~p & (s <= self.half)
            elif self.cls[j] == y:                                        # Erase Feedback (no patch needed)
                s -= (rng.random(len(s)) <= self.F) & (s > 1)


ytr, yte = rng.integers(0, 2, 300), rng.integers(0, 2, 300)
Ptr = [patches(make_image(c)) for c in ytr]
Pte = [patches(make_image(c)) for c in yte]
tm = ConvTM(n_literals=18)
for epoch in range(1, 21):
    for i in rng.permutation(len(Ptr)):
        tm.update(Ptr[i], ytr[i])
    if epoch in (1, 5, 20):
        acc = np.mean([tm.predict(P) == y for P, y in zip(Pte, yte)])
        print(f"epoch {epoch:2d}: test accuracy {acc:.3f}")

for j in range(len(tm.cls)):                                              # draw each rule as a 3x3 picture
    on, off = tm.state[j, :9] > tm.half, tm.state[j, 9:] > tm.half
    pic = np.where(on, "#", np.where(off, "o", "."))
    print(("Circle" if tm.cls[j] == 0 else "Cross "), " | ".join("".join(row) for row in pic.reshape(3, 3)))

epoch  1: test accuracy 0.990
epoch  5: test accuracy 1.000
epoch 20: test accuracy 1.000
Circle o#o | #o# | o#o
Circle ... | ... | #..
Circle o#o | #o# | o#o
Circle ... | ... | ...
Cross  o#o | ### | o#o
Cross  o#o | ### | o#o
Cross  o#o | ### | o#o
Cross  o#o | ### | o#o

# = must be black, o = must be white, . = don't care. Again the Circle and Cross pictures appear, each with white corners, plus two Circle rules that ended up (nearly) empty and so fire on (nearly) every image. To add position encoding, append the thermometer features of x and y to each patch in patches before the negations.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"The window makes the machine see less of the image.\"

The window is placed at every position, so every pixel is seen, in every patch that covers it. What the window removes is the pixel's absolute position, which is exactly what makes a rule reusable everywhere.

\"A rule that matches in three places casts three votes.\"

No. The matches are combined with OR, so a rule gives one truth value per image and at most one vote, however many patches match. In Step 3, painting a second Circle doesn't change \(R_5\)'s output.

\"Feedback updates the rule with every matching patch.\"

Recognize and Reject Feedback use one matching patch, chosen at random. Over many images, the random choices average out to what the matching patches have in common.

\"Position encoding turns it back into a standard Tsetlin machine.\"

Position literals are optional for each rule. A rule that forgets all of them is as position-free as before; a rule only memorizes them when restricting the region helps (like the upper-half rules in Step 6). And a region is a whole rectangle of window positions, not one fixed pixel.

\"Binary encoding would be just as good for positions, and shorter.\"

Two bits can hold the four positions 0 to 3, but then "rows 1 to 2" is not a single AND of literals. Thermometer encoding spends one feature per step so that every range, and so every rectangle, is one AND (Granmo, Ch. 4, §4.5).

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. How many window positions does a 3×3 window have on an 8×8 image? On a 28×28 image with a 10×10 window?

$(8 - 3 + 1)^2 = 6^2 = $ 36 positions. $(28 - 10 + 1)^2 = 19^2 = $ 361 positions. Each rule is matched against every one of them, and its output is the OR of all the matches.

2. A Circle rule matches no patch of a Circle image, and is selected for feedback. What happens, and which patch is used?

The rule belongs to the image's class and its output is False, so it gets Erase Feedback: every literal moves one step towards Forgotten with probability equal to the Forget Value. No patch is used, because Erase Feedback doesn't look at truth values.

3. A Circle rule matches 3 of the 16 patches of a Cross image, and is selected. What happens?

The rule fired on the wrong class, so it gets Reject Feedback. One of the 3 matching patches is picked at random, and every forgotten literal that is False in that patch moves one step towards Memorized. Once one of them crosses into Memorized, the rule no longer matches that kind of patch.

4. Window column x runs from 0 to 5. How many thermometer features do you need, and how do you write \"x is 2, 3 or 4\"?

Five features \(X_{\ge 1}, \dots, X_{\ge 5}\) (one per step above 0). "At least 2" is \(X_{\ge 2}\); "less than 5" is \(\lnot X_{\ge 5}\). So the range is \(X_{\ge 2} \wedge \lnot X_{\ge 5}\).

5. Why does the standard Tsetlin machine fail when it is trained on shapes in the left half and tested on shapes in the right half?

Its literals refer to fixed pixels. In training, the pixels of the right half were only ever background or noise, so no rule learned anything about shapes there. In our run it scored 49.0% (seed 1), a coin flip. The convolutional machine's rules talk about window pixels, which are the same wherever the window is, so it scored 100%.

6. In the Step 3 widget, the empty rule is True for every image. Why, and why is such a rule harmless in a trained machine?

With nothing memorized, no literal can be False, so it matches every patch, and the OR is True. An always-True rule adds the same vote to every image, so it carries no information about the class: the other rules simply have to outvote it, and the Voting Margin pushes learning to make them do so. In Step 5, the Cross rule that became a single black pixel behaves almost the same way: it fired on all 300 test images, and the machine still scored 100%.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Ole-Christoffer Granmo, An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines (free online), Ch. 4 "Convolution": §4.1 recognizing patterns in time and space, §4.2 input and patterns (the Circle/Cross images, convolution window, 1-D convolution), §4.3 rule evaluation, §4.4 rule learning (random matching patch, Voting Margin above 2), §4.5 position encoding (thermometer encoding). This lesson's diagrams and widgets are redrawn from the chapter's figures; the 6×6 noisy Circle/Cross task is our own extension of its example.
  • Ole-Christoffer Granmo, Sondre Glimsdal, Lei Jiao, Morten Goodwin, Christian W. Omlin and Geir Thore Berge, The Convolutional Tsetlin Machine (2019). The research paper, in the literature's terms (clauses, Type I/II feedback), with results on MNIST-style image benchmarks.

Next lessons: Confidence & composites: does a Tsetlin machine know when it is wrong, and how to combine several specialised machines.

docs.title: Deep Q-Networks (DQN)
docs.text:
TL;DR

A Deep Q-Network replaces the Q-table of Q-learning with a neural network \(Q(s, a; \theta)\) that takes a state and outputs one Q-value per action. Training it is ordinary regression: push \(Q(s,a;\theta)\) towards the target \(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \theta^-)\) with gradient descent. Two tricks made this stable enough to learn Atari games from pixels (2015): an experience replay buffer, so the network learns from random, decorrelated mini-batches of old experience, and a target network \(\theta^-\), a frozen copy that keeps the target still while the network chases it.

Level: intermediate · Prerequisites: Q-learning & SARSA, Gradient Descent

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
In 2015, a team at DeepMind published Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning in Nature. One agent, with the same network, the same algorithm and the same settings, learned to play 49 different Atari games from nothing but the screen pixels and the score. On many of them it played about as well as a professional human tester. Before that, RL with neural networks was known to be unstable, and most successes used hand-made features.

The algorithm was DQN. It is Q-learning from the previous lesson plus a neural network plus two stabilising tricks. Those tricks, a replay buffer and a target network, are still inside many modern RL methods, and the overestimation problem DQN ran into explains design choices you will meet again in actor-critic methods like SAC.

docs.title: Step 1 — Why Q-tables break
docs.text:
Tabular Q-learning keeps one number \(Q(s, a)\) for every state–action pair. On the cliff world that is a table of at most \(24 \times 4 = 96\) numbers, and each entry is learned separately. That stops working for two reasons.

1. There are far too many states. DQN's Atari input is the last 4 screen frames, shrunk to \(84 \times 84\) grey pixels with 256 shades each. That is \(84 \times 84 \times 4 = 28{,}224\) pixels, so the number of possible inputs is \(256^{28224}\), roughly \(10^{67970}\). No table can hold that, and the agent will never see the same screen twice anyway.

2. States can be continuous. In CartPole, the task we will solve at the end, a cart must keep a pole balanced by pushing left or right. The state is four real numbers: cart position, cart speed, pole angle and pole angular speed. There are infinitely many states.

What we really need is generalisation: if the agent learned that "pole tilting right, falling fast" is bad, it should assume that a slightly different tilt is also bad, without having visited it. A table cannot do this. A function with shared parameters can, because changing its parameters for one state also changes its output for similar states. That is exactly what neural networks are good at.

Q-table Q-network Stores one number per \((s, a)\) weights \(\theta\) shared by all states Unseen state knows nothing guesses from similar states Size grows with the number of states fixed (4,610 weights for our CartPole network) Update one state changes only that entry changes the outputs for many states

The last row is the blessing and the curse of this lesson. Generalisation is why DQN works; it is also why naive training is unstable (Steps 4 and 5).

docs.title: Step 2 — The Q-network: one output per action
docs.text:
We approximate the optimal action-value function with a network: \(Q(s, a; \theta) \approx Q^*(s, a)\), where \(\theta\) are the weights.

There are two ways to feed a network. You could give it \((s, a)\) and get back one number, but then choosing an action needs one forward pass per action. DQN instead takes only the state as input and has one output per action. A single forward pass gives all the Q-values, and acting greedily is just "pick the biggest output".

What to notice

  • The number of outputs is fixed by the number of actions (2 for CartPole, up to 18 for Atari). This is why DQN only works for discrete actions: with a continuous action like "steering angle", there is no finite list of outputs to take the max over. Continuous control needs the actor-critic methods of a later lesson.
  • Nothing about the network is special to RL. It is a plain regression network. All the RL lives in what we train it towards, which is the next step.

docs.title: Step 3 — Turning Q-learning into regression
docs.text:
Recall the tabular Q-learning update from the previous lesson:

\[ Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha \Big[\underbrace{r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')}_{\text{target}} - Q(s,a)\Big] \]

Read it as "move the estimate a little towards the target". With a network we cannot overwrite one entry, but we can do the next best thing: treat the target as a label and take a gradient step that moves \(Q(s,a;\theta)\) towards it. For one transition \((s, a, r, s')\):

\[ y = \begin{cases} r & \text{if } s' \text{ is terminal} \\ r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \theta^-) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad L(\theta) = \big(y - Q(s, a; \theta)\big)^2 \]

and then, exactly as in Gradient Descent, step downhill:

\[ \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\, \nabla_\theta L(\theta) = \theta + 2\eta\, \big(y - Q(s,a;\theta)\big)\, \nabla_\theta Q(s,a;\theta) \]

The bracket \(y - Q(s,a;\theta)\) is the TD error \(\delta\) from earlier lessons. For now read \(\theta^-\) as "the same weights \(\theta\)"; Step 5 explains why DQN uses a separate copy.

Three details matter:

  • The target is treated as a constant. We do not backpropagate through \(y\), even though it depends on the network too. (In code: compute \(y\) under torch.no_grad().) This is called a semi-gradient method. Differentiating through \(y\) as well is a different, usually worse, algorithm.
  • It is still Q-learning. If the "network" were a table with one weight per \((s,a)\), this gradient step would be the tabular update above, with step size \(2\eta\).
  • It is off-policy. The target uses \(\max_{a'}\), the greedy action, no matter which action the agent actually took next. So the transition can come from any behaviour, including old versions of the agent. That is what makes the replay buffer of Step 4 legal.

Huber loss

DQN on Atari clipped the TD error to \([-1, 1]\) in the gradient, which is the same as using the Huber loss (squared for small errors, linear for large ones). It stops a single surprising transition from producing a huge gradient. Our CartPole code uses the plain squared error, to match the formula above.

docs.title: Step 4 — Problem 1: consecutive samples are correlated → experience replay
docs.text:
The naive way to train is online: take one step in the environment, do one gradient step on that transition, repeat. This breaks an assumption that stochastic gradient descent relies on: that each mini-batch is a fair, random sample of the data.

Consecutive transitions are nearly identical (frame 1001 of a game looks almost exactly like frame 1000). Training on them in order is like fitting a regression line using only the points from one corner of the plot, then only from another corner. The network over-fits to whatever it saw last and forgets the rest. Worse, the data depends on the network: if it learns "always go left", it only sees left-hand states, which reinforces the habit.

Experience replay fixes this. Every transition \((s, a, r, s', \text{done})\) goes into a big replay buffer (DQN on Atari kept the last 1 million). For each gradient step, we sample a random mini-batch from the buffer.

Try it: the buffer below fills with real CartPole transitions from a random policy. Sample a mini-batch of 12 "in a row" (the last 12 steps, as online learning would see them) and "at random", and compare where they land in the state plot.

🗃️ Interactive: a replay buffer

What to notice

  • The 12 transitions in a row come from one or two episodes and trace one short, smooth path in the state plot: a single swing of the pole. Each one is almost a copy of its neighbour. A gradient step on them only teaches the network about that corner of the state space.
  • A random batch comes from several episodes, and its orange line zigzags across the whole cloud. It is much closer to an independent, representative sample, which is what SGD expects.
  • Every transition stays in the buffer for a long time and gets sampled many times. Experience is reused, which matters when collecting it is slow (a robot) or expensive (an Atari emulator running for days).

Replay only works because Q-learning is off-policy (Step 3). The old transitions were collected by older, worse versions of the policy, but the Q-learning target doesn't care who chose the action.

docs.title: Step 5 — Problem 2: chasing a moving target → the target network
docs.text:
Look at the target again: \(y = r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \theta)\). It is computed with the same network we are training. In a table that is harmless: updating \(Q(s, a)\) doesn't change \(Q(s', \cdot)\). With a network it is not, because of generalisation. A gradient step that raises \(Q(s, a)\) also raises \(Q\) for similar states, and \(s'\) is usually very similar to \(s\) (it is the next frame). So the target moves every time you step towards it, like a dog chasing its tail. Errors can feed on themselves and grow.

DQN's fix is a second network, the target network with weights \(\theta^-\). It is a copy of the online network that is only updated every \(C\) steps (\(\theta^- \leftarrow \theta\)) and frozen in between. For \(C\) steps, the targets \(y\) are fixed numbers, and learning is plain supervised regression towards fixed labels. Then the labels are refreshed. (DQN on Atari used \(C = 10{,}000\) updates.)

Try it: a tiny example with three states. From states A and B the agent gets reward +1 and moves to state C, which loops back to itself with reward 0 forever. With \(\gamma = 0.9\) the true values are \(Q(A) = Q(B) = 1\) and \(Q(C) = 0\) (green dashed lines). The "network" is linear with only two weights shared by all three states (\(Q(A) = w_1\), \(Q(B) = 2w_1 + w_2\), \(Q(C) = 2w_1 + 2w_2\)), so it can generalise and it can represent the true values exactly. The buffer holds A and B three times as often as C, and each step is one gradient step on the average squared TD error over the buffer. The slider \(C\) sets how often the target is synced; \(C = 1\) means the target is live.

🎯 Interactive: live target vs frozen target

What to notice

  • Live target (\(C = 1\)): it spirals out of control. With \(\alpha = 0.3\), after 300 steps the estimates are around \(-10^9\). A smaller step size does not save it: in this example the error grows by a constant factor every step for any \(\alpha\) (about 1.068 per step at \(\alpha = 0.3\), 1.002 at \(\alpha = 0.01\)), so a smaller \(\alpha\) only makes the explosion slower.
  • Frozen target: it converges. With \(\alpha = 0.3\) and \(C = 10\), all three estimates are within 0.01 of the truth after 300 steps. With \(C = 3\) the syncs are too frequent and it is still off by about 4.
  • Look at the staircase. Between syncs, each line glides towards a fixed label, then jumps when the target is refreshed. Each phase is an ordinary, well-behaved regression problem.
  • There is a price. With a small step size (\(\alpha = 0.05\)), even \(C = 100\) is still off by about 0.5 after 300 steps: values travel through the target only once per sync, so a large \(C\) learns slowly.

No guarantees, just much better odds

The divergence here is an instance of what Sutton and Barto call the deadly triad: function approximation + bootstrapping (targets built from your own estimates) + off-policy data. Any two are fine; all three together can diverge. DQN has all three. The target network and replay buffer don't remove the triad, and you can build examples where DQN still diverges. In practice they make it stable enough to work across dozens of games.

docs.title: Step 6 — Exploration: an ε schedule
docs.text:
DQN acts ε-greedily with respect to its own Q-network, like tabular Q-learning. The difference is that ε is annealed: at the start, the network's outputs are meaningless, so the agent explores a lot; later it mostly exploits what it has learned.

  • DQN on Atari: ε falls linearly from 1.0 to 0.1 over the first million frames, then stays at 0.1.
  • Our CartPole code: ε falls from 1.0 to 0.05 over the first 10,000 steps.

It also waits until the buffer has some data (1,000 transitions in our code) before the first gradient step, so the first mini-batches are not all from the same episode.

The Atari agent used a few more engineering tricks that are worth knowing by name: it stacked the last 4 frames as the state (one frame can't show which way the ball is moving), repeated each action for 4 frames (frame skipping), and clipped rewards to \(-1, 0, +1\) so one set of hyperparameters worked for games with very different score scales.

docs.title: Step 7 — Improvements: Double DQN, dueling networks, prioritised replay
docs.text: DQN started a long line of improvements. Three are especially common.

docs.title: Double DQN: the max is too optimistic
docs.text:
The target uses \(\max_{a'} Q(s', a')\). If the estimates are noisy, the max tends to pick an action whose estimate happens to be too high. So even when the noise averages out to zero for each action, the max is biased upwards. The bias feeds into the targets, then into other estimates through bootstrapping, and DQN's Q-values can end up far higher than the returns the agent really gets.

Try it: every action below is truly worth 0. Each draw gives two independent noisy estimates of all actions (blue and purple). DQN's target takes the max of the blue estimates. Double DQN uses the blue estimates only to choose the action, then reads that action's value from the purple estimate.

📈 Interactive: why the max overestimates

What to notice

  • The max of the blue estimates is almost always positive, although every true value is 0. In a simulation with 200,000 draws and noise \(\sigma = 1\), the average of the max was 0.57 with 2 actions, 1.03 with 4 and 1.54 with 10. More actions → more chances to be lucky → more overestimation.
  • The Double estimate averages about 0 (to within 0.003 in the same simulation), whatever the number of actions. Choosing with one estimate and judging with an independent one removes the "winner was lucky" bias.

DQN already has a second network, so Double DQN costs one line. The target becomes

\[ y = r + \gamma\, Q\big(s',\ \underbrace{\arg\max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \theta)}_{\text{online net chooses}};\ \theta^-\big) \quad (\text{target net evaluates}) \]

docs.title: Dueling networks
docs.text: Split the last layer into two streams: one estimates the state value \(V(s)\), one estimates how much better each action is than average, the advantage \(A(s, a)\). They are recombined as \(Q(s,a) = V(s) + A(s,a) - \tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{a'} A(s,a')\). In many states the action barely matters (nothing is happening on screen), and the \(V\) stream can learn that without learning every action separately.

docs.title: Prioritised experience replay
docs.text:
Sample transitions with large TD error \(|\delta|\) more often, because that is where the network is most wrong and has the most to learn. Importance-sampling weights correct the bias this introduces.

Rainbow (2018) combined these with three more ideas (multi-step targets, distributional values, noisy networks) and beat each of them alone on Atari.

What DQN can't do

DQN needs a lot of data (the Atari agents trained on 50 million frames per game, about 38 days of play), it only handles discrete actions, and it can be brittle: results vary a lot between random seeds, as you'll see below. Policy-gradient and actor-critic methods (the next lessons) address the continuous-action problem; model-based methods address data efficiency.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Here is a complete DQN in PyTorch. CartPole is written out in plain Python with the standard physics (it is Gym's CartPole-v1: reward +1 for every step the pole stays up, episodes end when it falls or after 500 steps). The two flags use_replay and use_target let us switch the two tricks off.

import math, random
from collections import deque

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn


class CartPole:
    """The classic cart-pole task (same physics as Gym's CartPole-v1). Reward +1 per step, max 500 steps."""

    def reset(self):
        self.s = np.random.uniform(-0.05, 0.05, size=4)     # cart position, cart speed, pole angle, pole speed
        self.t = 0
        return self.s.astype(np.float32)

    def step(self, action):                                  # 0 = push left, 1 = push right
        x, x_dot, th, th_dot = self.s
        force = 10.0 if action == 1 else -10.0
        cos, sin = math.cos(th), math.sin(th)
        temp = (force + 0.05 * th_dot**2 * sin) / 1.1
        th_acc = (9.8 * sin - cos * temp) / (0.5 * (4 / 3 - 0.1 * cos**2 / 1.1))
        x_acc = temp - 0.05 * th_acc * cos / 1.1
        self.s = np.array([x + 0.02 * x_dot, x_dot + 0.02 * x_acc, th + 0.02 * th_dot, th_dot + 0.02 * th_acc])
        self.t += 1
        fell = abs(self.s[0]) > 2.4 or abs(self.s[2]) > 12 * math.pi / 180
        return self.s.astype(np.float32), 1.0, fell, self.t >= 500   # s', r, terminal?, time limit?


def q_network():                                             # Q(s, ·; θ): 4 numbers in, one Q-value per action out
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 2))


def greedy_test(q_net, episodes=20):                         # play with ε = 0, return the average episode length
    env, lengths = CartPole(), []
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s, done = env.reset(), False
        while not done:
            with torch.no_grad():
                a = q_net(torch.tensor(s)).argmax().item()
            s, r, term, trunc = env.step(a)
            done = term or trunc
        lengths.append(env.t)
    return np.mean(lengths)


def train_dqn(seed=0, total_steps=50_000, gamma=0.99, batch_size=64, sync_every=500,
              use_replay=True, use_target=True):
    random.seed(seed); np.random.seed(seed); torch.manual_seed(seed)
    env = CartPole()
    q_net, target_net = q_network(), q_network()
    target_net.load_state_dict(q_net.state_dict())            # θ⁻ ← θ
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(q_net.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    buffer = deque(maxlen=50_000 if use_replay else 1)        # no replay = learn from the newest transition only
    untrained_score = greedy_test(q_net)
    lengths, step = [], 0

    while step < total_steps:
        s, done = env.reset(), False
        while not done:
            # 1. act ε-greedily; ε falls from 1.0 to 0.05 over the first 10,000 steps
            eps = max(0.05, 1.0 - step / 10_000)
            if random.random() < eps:
                a = random.randrange(2)
            else:
                with torch.no_grad():
                    a = q_net(torch.tensor(s)).argmax().item()
            s2, r, terminal, truncated = env.step(a)

            # 2. store the transition in the replay buffer
            buffer.append((s, a, r, s2, terminal))
            s, done, step = s2, terminal or truncated, step + 1

            # 3. learn from a random mini-batch of old transitions
            if len(buffer) >= (1_000 if use_replay else 1):
                batch = random.sample(buffer, min(batch_size, len(buffer)))
                S, A, R, S2, T = (torch.tensor(np.array(x), dtype=torch.float32) for x in zip(*batch))
                with torch.no_grad():                                         # the target is a fixed label
                    net = target_net if use_target else q_net
                    y = R + gamma * (1 - T) * net(S2).max(dim=1).values      # y = r + γ max_a' Q(s', a'; θ⁻)
                q = q_net(S).gather(1, A.long()[:, None]).squeeze(1)        # Q(s, a; θ)
                loss = ((y - q) ** 2).mean()                                  # (y − Q(s, a; θ))²
                optimizer.zero_grad()
                loss.backward()
                optimizer.step()                                              # one gradient step on θ

            # 4. every C steps, copy the online network into the target network
            if use_target and step % sync_every == 0:
                target_net.load_state_dict(q_net.state_dict())
        lengths.append(env.t)

    return untrained_score, lengths, greedy_test(q_net)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    torch.set_num_threads(1)
    before, lengths, after = train_dqn(seed=0)
    print(f"episodes played: {len(lengths)}")
    for i in range(0, len(lengths) - 99, 100):
        print(f"  episodes {i + 1:3d}-{min(i + 100, len(lengths)):3d}: average length {np.mean(lengths[i:i + 100]):6.1f}")
    print(f"average length, first 20 training episodes: {np.mean(lengths[:20]):6.1f}")
    print(f"average length, last 20 training episodes:  {np.mean(lengths[-20:]):6.1f}")
    print(f"greedy test (20 episodes), untrained network: {before:6.1f}")
    print(f"greedy test (20 episodes), trained network:   {after:6.1f}   (500 = never fell)")

On one CPU core this takes about 70 seconds:

episodes played: 503
  episodes   1-100: average length   22.2
  episodes 101-200: average length   64.8
  episodes 201-300: average length  128.6
  episodes 301-400: average length  130.8
  episodes 401-500: average length  149.1
average length, first 20 training episodes:   27.1
average length, last 20 training episodes:   145.5
greedy test (20 episodes), untrained network:    9.3
greedy test (20 episodes), trained network:    136.7   (500 = never fell)

The untrained network drops the pole after about 9 steps; the trained one keeps it up for 137 steps on average with no exploration, and the training episodes grew from about 22 steps to about 150. It learns, but it doesn't reach the maximum of 500 within 50,000 steps on this seed.

Ablation. Same code, three random seeds each, switching off one trick at a time (average length of the last 20 training episodes, and of 20 greedy test episodes, one number per seed). The script below imports train_dqn from the code above (saved as dqn_cartpole.py) and runs the nine trainings in parallel:

import multiprocessing as mp
import numpy as np, torch
from dqn_cartpole import train_dqn

CONFIGS = {"full DQN": {}, "no target network": {"use_target": False},
           "no replay buffer": {"use_replay": False}}

def job(args):
    torch.set_num_threads(1)
    name, seed = args
    _, lengths, after = train_dqn(seed=seed, **CONFIGS[name])
    return name, seed, np.mean(lengths[-20:]), after

if __name__ == "__main__":
    jobs = [(n, s) for n in CONFIGS for s in range(3)]
    with mp.Pool(len(jobs)) as pool:
        res = pool.map(job, jobs)
    for name in CONFIGS:
        rows = [r for r in res if r[0] == name]
        last = "  ".join(f"{r[2]:5.1f}" for r in rows)
        test = "  ".join(f"{r[3]:5.1f}" for r in rows)
        print(f"{name:18s} last 20 episodes: {last}   greedy test: {test}")

full DQN           last 20 episodes: 145.5  412.4  223.3   greedy test: 136.7  215.4  357.5
no target network  last 20 episodes: 213.4  228.3  457.7   greedy test: 234.8  148.8  181.3
no replay buffer   last 20 episodes:  36.1   17.8   69.9   greedy test:   9.7  125.8   69.8

What this shows, and what it doesn't:

  • Seeds matter a lot. The full DQN ended between 145 and 412 depending only on the random seed. DQN is famous for this; always run several seeds before believing a comparison.
  • Replay mattered clearly. Learning from each transition once, in order, ended far lower on every seed (18 to 70 steps in training).
  • The target network didn't help on CartPole in these runs: without it, the results were similar or even better. CartPole is tiny and its values are smooth, so the chasing effect of Step 5 didn't hurt here. On Atari it was different: the DQN paper's ablation on five games shows the score dropping on every game without the target network, and dropping much further without replay. Tricks that are essential at scale can be invisible on a toy problem, and the other way round.

The DQN paper's own network for Atari is the same idea with convolutions in front:

atari_q_net = nn.Sequential(                       # input: 4 stacked 84×84 grey frames
    nn.Conv2d(4, 32, kernel_size=8, stride=4), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=4, stride=2), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=1), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64 * 7 * 7, 512), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(512, n_actions),                     # one Q-value per joystick action
)

For real projects, use a tested implementation such as CleanRL's dqn.py or Stable-Baselines3's DQN with Gymnasium environments.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"DQN is a new learning rule.\"

It is Q-learning. The update target \(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s',a')\) is the same; only the way the Q-function is stored (a network instead of a table) and two stabilisers (replay, target network) are new.

\"The target network is a second network that is trained too.\"

It is never trained. It is a periodic copy of the online network, used only to compute targets. All gradient steps go into \(\theta\).

\"Experience replay works with any RL algorithm.\"

Only with off-policy methods. Replayed transitions were chosen by an older policy. Q-learning's target doesn't care (it uses the max), but on-policy methods like SARSA or vanilla policy gradients assume the data comes from the current policy, and naive replay breaks them.

\"Higher Q-values mean the agent is doing better.\"

Not necessarily. Because of the max in the target, DQN's Q-values tend to overestimate the real returns. Judge an agent by the returns it actually collects, not by its own value estimates.

\"With a target network, DQN is guaranteed to converge.\"

No. Function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy data together (the deadly triad) can still diverge. The tricks make training stable in practice, not in theory.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. Why does a DQN have one output per action instead of taking the action as an input?

So that one forward pass gives \(Q(s, a)\) for all actions. Both acting greedily and computing the target \(\max_{a'} Q(s', a')\) need every action's value, and with the action as input that would take one forward pass per action.

2. A transition ends the episode (the pole fell). What is its target y, and why?

\(y = r\). There is no next state to bootstrap from: the return after a terminal state is 0. In the code this is the (1 - T) factor. Forgetting it makes the agent believe falling is followed by more reward.

3. Which of DQN's two tricks addresses which problem?

Experience replay addresses correlated, non-stationary training data: random mini-batches from a large buffer are close to independent samples, and each transition is reused many times. The target network addresses the moving target: freezing \(\theta^-\) for \(C\) steps makes the labels fixed, so each phase is ordinary regression.

4. In the moving-target widget, why does the live target diverge even though the network can represent the true values exactly?

The weights are shared. A step that fixes the error at A or B also changes \(Q(C)\), which is the target for A and B. With the target live, the update keeps chasing its own effect, and here the errors grow by a fixed factor each step for every step size. Freezing the target for enough steps lets each regression phase finish before the target moves.

5. What does Double DQN change, and what problem does it fix?

The target action is chosen by the online network but evaluated by the target network: \(y = r + \gamma Q(s', \arg\max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \theta); \theta^-)\). Taking a max over noisy estimates is biased upwards (overestimation); using one estimate to choose and an independent one to evaluate removes most of that bias.

docs.title: Dynamic Programming: Policy and Value Iteration
docs.text:
TL;DR

If you know the model of the environment, the rules \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\), you don't need trial and error. You can compute the best policy. Dynamic programming (DP) turns the Bellman equations into update rules and applies them to every state, over and over, until nothing changes. Policy iteration alternates "how good is my policy?" (evaluation) with "act greedily on that" (improvement). Value iteration folds both into one update. Both find the optimal policy for the cliff world in a fraction of a second.

Level: intermediate · Prerequisites: What is RL? (the cliff world, policies and values) and MDPs & Bellman equations (the model \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\) and the Bellman equations).

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
In the MDP lesson we wrote down the Bellman equations: what the values of a policy, and the optimal values, must satisfy. That tells us what the answer looks like. It doesn't tell us how to find it.

Dynamic programming is the "how", for the case where we know the rules of the world:

  • Planning problems with known rules: inventory and stock control, maintenance schedules, queues, small robot navigation tasks, board-game endgames. If you can write down the transition probabilities, DP gives you the provably optimal policy.
  • The blueprint for everything that follows. Monte Carlo, TD learning, Q-learning, DQN and actor-critic are all, at heart, DP with the exact sums replaced by samples from experience. Q-learning is "value iteration from samples". Actor-critic is "policy iteration with a neural network". If you understand this lesson, the rest of the course is variations on a theme.

The name is historical (Richard Bellman, 1950s). "Programming" here means planning, as in "a TV programme", not writing code. "Dynamic" means it unfolds over time steps.

docs.title: Step 1 — Turn the Bellman equation into an update rule: policy evaluation
docs.text:
The first job: given a policy \(\pi\), compute its values \(V^\pi(s)\) for every state. The Bellman expectation equation from the last lesson says the value of a state is the expected reward of one step plus the discounted value of where you land:

\[ V^\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[\, r + \gamma\, V^\pi(s') \,\big] \]

That is one equation per state, and \(V^\pi\) appears on both sides. The trick of iterative policy evaluation is almost embarrassingly simple: use the equation as an assignment. Start with any guess, say \(V_0(s) = 0\) everywhere, and repeatedly overwrite every state with the right-hand side, computed from the previous guess:

\[ V_{k+1}(s) \;\leftarrow\; \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[\, r + \gamma\, V_k(s') \,\big] \qquad \text{for every state } s \]

One pass over all states is called a sweep. Each single update is called a backup, because it copies ("backs up") value information from the next states into the current one. We stop when the biggest change in a sweep, \(\Delta = \max_s |V_{k+1}(s) - V_k(s)|\), falls below a small threshold \(\theta\) (we use \(10^{-6}\)).

Why does this converge? Each sweep shrinks the distance to the true \(V^\pi\) by at least a factor \(\gamma\). With \(\gamma < 1\), errors die out geometrically, wherever you start. (In maths language, the update is a contraction.)

You have already seen this algorithm: the policy widget in lesson 1 secretly ran it every time you changed an arrow. Here you can watch it, sweep by sweep.

🧮 Interactive: policy evaluation, one sweep at a time

What to notice

  • Information flows backwards from the end. After sweep 1, every cell knows only about the −1 step cost, except the cells next to the goal or the cliff, which have seen the +10 or −20. Each sweep pushes that news one more step away. That is the backup, made visible.
  • The random policy is slow to evaluate. With \(\gamma = 0.95\) it takes 155 sweeps to reach \(\Delta < 10^{-6}\), ending at \(V(\text{start}) = -19.88\) (the same number as lesson 1). Lower \(\gamma\) to 0.5 and it needs only 21; at \(\gamma = 0.99\) it needs 272. A larger \(\gamma\) means a longer memory, so errors fade more slowly.
  • Deterministic paths settle exactly. Edge of the cliff at slip 0 needs only 9 sweeps (\(V(\text{start}) = 2.05\)): once the goal's value has travelled back along every path, nothing changes any more. At slip 0.2 it needs 32 sweeps and ends at \(-9.08\), as in lesson 1.

docs.title: Step 2 — Policy improvement: act greedily on the values
docs.text:
Knowing \(V^\pi\) is useful only if it helps us do better. Here's how. In any state \(s\), look one step ahead at each action, using the values of \(\pi\) for whatever comes after:

\[ Q^\pi(s, a) = \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[\, r + \gamma\, V^\pi(s') \,\big] \]

\(Q^\pi(s, a)\) is the return you expect if you take action \(a\) once, then go back to following \(\pi\). Now build a new policy \(\pi'\) that simply picks the best-looking action everywhere. It is greedy with respect to \(V^\pi\):

\[ \pi'(s) = \arg\max_a \; Q^\pi(s, a) \]

Here is one real example: the cell just above the last cliff square, under the random policy (slip 0, \(\gamma = 0.95\)).

Why is \(\pi'\) never worse than \(\pi\)? In every state, the greedy action is at least as good as what \(\pi\) would do on average: \(Q^\pi(s, \pi'(s)) \ge V^\pi(s)\). So "follow \(\pi'\) for one step, then \(\pi\)" is at least as good as \(\pi\). Apply the same argument at the next step, and the next, and you get "follow \(\pi'\) forever" is at least as good too. This is the policy improvement theorem:

\[ Q^\pi\big(s, \pi'(s)\big) \ge V^\pi(s) \;\text{ for all } s \quad\Longrightarrow\quad V^{\pi'}(s) \ge V^\pi(s) \;\text{ for all } s \]

And if the greedy policy is the same as \(\pi\), then \(\pi\) already satisfies the Bellman optimality equation, so it is optimal. No better policy exists.

What to notice

Go back to the widget in Step 1, evaluate the Random policy to convergence, and tick show the greedy policy. The green arrows are \(\pi'\). Even though the random policy is terrible (\(-19.88\)), one greedy step on its values already gives a sensible route around the top (it is the safe detour, worth \(-2.04\) at slip 0). Click cells to see the four Q-values behind each arrow.

docs.title: Step 3 — Policy iteration: evaluate, improve, repeat
docs.text:
Put Steps 1 and 2 in a loop and you have policy iteration:

  1. Evaluate the current policy \(\pi_k\) to get \(V^{\pi_k}\) (many sweeps, Step 1).
  2. Improve: $\pi_{k+1} = $ greedy with respect to \(V^{\pi_k}\) (Step 2).
  3. If \(\pi_{k+1} = \pi_k\), stop: it is optimal. Otherwise go back to 1.

Each new policy is at least as good as the last. There are only finitely many deterministic policies (\(4^{18}\) here, about 69 billion), so the loop must end. In practice it ends after a handful of rounds.

🔁 Interactive: policy iteration on the cliff world

What to notice

  • Very few rounds. At slip 0 the values of the start cell go \(-19.88 \to -2.04 \to 2.05 \to 2.05\): random, then the safe detour, then the cliff-edge route. The fourth improvement changes nothing, so it stops. At slip 0.2 it goes \(-19.88 \to -6.49 \to -6.30\) and stops after the third.
  • The expensive part is evaluation. Evaluating the random policy takes 155 sweeps; later policies need far fewer (12, 10 and 9 at slip 0). Improvement is a single cheap pass.
  • The answer depends on the world. Slip 0 gives the cliff-edge route (\(V^* = 2.05\)). Slip 0.2 gives a cautious policy worth \(-6.30\), better than both hand-written policies from lesson 1 (\(-9.08\) for the edge, \(-6.97\) for the detour).

docs.title: Step 4 — Value iteration: one sweep, then improve
docs.text:
Policy iteration waits for evaluation to converge before improving. Does it have to? What if we improve after every single sweep? Then evaluation and improvement merge into one update, which is the Bellman optimality equation used as an assignment:

\[ V_{k+1}(s) \;\leftarrow\; \max_a \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[\, r + \gamma\, V_k(s') \,\big] \qquad \text{for every state } s \]

Compare it with policy evaluation in Step 1: the average over the policy's actions, \(\sum_a \pi(a \mid s)\), has become a \(\max_a\). That's all. This is value iteration. It converges to \(V^*\) for the same reason as before (each sweep shrinks the error by at least \(\gamma\)). When it stops, read off the optimal policy greedily: \(\pi^*(s) = \arg\max_a Q(s, a)\).

⚡ Interactive: value iteration, sweep by sweep

What to notice

  • Slip 0: value iteration needs 9 sweeps (\(\Delta\) drops to exactly 0 on the 9th) and finds \(V^*(\text{start}) = 2.05\), the cliff-edge route. The greedy arrows are already final after sweep 7, before the values have finished.
  • Slip 0.2: it needs 37 sweeps and gives \(V^*(\text{start}) = -6.30\), the same answer as policy iteration. The arrows stop changing after sweep 11. Policies often converge long before values do.
  • The route switches at slip ≈ 0.112. Drag the slip slider slowly: at 0.11 the optimal route still hugs the cliff (\(V^* = -4.17\)); at 0.12 it climbs over the top (\(V^* = -4.46\)). Nobody told the agent "be careful"; it falls out of the maths.
  • Above slip ≈ 0.327 the start cell points ← into the wall. Bumping into the wall keeps you in place, and a slip from "left" only goes up or down (down is also a wall). It is the one action from the start that can never slide you into the cliff.
  • The chart: \(\Delta\) falls roughly in a straight line on the log scale, i.e. geometrically. Changing \(\gamma\) at slip 0.2 moves the sweep count only a little (19 at \(\gamma = 0.5\), 34 at 0.9, 39 at 0.99), because most paths end at the goal or the cliff long before discounting matters.

docs.title: Step 5 — The big picture: generalized policy iteration
docs.text:
Policy iteration and value iteration are two ends of one idea. There are two processes, and they push each other along:

  • Evaluation makes the values consistent with the current policy.
  • Improvement makes the policy greedy with respect to the current values.

Each one, by doing its job, spoils the other a little: a new policy makes the old values out of date, and new values make the old policy no longer greedy. Yet the back-and-forth only stops when both are satisfied at once. A policy that is greedy with respect to its own values satisfies the Bellman optimality equation. So the only resting point is \(\pi^*\) and \(V^*\).

Sutton and Barto call this generalized policy iteration (GPI). Almost every RL method fits it. You can evaluate fully or partially, update all states or just one, compute exact sums or use samples. As long as both processes keep running, things tend towards the optimum. Later lessons are all GPI:

Method Evaluation Improvement Policy iteration (this lesson) exact, all sweeps greedy, all states Value iteration (this lesson) one sweep greedy, built into the max Monte Carlo control, SARSA, Q-learning from sampled episodes or steps ε-greedy Actor-critic (PPO, SAC) a critic network learns \(V\) or \(Q\) a gradient step on the actor network

docs.title: Step 6 — The catch: you need the model, and you need every state
docs.text:
DP is exact and fast on the cliff world. Two things stop it from solving everything:

  1. It needs the model. Every backup sums over \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\). For a robot, a stock market or a conversation with a person, nobody can write those probabilities down. We only get to try things and see what happens.
  2. It sweeps over every state. The cliff world has 18 states. Backgammon has about \(10^{20}\). Even at a billion backups per second, one sweep over \(10^{20}\) states would take about 3,200 years. Go has around \(10^{170}\) positions; an image-based game has astronomically more. The number of states grows exponentially with the number of variables that describe a state. Bellman called this the curse of dimensionality.

The way out is to keep the GPI idea but change how the backups are done:

  • Sample instead of summing. Replace \(\sum_{s',r} p(s', r \mid s, a)[\dots]\) with what actually happened on one step or one episode. No model needed. This is Monte Carlo and TD learning, the next lesson.
  • Only visit states that matter. An agent following its policy spends its time in relevant states, not in all \(10^{20}\).
  • Generalize between states. Replace the table of values with a function, e.g. a neural network, so that learning about one state teaches you about similar ones (the DQN lesson).

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Value iteration, the shortest route from a known model to an optimal policy:

Here are both algorithms in numpy. The model is stored as two arrays: P[s, a, s'], the probability of landing in non-terminal state s', and R[s, a], the expected immediate reward. Terminal states (goal, cliff) have value 0, so they don't need a column in P. Policies are tables pi[s, a] of action probabilities, so the random policy and a deterministic one use the same code.

import numpy as np

MAP = ["......",
       "..#...",
       "......",
       "SCCCCG"]
MOVES = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]          # up, right, down, left
ARROWS = "↑→↓←"
STATES = [(r, c) for r in range(4) for c in range(6) if MAP[r][c] in ".S"]
INDEX = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(STATES)}         # 18 non-terminal states
nS, nA = len(STATES), 4


def build_model(slip):
    """The model p(s', r | s, a) as two arrays:
    P[s, a, s'] = probability of landing in non-terminal state s'
    R[s, a]     = expected immediate reward."""
    P, R = np.zeros((nS, nA, nS)), np.zeros((nS, nA))
    for (r, c), s in INDEX.items():
        for a in range(nA):
            for p, d in [(1 - slip, a), (slip / 2, (a + 1) % 4), (slip / 2, (a + 3) % 4)]:
                nr, nc = r + MOVES[d][0], c + MOVES[d][1]
                if not (0 <= nr < 4 and 0 <= nc < 6) or MAP[nr][nc] == "#":
                    nr, nc = r, c                                    # bump: stay put
                tile = MAP[nr][nc]
                R[s, a] += p * (10 if tile == "G" else -20 if tile == "C" else -1)
                if tile in ".S":                                     # terminal states have value 0
                    P[s, a, INDEX[(nr, nc)]] += p
    return P, R


def policy_evaluation(P, R, pi, gamma, tol=1e-6):
    """Sweep V(s) <- sum_a pi(a|s) [R(s,a) + gamma * sum_s' P(s'|s,a) V(s')] until it stops changing."""
    V, sweeps = np.zeros(nS), 0
    while True:
        V_new = (pi * (R + gamma * P @ V)).sum(axis=1)  # pi[s, a] = probability of a in s
        delta, V, sweeps = np.abs(V_new - V).max(), V_new, sweeps + 1
        if delta < tol:
            return V, sweeps


def greedy(P, R, V, gamma):
    """One-step lookahead: the best action in every state, as a one-hot policy table."""
    Q = R + gamma * P @ V
    return np.eye(nA)[Q.argmax(axis=1)]


def policy_iteration(P, R, gamma):
    pi = np.full((nS, nA), 1 / nA)                       # start from the random policy
    for it in range(1, 100):
        V, sweeps = policy_evaluation(P, R, pi, gamma)   # 1. evaluate
        new_pi = greedy(P, R, V, gamma)                  # 2. improve
        print(f"  iteration {it}: evaluation took {sweeps:3d} sweeps, V(start) = {V[INDEX[(3, 0)]]:6.2f}")
        if np.array_equal(new_pi, pi):                   # 3. stable? then it is optimal
            return pi, V
        pi = new_pi


def value_iteration(P, R, gamma, tol=1e-6):
    V, sweeps = np.zeros(nS), 0
    while True:
        V_new = (R + gamma * P @ V).max(axis=1)          # Bellman optimality backup, all states at once
        delta, V, sweeps = np.abs(V_new - V).max(), V_new, sweeps + 1
        if delta < tol:
            return greedy(P, R, V, gamma), V, sweeps


def show(pi):
    grid = [list(row) for row in MAP]
    for (r, c), s in INDEX.items():
        grid[r][c] = ARROWS[pi[s].argmax()]
    return "\n".join("".join(row) for row in grid)


gamma = 0.95
for slip in [0.0, 0.2]:
    P, R = build_model(slip)
    print(f"slip = {slip}")
    print(" policy iteration:")
    pi_pi, V_pi = policy_iteration(P, R, gamma)
    pi_vi, V_vi, sweeps = value_iteration(P, R, gamma)
    print(f" value iteration: {sweeps} sweeps, V*(start) = {V_vi[INDEX[(3, 0)]]:.2f}")
    print(" same policy from both:", np.array_equal(pi_pi, pi_vi))
    print(show(pi_vi), "\n")

slip = 0.0
 policy iteration:
  iteration 1: evaluation took 155 sweeps, V(start) = -19.88
  iteration 2: evaluation took  12 sweeps, V(start) =  -2.04
  iteration 3: evaluation took  10 sweeps, V(start) =   2.05
  iteration 4: evaluation took   9 sweeps, V(start) =   2.05
 value iteration: 9 sweeps, V*(start) = 2.05
 same policy from both: True
→→→→→↓
→↓#→→↓
→→→→→↓
↑CCCCG

slip = 0.2
 policy iteration:
  iteration 1: evaluation took 155 sweeps, V(start) = -19.88
  iteration 2: evaluation took  37 sweeps, V(start) =  -6.49
  iteration 3: evaluation took  37 sweeps, V(start) =  -6.30
 value iteration: 37 sweeps, V*(start) = -6.30
 same policy from both: True
→→→→→↓
↑↑#→→↓
↑↑→↑→↓
↑CCCCG

The whole thing runs in well under a second. Notice the line R + gamma * P @ V: it computes \(Q(s, a)\) for every state and action at once. Policy evaluation averages it over the policy, value iteration takes the max, and improvement takes the argmax. Three algorithms, one backup.

Two variations you will meet in other code:

  • In-place sweeps (Gauss–Seidel): overwrite V[s] immediately, so later states in the same sweep already use the new values. Often converges in fewer sweeps; lesson 1's widget did this.
  • Q-value iteration: keep a table \(Q(s, a)\) instead of \(V(s)\) and back up \(Q(s, a) \leftarrow \sum p\,[r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')]\). Replace that sum by a single sampled transition and you get Q-learning.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"Dynamic programming is a learning algorithm.\"

DP is planning, not learning. It never interacts with the environment: it reads the rules \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\) and computes. RL methods proper (from the next lesson on) learn from experience because they don't have the rules.

\"You have to evaluate a policy exactly before you can improve it.\"

No. Improvement works with any values, and value iteration improves after a single sweep. Policy iteration's full evaluation buys fewer, bigger improvement steps; value iteration buys cheap steps. Both reach the same \(\pi^*\), and the arrows often settle long before the values (sweep 11 of 37 at slip 0.2).

\"The greedy policy only maximises the next reward.\"

Greedy here means greedy with respect to \(Q\), which includes \(\gamma V(s')\), the value of everything that comes after. Acting greedily on good values is far-sighted. Acting greedily on rewards alone would be short-sighted.

\"Value iteration tells you how many steps to the goal.\"

It tells you the expected discounted return. On a slippery floor the optimal policy can deliberately take a longer route, or even walk into a wall (slip above about 0.33), because that maximises the expected return, not the path length.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. What is the only difference between the policy evaluation update and the value iteration update?

Policy evaluation averages over the policy's actions, \(\sum_a \pi(a \mid s)[\dots]\). Value iteration takes the maximum over actions, \(\max_a [\dots]\). Everything inside the brackets, the one-step lookahead \(\sum_{s',r} p(s',r \mid s,a)[r + \gamma V(s')]\), is the same.

2. Policy iteration produced the same policy twice in a row. Why can we stop and call it optimal?

If \(\pi\) is greedy with respect to its own values \(V^\pi\), then \(V^\pi(s) = \max_a \sum p\,[r + \gamma V^\pi(s')]\) for every state. That is exactly the Bellman optimality equation, whose only solution is \(V^*\). So \(V^\pi = V^*\) and \(\pi\) is optimal.

3. At slip 0.2, why is the optimal value of the start (−6.30) better than both hand-written policies from lesson 1 (−9.08 and −6.97)?

The optimal policy is free to choose cell by cell. From the start it climbs over the top like the safe detour, but it differs from the detour in 4 cells: two cells in row 1 (columns 3 and 4) point → towards the goal column instead of ↑, and two cells in row 2 (columns 2 and 4) point →. Neither hand-written policy is greedy with respect to its own values, so policy improvement can still make each of them better, and DP keeps improving until no cell can.

4. Your problem has 30 binary sensors, and the state is all 30 readings. How many states are there, and is DP practical?

\(2^{30} \approx 10^9\) states. A table of that size fits in memory, and a sweep at a billion backups per second takes about a second, so it is borderline feasible if you know the model. With 60 sensors it would be \(2^{60} \approx 10^{18}\) states, about 37 years per sweep. That exponential growth is the curse of dimensionality.

5. Value iteration on the cliff world at slip 0 stops after 9 sweeps no matter what γ is. Why doesn't a larger γ slow it down here?

With no slip everything is deterministic and every optimal path ends at the goal within a few steps. The longest optimal path from any cell is 8 steps. After 8 sweeps every state's value is exactly right and the next sweep changes nothing (\(\Delta = 0\)). The "shrink by \(\gamma\) per sweep" rule is only a worst-case guarantee; it bites when episodes can last a long time, as with the random policy (155 sweeps at \(\gamma = 0.95\), 272 at \(0.99\)).
