  • David Silver, UCL Course on RL, Lecture 3: Planning by Dynamic Programming (video + slides)
  • Richard Bellman, Dynamic Programming (1957), the original book, where the "curse of dimensionality" was named
  • Andrej Karpathy, REINFORCEjs: GridWorld with Dynamic Programming, another interactive grid world with policy and value iteration

Next lessons: Monte Carlo & TD learning: the same evaluate-and-improve loop, learned from sampled experience instead of a known model.

docs.title: Gradient Descent
docs.text:
TL;DR

Gradient descent is how almost every AI model learns. You measure how wrong the model is (the loss), work out which direction makes it less wrong (the gradient), and take a small step that way. Repeat thousands of times, and the model gets good.

Level: beginner · Prerequisites: basic algebra; knowing that a derivative is "the slope" helps but is not required.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text: When people say a neural network "learns", what is really happening is gradient descent (or one of its close relatives, such as Adam). ChatGPT, image classifiers and medical-image segmentation models are all trained this way. Once you understand this lesson, "training a model" stops being magic.

docs.title: Step 1 — The intuition: walking down a foggy mountain
docs.text:
Imagine you are standing on a mountain in thick fog. You want to reach the lowest point of the valley, but you can only see the ground right under your feet. What do you do?

  1. Feel which way the ground slopes.
  2. Take a step downhill.
  3. Repeat until the ground is flat.

That is the whole algorithm. In AI:

Mountain Machine learning Your position The model's parameters (its adjustable numbers, also called weights) Height of the ground The loss: how wrong the model is Slope under your feet The gradient Size of your step The learning rate Bottom of the valley The best parameters (lowest loss)

docs.title: Step 2 — What are we trying to make small? The loss
docs.text:
Let's use a tiny example. We have 7 data points (blue dots) and want to fit a straight line through the origin:

\[ \hat{y} = w \cdot x \]

There is only one parameter, the slope \(w\). For each point the model makes an error \(\hat{y}_i - y_i\) (the dashed red lines). We square the errors (so negative and positive errors don't cancel out, and big errors count extra) and take their average. This is the mean squared error (MSE) loss:

\[ L(w) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(w\,x_i - y_i\right)^2 \]

Try it: drag the slider. Watch the line on the left and the orange dot on the right. The right plot shows the loss for every possible value of \(w\). It is a bowl, and we want the bottom of it.

🎚️ Interactive: find a good w by hand

What to notice

  • When the line fits the dots well, the dashed error lines are short and the orange dot is near the bottom of the bowl.
  • You found the minimum by looking at the whole curve. A real model has millions of parameters, so we can never draw the whole curve. We need a method that only uses local information. That method is gradient descent.

docs.title: Step 3 — Which way is downhill? The gradient
docs.text:
Look at the red line touching the curve in the widget above. That is the slope of the loss at your current \(w\), written \(\frac{dL}{dw}\). It is the "feel the ground under your feet" step.

  • Slope positive → loss goes up as \(w\) increases → move \(w\) left (decrease it).
  • Slope negative → loss goes down as \(w\) increases → move \(w\) right (increase it).
  • Slope ≈ 0 → the ground is flat → you're at the bottom.

So the rule is simple: always move opposite to the slope.

For our loss, calculus gives the slope directly:

\[ \frac{dL}{dw} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} 2\,x_i\left(w\,x_i - y_i\right) \]

You don't need to derive this yourself. In practice libraries like PyTorch compute it automatically (this is called automatic differentiation, and backpropagation in neural networks). What matters is the meaning: it tells us which way is uphill, and how steep it is.

Gradient vs. derivative

With one parameter we call it the derivative or slope. With many parameters we get one slope per parameter. That list of slopes is called the gradient, written \(\nabla L\). It points in the direction of steepest ascent, so we walk the opposite way.

docs.title: Step 4 — Taking the step: the update rule
docs.text:
Now combine everything into one line, the heart of gradient descent:

\[ w_{\text{new}} = w_{\text{old}} - \eta \cdot \frac{dL}{dw} \]
  • The minus sign means "go opposite to the slope", i.e. downhill.
  • \(\eta\) (Greek letter eta) is the learning rate: how big a step to take.
  • Steep slope → big step; gentle slope → small step. The algorithm slows down by itself as it nears the bottom.

Try it: press Run 30 steps, then try the preset learning rates. The green ring marks the true minimum.

🏃 Interactive: gradient descent in action

What to notice: the learning rate matters a lot

Learning rate What happens Too small (0.01) Safe but slow: after 30 steps it still hasn't arrived. Good (0.05) Gets to the bottom quickly and smoothly. Big (0.18) Overshoots and bounces from side to side, but slowly settles. Too big (0.22) Every jump lands higher than the last one, and the loss explodes. This is called divergence.

Choosing the learning rate is one of the most important practical decisions when training a model.

docs.title: Step 5 — More parameters: a landscape instead of a curve
docs.text:
Real models have more than one parameter. Let's add an intercept \(b\), so the line no longer has to pass through the origin:

\[ \hat{y} = w \cdot x + b \]

Now the loss depends on two numbers, \(L(w, b)\). Instead of a curve, it is a surface, like a real valley. Below, we view it from above as a contour map: the stronger the purple, the lower the loss. The green ring marks the minimum. The gradient now has two parts, one per parameter:

\[ \nabla L = \left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial w},\; \frac{\partial L}{\partial b}\right), \qquad \begin{aligned} w &\leftarrow w - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}\\ b &\leftarrow b - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial b} \end{aligned} \]

Exactly the same rule, applied to each parameter at the same time.

🗺️ Interactive: descending a 2-D loss landscape

What to notice

  • Click different starting points. Every path ends at the green ring, because this bowl has only one bottom.
  • The valley is long and narrow. With a learning rate around 0.15 the path zig-zags across the narrow direction while crawling along the long one. This exact problem is what improved optimizers like Momentum and Adam were invented to fix (a future lesson).
  • Push the learning rate to 0.2 and the path diverges, just as in 1-D.

docs.title: Step 6 — Real data is big: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)
docs.text:
To compute the exact gradient we averaged over all data points. With 7 points that's easy. With 10 million images it is far too slow to do for every single step.

The trick is to estimate the gradient from a small random subset of the data, called a mini-batch, at every step:

Variant Gradient computed from Each step is… Batch gradient descent all \(N\) examples accurate but slow Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) 1 random example very cheap but noisy Mini-batch gradient descent e.g. 32–512 examples the practical sweet spot, used almost everywhere

Try it: in the 2-D widget above, switch gradient from to 1 random point (SGD) and press Run. The path becomes wobbly, because each step only "sees" one point. It still heads towards the minimum on average. That noise is not all bad: in deep learning it can even help the model escape poor regions.

Vocabulary: epoch

One epoch is one full pass over the training data. With 10,000 examples and a mini-batch of 100, one epoch is 100 steps.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Here is the full algorithm from the 2-D widget, in a few lines of NumPy:

import numpy as np

x = np.array([0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5])
y = np.array([1.3, 1.6, 3.2, 4.5, 4.7, 6.1, 6.8])

w, b = -0.5, 5.0        # starting point
lr = 0.1                # learning rate (η)

for step in range(200):
    y_hat = w * x + b                     # 1. predict
    error = y_hat - y
    loss = np.mean(error ** 2)            # 2. measure loss (MSE)
    grad_w = np.mean(2 * error * x)       # 3. gradient
    grad_b = np.mean(2 * error)
    w -= lr * grad_w                      # 4. step downhill
    b -= lr * grad_b

print(f"w = {w:.3f}, b = {b:.3f}, loss = {loss:.4f}")

And the same thing in PyTorch, which computes the gradient for you:

import torch

x = torch.tensor([0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5])
y = torch.tensor([1.3, 1.6, 3.2, 4.5, 4.7, 6.1, 6.8])
w = torch.tensor(-0.5, requires_grad=True)
b = torch.tensor(5.0, requires_grad=True)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD([w, b], lr=0.1)

for step in range(200):
    loss = ((w * x + b - y) ** 2).mean()
    optimizer.zero_grad()   # clear old gradients
    loss.backward()         # compute gradients automatically
    optimizer.step()        # w ← w − lr · grad

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"Gradient descent always finds the best possible answer.\"

Only for bowl-shaped (convex) losses like the ones in this lesson. Neural-network loss landscapes have many hills, valleys and flat regions. Gradient descent finds a low point, not necessarily the lowest. In practice, these low points are usually good enough.

\"A bigger learning rate means faster training.\"

Only up to a point. Past it, training oscillates or diverges (you saw this in Step 4). That's why practitioners often use learning-rate schedules that start larger and shrink over time.

\"The gradient points towards the minimum.\"

It points in the direction of steepest local descent, which is not necessarily straight at the minimum. The zig-zag in the 2-D widget shows this clearly.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. At the current w, the slope dL/dw = +3. Should w increase or decrease?

Decrease. A positive slope means the loss rises as \(w\) grows, so we move the opposite way: \(w_{\text{new}} = w - \eta \cdot 3\).

2. Your training loss gets bigger every step and eventually becomes NaN. What is the most likely cause?

The learning rate is too large, so gradient descent is diverging. Try reducing it by a factor of 10.

3. Why does gradient descent automatically take smaller steps near the minimum, even with a fixed learning rate?

Because the step is \(\eta \times\) gradient, and the gradient (the slope) gets close to zero near the bottom of the bowl.

4. What is the difference between batch GD and SGD?

Batch GD computes the gradient from all training examples: it is accurate but slow per step. SGD uses one (or a small mini-batch of) random examples: each step is cheap and noisy, but on average it still points downhill.

5. With 50,000 training images and a mini-batch size of 250, how many update steps are in one epoch?

$50{,}000 / 250 = $ 200 steps.

docs.text:

docs.title: Markov Decision Processes and the Bellman Equations
docs.text:
TL;DR

A Markov decision process (MDP) is the precise maths of an RL problem: states, actions, a table of transition probabilities \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\), and a discount \(\gamma\). Because the return is recursive (\(G_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma G_{t+1}\)), the value of a state equals the expected reward of one step plus the discounted value of where you land. That is the Bellman equation. Every RL method in this course is a way of solving it, exactly or approximately.

Level: beginner–intermediate · Prerequisites: What is RL? (states, rewards, return, policy, value), Multi-armed bandits. Knowing what a matrix and a linear system (\(Ax = b\)) are helps for Step 7.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
In the first lesson the cliff-world widget showed a value \(V^\pi(s)\) in every cell. It got those numbers without playing a single episode. How? It used the Bellman equation: a rule that ties the value of each cell to the values of its neighbours.

In the bandits lesson every action was a one-shot decision: pull an arm, get a reward, done. Real problems have consequences: the action you take now changes the situation you face next. MDPs are the language for that, and the Bellman equations are the one idea behind:

  • Dynamic programming (next lesson): solve the Bellman equation when you know the rules of the world.
  • Q-learning, SARSA, DQN: solve it from samples, without knowing the rules.
  • Actor-critic methods (PPO, used in RLHF): a value network trained on a Bellman target judges the policy.

If you understand this lesson, every later update rule will look familiar.

docs.title: Step 1 — The Markov property: the state is all you need
docs.text:
A state should contain everything about the past that matters for the future. If it does, we say the state has the Markov property:

\[ \Pr(s_{t+1}, r_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t) \;=\; \Pr(s_{t+1}, r_{t+1} \mid s_0, a_0, r_1, \dots, s_t, a_t) \]

In words: once you know the current state and action, the rest of the history adds nothing to your prediction of what happens next. "The future is independent of the past, given the present."

The cliff world is Markov: if you know which cell you are in, how you got there does not change where your next step can take you. Here is a state that is not Markov:

Real states are often only approximately Markov. A robot's camera image doesn't show what is behind it; a chatbot's "state" is the whole conversation so far precisely so that nothing important is lost. When the state misses something important, the problem is called partially observable (a POMDP), and the usual fix is the one above: put more history into the state.

What to notice

  • The Markov property is a property of how you define the state, not of the world. The same game is non-Markov with one frame and (close to) Markov with two.
  • It is what makes everything else in this lesson possible: if the state is all you need, then the value of a state can depend only on that state, not on how you got there.

docs.title: Step 2 — The Markov decision process
docs.text:
A Markov decision process packs the whole RL problem into five ingredients:

Ingredient Symbol Recycling robot (below) States \(\mathcal{S}\) battery high, battery low Actions \(\mathcal{A}(s)\) search for cans, wait for someone to bring one, recharge (only when low) Dynamics \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\) the probabilities on the arrows Rewards part of \(p\) +2 per search, +1 per wait, −3 if the battery dies and a human must rescue it Discount \(\gamma\) 0.9

The heart of an MDP is the dynamics function

\[ p(s', r \mid s, a) = \Pr(s_{t+1} = s',\ r_{t+1} = r \mid s_t = s,\ a_t = a), \]

the probability that taking action \(a\) in state \(s\) lands you in \(s'\) with reward \(r\). For each \((s, a)\) these probabilities sum to 1. It is the "rules of the game": in the bandits lesson it was one reward distribution per arm; here it also says where you go next.

Our example is a little robot that collects empty cans (a classic from Sutton & Barto's textbook, with our own numbers). Searching finds cans (+2) but drains the battery: from high it stays high with probability 0.7. From low, searching is risky: with probability 0.4 the battery dies, a human carries the robot back to the charger (−3), and it starts again at high.

Try it: the orange ring marks the state the robot is in. Press Take one step a few times. The policy (orange arrows) picks an action, then the environment (blue arrows) rolls the dice.

🤖 Interactive: the recycling-robot MDP

What to notice

  • Two kinds of randomness. The agent chooses the action, possibly at random (\(\pi(a \mid s)\), orange). The environment chooses the outcome (\(p(s', r \mid s, a)\), blue). The agent controls only the first.
  • The default Coin flip policy always searches when the battery is high, and flips a coin between searching and recharging when it is low.
  • Change the policy and the values \(V\) in the circles change. The MDP (blue arrows) stays the same. A value always belongs to a policy.
  • We will come back to the Sample buttons in the next step.

docs.title: Step 3 — The return is recursive
docs.text:
In lesson 1 the return was the discounted sum of future rewards. Look at what happens when we pull the first reward out of the sum:

\[ \begin{aligned} G_t &= r_{t+1} + \gamma\, r_{t+2} + \gamma^2\, r_{t+3} + \dots \\ &= r_{t+1} + \gamma \left( r_{t+2} + \gamma\, r_{t+3} + \dots \right) \\ &= r_{t+1} + \gamma\, G_{t+1} \end{aligned} \]

The return from now is the next reward plus \(\gamma\) times the return from the next step. This one line is the seed of the whole lesson.

The value of a state is the expected return: \(V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t \mid s_t = s]\). Taking the expectation of both sides of the recursion gives

\[ V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\left[\, r_{t+1} + \gamma\, V^\pi(s_{t+1}) \;\middle|\; s_t = s \,\right]. \]

(The step from \(G_{t+1}\) to \(V^\pi(s_{t+1})\) uses the Markov property: from \(s_{t+1}\) on, the future depends only on \(s_{t+1}\), so the expected value of \(G_{t+1}\) is just \(V^\pi(s_{t+1})\).)

Try it: in the robot widget above, press Sample 1 return. The readout shows one sampled run's rewards, its return \(G_0\), and checks that \(G_0 = r_1 + 0.9\, G_1\). Then press Sample 1000 returns and watch the running average (orange) settle onto the dashed line.

What to notice

  • Single returns are noisy. For the Coin flip policy they spread out with a standard deviation of about 2.2 around their mean.
  • Their average still lands on the exact value \(V^\pi(\text{high}) = 14.60\) (usually within about 0.15 after 1000 samples). The robot task never ends, so each sample is cut off after 200 steps; the rewards after that are weighted by \(0.9^{200} \approx 7 \times 10^{-10}\), which is nothing.
  • So where does the exact 14.60 come from, if not from averaging? From the Bellman equation, next.

docs.title: Step 4 — The Bellman expectation equation for \(V^\pi\)
docs.text:
Write out the expectation in Step 3. Two random things happen in one step: the policy picks \(a\) with probability \(\pi(a \mid s)\), then the environment picks \((s', r)\) with probability \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\). Average over both:

\[ \boxed{\;V^\pi(s) = \sum_{a} \pi(a \mid s) \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[\, r + \gamma\, V^\pi(s') \,\big]\;} \]

This is the Bellman expectation equation. Read it as a one-step lookahead: list everything that can happen in one step, score each outcome by "reward now + discounted value of where I land", and take the probability-weighted average. Computing this right-hand side for a state is called a backup, because it carries value information back from the next states to the current one. Drawn as a tree it is a backup diagram:

The values in that tree are consistent: plug \(V(\text{low}) = 12.6\) and \(V(\text{high}) = 14.6\) into the right-hand side and you get \(12.6\) back. That is what it means for \(V^\pi\) to satisfy the Bellman equation. A wrong guess (say all zeros) would not.

Now the same thing on the cliff world from lesson 1, with real numbers for every cell.

Try it: click any floor cell. The readout writes out its Bellman equation: one line per possible outcome, \(p \times (r + \gamma V(s'))\), summed up and compared with the stored value. Then raise the slip chance.

🔍 Interactive: Bellman backup explorer

What to notice

  • Edge policy, slip 0, cell (2,1) (just above the cliff): only one outcome, so the equation is a single line: \(V = -1 + 0.95 \times 5.72 = 4.44\).
  • Raise the slip chance to 0.2. The same cell now has three outcomes: \(0.8 \times (-1 + 0.95 \times (-2.97)) + 0.1 \times (-20) + 0.1 \times (-1 + 0.95 \times (-6.78)) = -3.055 - 2.000 - 0.744 = -5.80\). The cliff line costs a full 2 points on its own, even though it only happens one time in ten.
  • Every cell's residual is 0 or about \(10^{-15}\) (floating-point rounding): the value table satisfies all 18 Bellman equations at once. That is the defining property of \(V^\pi\).
  • Random policy, start cell: four actions with \(\pi = 0.25\) each. One of them (→) walks straight into the cliff, which drags \(V(\text{start})\) down to \(-19.88\), the number you saw in lesson 1.

docs.title: Step 5 — The same idea for \(Q^\pi\)
docs.text:
In lesson 1 we met the action-value \(Q^\pi(s, a)\): the expected return if you take action \(a\) in \(s\) first, then follow \(\pi\). It is the middle layer of the backup diagram: the value of a node after the agent has chosen but before the environment has rolled the dice. Two short equations link \(V\) and \(Q\):

\[ Q^\pi(s, a) = \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[\, r + \gamma\, V^\pi(s') \,\big] \qquad\qquad V^\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s)\, Q^\pi(s, a) \]

The first is the environment's half of the tree, the second the agent's half. Substituting one into the other gives the Bellman expectation equation for \(Q^\pi\):

\[ Q^\pi(s, a) = \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\Big[\, r + \gamma \sum_{a'} \pi(a' \mid s')\, Q^\pi(s', a') \,\Big] \]

Why bother with \(Q\) when we have \(V\)? Because \(Q\) compares actions. For the robot's coin-flip policy in state low:

action \(Q^\pi(\text{low}, a)\) search 12.06 wait 12.34 recharge 13.14

The policy is averaging a 12.06 action with a 13.14 action and gets \(V^\pi(\text{low}) = 12.6\). Recharging every time would clearly do better. Reading \(Q\) and switching to the best action is exactly how policy improvement works in the next lesson. In the backup explorer above, the "→ Q = …" header of each action is this \(Q^\pi(s, a)\).

What to notice

  • \(V\) needs the model \(p\) to compare actions: you must look one step ahead. \(Q\) has that lookahead built in, so you can pick the best action with a simple \(\arg\max_a Q(s, a)\). That is why model-free methods like Q-learning learn \(Q\), not \(V\).
  • \(Q^\pi(\text{low, wait}) = 12.34\) even though this policy never waits. \(Q^\pi\) answers "what if I tried \(a\) just once, then went back to \(\pi\)?"

docs.title: Step 6 — The Bellman optimality equations
docs.text:
So far the policy was given. Now we want the best one. Define the optimal value functions as the best value any policy can achieve:

\[ V^*(s) = \max_\pi V^\pi(s), \qquad Q^*(s, a) = \max_\pi Q^\pi(s, a) \]

An optimal agent doesn't average over its actions; it takes the best one. So in the backup diagram, the agent's branch becomes a max while the environment's branch stays an average (you can't choose the dice):

\[ \boxed{\;V^*(s) = \max_a \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[\, r + \gamma\, V^*(s') \,\big]\;} \] \[ \boxed{\;Q^*(s, a) = \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\Big[\, r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^*(s', a') \,\Big]\;} \]

These are the Bellman optimality equations. Once you have \(Q^*\), acting optimally is trivial: be greedy,

\[ \pi^*(s) = \arg\max_a Q^*(s, a). \]

No lookahead and no model are needed. A one-step greedy choice is globally optimal because \(Q^*\) already accounts for acting optimally ever after. For the robot, \(Q^*(\text{low}, \cdot)\) is 13.32 (search), 13.76 (wait) and 14.17 (recharge), so \(\pi^*\) recharges when low and searches when high, with \(V^*(\text{high}) = 15.75\) and \(V^*(\text{low}) = 14.17\). That is the Cautious preset in the robot widget.

Try it: here is \(Q^*\) for the cliff world. Each cell is split into four triangles, one per action, coloured by \(Q^*(s, a)\). The arrows mark the greedy action (two arrows mean a tie), and the orange line follows them from the start. Slide the slip chance slowly from 0 to 0.4.

🧭 Interactive: optimal action-values Q* and the greedy policy

What to notice

  • Slip 0: the greedy path hugs the cliff and \(V^*(\text{start}) = 2.05\), the same as the hand-written Edge policy from lesson 1. That policy was already optimal.
  • The route flips between slip 0.10 and 0.15. At 0.10 the path still hugs the edge (\(V^* = -3.68\)); at 0.15 it takes the top row (\(V^* = -5.13\)).
  • Slip 0.2: \(V^*(\text{start}) = -6.30\), better than both lesson-1 policies (edge \(-9.08\), safe \(-6.97\)). The main route is the safe detour, but \(Q^*\) also knows the best move in cells you only reach by slipping.
  • Slip 0.35 or more: the greedy action at the start is ←, into the wall! At slip 0.4, \(Q^*(\text{start}, ←) = -10.34\) beats \(Q^*(\text{start}, ↑) = -11.21\). Bumping the wall keeps you put, and a sideways slip then goes up (good) or down (also a wall), never into the cliff. Trying ↑ risks slipping right, into the cliff. Nobody wrote that trick in; it falls out of the equations.
  • The cliff triangles (pointing down from the edge row) stay deep red at every slip: \(Q^*\) knows that action is a disaster, while \(V^*\) would hide it behind the max.

docs.title: Step 7 — A system of equations you can solve
docs.text:
Look again at the Bellman expectation equation. There is one equation per state, and the unknowns are the values \(V^\pi(s)\). The robot has two states, so two equations (coin-flip policy, \(\gamma = 0.9\)):

\[ \begin{aligned} V(\text{high}) &= 0.7\,[2 + 0.9\,V(\text{high})] + 0.3\,[2 + 0.9\,V(\text{low})] \\ V(\text{low}) &= 0.5\,\big(0.6\,[2 + 0.9\,V(\text{low})] + 0.4\,[-3 + 0.9\,V(\text{high})]\big) + 0.5\,[0 + 0.9\,V(\text{high})] \end{aligned} \]

Every equation is linear in the unknowns. Collect the policy's average reward per state in a vector \(r^\pi\) and its state-to-state transition probabilities in a matrix \(P^\pi\), and all of them become one matrix equation:

\[ V^\pi = r^\pi + \gamma P^\pi V^\pi \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (I - \gamma P^\pi)\, V^\pi = r^\pi \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad V^\pi = (I - \gamma P^\pi)^{-1} r^\pi. \]

For \(\gamma < 1\) the matrix \(I - \gamma P^\pi\) is always invertible, so there is exactly one solution. NumPy solves it in one line:

import itertools
import numpy as np

gamma = 0.9
states = ["high", "low"]
actions = {"high": ["search", "wait"], "low": ["search", "wait", "recharge"]}
# p(s', r | s, a) written as a list of (probability, next state, reward)
dynamics = {
    ("high", "search"):   [(0.7, "high", 2), (0.3, "low", 2)],
    ("high", "wait"):     [(1.0, "high", 1)],
    ("low", "search"):    [(0.6, "low", 2), (0.4, "high", -3)],   # battery dies: rescued
    ("low", "wait"):      [(1.0, "low", 1)],
    ("low", "recharge"):  [(1.0, "high", 0)],
}


def evaluate(policy):
    """Solve V = r_pi + gamma * P_pi V exactly. policy[s] = {action: probability}."""
    n = len(states)
    P = np.zeros((n, n))   # P[s, s'] = probability of moving s -> s' under the policy
    r = np.zeros(n)        # r[s]     = expected immediate reward in s under the policy
    for i, s in enumerate(states):
        for a, pa in policy[s].items():
            for p, s2, reward in dynamics[(s, a)]:
                P[i, states.index(s2)] += pa * p
                r[i] += pa * p * reward
    return np.linalg.solve(np.eye(n) - gamma * P, r)   # V = (I - gamma P)^-1 r


coin_flip = {"high": {"search": 1.0}, "low": {"search": 0.5, "recharge": 0.5}}
print("coin-flip policy: V =", evaluate(coin_flip).round(3))

# Bellman optimality by brute force: try every deterministic policy (2 x 3 = 6 of them)
for a_high, a_low in itertools.product(actions["high"], actions["low"]):
    V = evaluate({"high": {a_high: 1.0}, "low": {a_low: 1.0}})
    print(f"high: {a_high:6s}  low: {a_low:8s}  V = {V.round(3)}")

coin-flip policy: V = [14.6 12.6]
high: search  low: search    V = [12.603  9.863]
high: search  low: wait      V = [12.703 10.   ]
high: search  low: recharge  V = [15.748 14.173]
high: wait    low: search    V = [10.     7.826]
high: wait    low: wait      V = [10. 10.]
high: wait    low: recharge  V = [10.  9.]

The first line reproduces the values from the backup diagram. The loop finds the optimal policy (search when high, recharge when low) by brute force: its values \([15.748, 14.173]\) are the highest in both states at once, and they match \(V^*\) from Step 6.

So why do we need the rest of the course?

  • The optimality equation is not linear. The \(\max\) breaks the matrix trick, so there is no single np.linalg.solve for \(V^*\).
  • Brute force explodes. The robot has 6 deterministic policies. The tiny cliff world has 18 floor cells with 4 actions each: \(4^{18} \approx 6.9 \times 10^{10}\) policies.
  • Solving is expensive for big problems. A linear solve costs about \(n^3\) operations for \(n\) states. Backgammon has around \(10^{20}\) states, Go more than \(10^{170}\).
  • Usually we don't even know \(p\). The equations need the dynamics. A real agent only sees samples.

The next lesson, dynamic programming, attacks the first three problems: it solves both Bellman equations by repeating the backup over and over (policy iteration, value iteration). The lessons after that attack the last one by replacing the sum over \(p\) with samples.

What to notice

  • The Bellman expectation equation is a linear system with exactly one solution, \(V^\pi\). Evaluating a policy, when you know the MDP, is "just" linear algebra.
  • The Bellman optimality equation also has exactly one solution, \(V^*\), but you need an iterative method (or a search over policies) to find it.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Here is the cliff world as an MDP in NumPy. outcomes() is the dynamics function \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\), evaluate() solves the Bellman expectation equation as a linear system, and the residual check confirms that the solution satisfies the equation in every cell:

import numpy as np

MAP = ["......",
       "..#...",
       "......",
       "SCCCCG"]
MOVES = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]                 # up, right, down, left
cells = [(r, c) for r in range(4) for c in range(6) if MAP[r][c] in ".S"]   # non-terminal states
index = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(cells)}


def outcomes(s, a, slip):
    """p(s', r | s, a): list of (probability, next cell, reward, episode over?)."""
    result = []
    for p, d in [(1 - slip, a), (slip / 2, (a + 1) % 4), (slip / 2, (a + 3) % 4)]:
        r, c = s[0] + MOVES[d][0], s[1] + MOVES[d][1]
        if not (0 <= r < 4 and 0 <= c < 6) or MAP[r][c] == "#":
            r, c = s                                         # bump: stay put
        tile = MAP[r][c]
        reward = 10 if tile == "G" else -20 if tile == "C" else -1
        if p > 0:
            result.append((p, (r, c), reward, tile in "GC"))
    return result


def evaluate(policy, slip, gamma=0.95):
    """Bellman expectation equation as a linear system: (I - gamma P) V = r."""
    n = len(cells)
    P, r = np.zeros((n, n)), np.zeros(n)
    for s in cells:
        for a, pa in policy(s).items():
            for p, s2, reward, done in outcomes(s, a, slip):
                r[index[s]] += pa * p * reward
                if not done:                                 # terminal states have value 0
                    P[index[s], index[s2]] += pa * p
    return np.linalg.solve(np.eye(n) - gamma * P, r)


def q_values(V, s, slip, gamma=0.95):
    """One-step lookahead: Q(s, a) = sum over outcomes of p * (r + gamma * V(s'))."""
    return [sum(p * (reward + (0 if done else gamma * V[index[s2]]))
                for p, s2, reward, done in outcomes(s, a, slip)) for a in range(4)]


EDGE = ["↓↓→↓↓↓", "↓↓.↓↓↓", "→→→→→↓", "↑....."]
edge = lambda s: {"↑→↓←".index(EDGE[s[0]][s[1]]): 1.0}
random_policy = lambda s: {a: 0.25 for a in range(4)}

start = index[(3, 0)]
for slip in [0.0, 0.2]:
    for name, policy in [("edge", edge), ("random", random_policy)]:
        V = evaluate(policy, slip)
        # Bellman residual: does V really satisfy V(s) = sum_a pi(a|s) Q(s, a) in every cell?
        residual = max(abs(V[index[s]] - sum(pa * q_values(V, s, slip)[a] for a, pa in policy(s).items()))
                       for s in cells)
        print(f"slip={slip}  {name:6s}  V(start) = {V[start]:6.2f}   max Bellman residual = {residual:.1e}")

V = evaluate(edge, 0.2)
print("Q_edge(start, ·) at slip 0.2 [up, right, down, left]:", np.round(q_values(V, (3, 0), 0.2), 2))

slip=0.0  edge    V(start) =   2.05   max Bellman residual = 4.4e-16
slip=0.0  random  V(start) = -19.88   max Bellman residual = 3.6e-15
slip=0.2  edge    V(start) =  -9.08   max Bellman residual = 1.8e-15
slip=0.2  random  V(start) = -19.88   max Bellman residual = 3.6e-15
Q_edge(start, ·) at slip 0.2 [up, right, down, left]: [ -9.08 -17.73 -10.67  -9.43]

These are the same values as the Monte Carlo averages in lesson 1 (2.05, −9.08, −19.88), now computed exactly, without playing a single episode. The last line is a hint of what comes next: at the start, the edge policy's own action "up" (\(-9.08\)) is already the best of the four. But run q_values on every cell and in 7 of the 18 cells another action beats the policy's choice (at (1,4), for example, → scores 4.71 against the policy's ↓ at 2.83). Switching to those better actions and repeating is policy iteration, in the next lesson.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"The Bellman equation is an algorithm.\"

It is a condition that the true values must satisfy, like "\(x^2 = 2\)" is a condition that \(\sqrt 2\) satisfies. Algorithms (dynamic programming, TD learning, Q-learning) are different ways of finding values that satisfy it.

\"Markov means the agent has no memory.\"

Markov is a property of the state, not of the agent. If memory matters, put it into the state (stack frames, add velocity, keep the conversation history). Then the state is Markov again.

\"V(s) is the value of the best action, so V tells me what to do.\"

\(V^*\) tells you how good a state is, not which action gets you there. To act on \(V^*\) you still need a one-step lookahead with the model \(p\). \(Q^*\) has the action built in: \(\arg\max_a Q^*(s, a)\) needs no model.

\"The optimal policy maximises the next reward.\"

The greedy policy maximises \(Q^*\), which already includes all future rewards. In the cliff world at high slip the best first move is to walk into a wall: the worst-looking action locally, but the safest long-run choice.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. A state in a card game is \"the cards in my hand\". Why might this not be Markov, and how would you fix it?

The cards already played matter: they change which cards are left in the deck and so what can happen next. A state with only your hand forgets them. Fix it by adding the history that matters (the cards already played, or counts of what remains) to the state.

2. An episode gives rewards r₁ = 1, r₂ = 0, r₃ = 4 and then ends. With γ = 0.5, compute G₂, G₁ and G₀ using the recursion.

Work backwards. \(G_3 = 0\) (the episode is over). \(G_2 = r_3 + \gamma G_3 = 4\). \(G_1 = r_2 + \gamma G_2 = 0 + 0.5 \times 4 = 2\). $G_0 = r_1 + \gamma G_1 = 1 + 0.5 \times 2 = $ 2. Check: \(1 + 0.5 \cdot 0 + 0.25 \cdot 4 = 2\).

3. In a state s, a policy picks action A with probability 0.25 and B with probability 0.75. Q(s, A) = 8 and Q(s, B) = 4. What is V^π(s)? What is the best possible value of s if these Q-values were Q* values?

$V^\pi(s) = 0.25 \times 8 + 0.75 \times 4 = 2 + 3 = $ 5. If they were \(Q^*\) values, $V^*(s) = \max(8, 4) = $ 8, achieved by always taking A.

4. What changes between the Bellman expectation equation and the Bellman optimality equation, and why does that stop us from solving the second one with a single linear solve?

The average over the agent's actions, \(\sum_a \pi(a \mid s)\,\cdot\), is replaced by a \(\max_a\). The environment's average over outcomes stays. A max is not linear, so the equations can no longer be written as \((I - \gamma P)V = r\) with a fixed \(P\); you need an iterative method such as value iteration (next lesson).

5. In the Q* widget at slip 0.4, why is walking into the wall the best first move from the start?

Moving left from the start bumps the wall, so the intended move keeps you put. The sideways slips go up (towards safety) or down (another wall, stay put). No outcome ends in the cliff. Moving up instead has a 0.2 chance of slipping right, straight into the cliff for −20. Paying −1 per step to wait for a safe slip is worth more: \(Q^*(\text{start}, ←) = -10.34\) vs \(Q^*(\text{start}, ↑) = -11.21\).

docs.title: Model-Based RL and Planning: Dyna, MCTS and AlphaZero
docs.text:
TL;DR

A model of the environment predicts what happens next: given a state and an action, it returns the next state and the reward. An agent that has a model can plan: it can try things out in its head instead of in the real world. Dyna-Q learns a model from its own experience and uses it to replay imagined steps, so it needs far fewer real steps. Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) plans at the moment of choosing a move, by growing a search tree of possible futures. AlphaZero guides that search with a neural network trained by self-play, and MuZero even learns the model itself.

Level: intermediate · Prerequisites: Q-learning & SARSA, Actor-critic. The UCB rule from Multi-armed bandits comes back in Step 5.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
Every method so far in this series was model-free. Q-learning, DQN, policy gradients and actor-critic all learn what to do straight from experience, and they need a lot of it. The original DQN trained on 50 million frames per Atari game, roughly 38 days of non-stop play for a human.

Real experience is often expensive or slow: a robot wears out, a chemistry experiment takes a day, a patient cannot be used for trial and error. People don't learn like that either. Before you cross a busy road, you imagine what would happen if you stepped out now. That imagined experience is free.

Model-based RL gives agents the same ability. It is behind some of RL's biggest successes:

  • AlphaGo beat Go world champion Lee Sedol in 2016, and AlphaZero (2017) beat the strongest chess, shogi and Go programs. Both search ahead, using the game's rules as the model.
  • MuZero (2019) reached the same level without being told the rules, by learning its own model, and also mastered Atari.
  • Planning with learned models is how many robot-control systems squeeze good behaviour out of a few hours of real data.

docs.title: Step 1 — What is a model?
docs.text:
In the first lesson the environment was a black box: you send an action, it sends back a reward and a next state. A model is the agent's own copy of that black box. It answers the question "if I am in state \(s\) and take action \(a\), what happens?"

\[ \text{model}(s, a) \;\to\; \hat{p}(s', r \mid s, a) \]

The hat on \(\hat p\) means "estimated": the model is the agent's belief about the true dynamics \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\) from the MDP lesson. There are two kinds:

Distribution model Sample model What it gives all outcomes with their probabilities one random outcome, like a dice roll Example "80% → next cell, 10% → slide up, 10% → slide into the cliff" "this time you slid up" Used by dynamic programming (it sums over all outcomes) Dyna, MCTS (they just need samples)

And two places a model can come from:

  • Given: the rules are known exactly. Board games, physics simulators, the cliff world when we read its code.
  • Learned: the agent builds it from its own experience. That is what Dyna (Step 3) and MuZero (Step 6) do.

With a model, the agent can do planning: compute or improve a policy using imagined experience instead of real experience. Dynamic programming was already planning: value iteration loops over the model's probabilities and never touches the real environment. The new question in this lesson is how to plan when the model has to be learned, or when the state space is far too big to sweep through.

What to notice

Model-free agents learn what to do (Q-values or a policy). Model-based agents also learn how the world works, and then work out what to do. The second kind of knowledge can be reused: if the goal moves, a model of the walls and the cliff is still correct.

docs.title: Step 2 — Learning a model by counting
docs.text:
In a small, discrete world, learning a model is just counting. Every time the agent takes action \(a\) in state \(s\) and sees reward \(r\) and next state \(s'\), it adds one to a counter \(n(s, a, s', r)\). The estimated probability of an outcome is how often it happened:

\[ \hat{p}(s', r \mid s, a) = \frac{n(s, a, s', r)}{n(s, a)} \]

where \(n(s, a)\) is how often the agent tried \(a\) in \(s\) at all. This is the same "average of what you saw" idea as the Monte Carlo value estimates, applied to outcomes instead of returns.

Here is what that looks like on the slippery cliff world (slip chance 0.2), for one state-action pair: standing at row 2, column 1 (just above the cliff) and moving right. The true answer is 80% to the next cell, 10% sliding up and 10% sliding down into the cliff, an expected reward of \(0.9 \cdot (-1) + 0.1 \cdot (-20) = -2.9\).

Tries \(n(s, a)\) → next cell (−1) ↑ slide up (−1) ↓ into the cliff (−20) estimated expected reward 10 10 (1.00) 0 (0.00) 0 (0.00) −1.00 100 86 (0.86) 6 (0.06) 8 (0.08) −2.52 1000 779 (0.78) 104 (0.10) 117 (0.12) −3.22 true 0.80 0.10 0.10 −2.90

What to notice

  • After 10 tries the model has never seen a slip, so it believes that walking along the cliff edge is perfectly safe. A planner that trusts this model will happily plan routes along the edge. Small amounts of data give confident, wrong models.
  • With more data the counts approach the true probabilities. In a deterministic world (slip 0), a single try per state-action pair gives the exact model.
  • For big or continuous state spaces (images, robot joints) you can't count. You train a neural network \(\hat f_\phi(s, a) \to (\hat s', \hat r)\) by supervised learning on the agent's transitions instead. The idea stays the same.

docs.title: Step 3 — Dyna-Q: learn, model, plan
docs.text:
Dyna (Sutton, 1990) is the simplest way to mix the two worlds. It is plain Q-learning with one addition. After every real step, the agent:

  1. updates \(Q\) from the real transition, exactly as Q-learning does (direct RL),
  2. records the transition in its model (model learning),
  3. then performs \(n\) extra Q-learning updates on transitions imagined by the model (planning).

Each planning update picks a state-action pair \((s, a)\) the agent has already tried, asks the model for an outcome \((r, s')\), and applies the usual update:

\[ Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha \big[\, r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a) \,\big] \]

That's all. Real and imagined experience go through the same update rule; the model is just a free source of extra experience.

Try it: below is one Dyna-Q agent on the (non-slippery) cliff world from lesson 1, with \(\alpha = 0.1\), \(\gamma = 0.95\), \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and all Q-values starting at 0. Pick \(n\), then run one episode at a time. The orange ticks are the model: one tick on the side of a cell for each action the agent has tried there.

🎚️ Interactive: inside a Dyna-Q agent

What to notice

  • The first episode is a stumble for every n. The model starts empty and the agent has no idea where the goal is, so the first episode usually ends in the cliff after a few random steps.
  • Planning spreads news backwards. Each real step changes one Q-value. Each planning step can update any pair the model knows, so the +10 of the goal travels back along known paths without the agent walking them again. Compare the green cells after 10 episodes with n = 0 and with n = 50: over 100 Python runs, the median number of cells with a positive value was 1 for n = 0, 3 for n = 5 and 8 for n = 50.
  • The model fills up fast. After a few episodes most cells have ticks on all four sides. In this deterministic world one visit is enough to know an outcome exactly.
  • Watch the dashed green line. With n = 50 the greedy route usually becomes the optimal 7-step path along the cliff edge within a handful of episodes. With n = 0 it takes dozens.

docs.title: Step 4 — How much does planning buy?
docs.text:
One episode is noisy. To compare fairly, we run many independent agents for each value of \(n\) and ask: after how many episodes is the greedy route the optimal 7-step route? The widget runs 50 agents per curve right in your browser.

📈 Interactive: Dyna-Q learning curves for different n

The Python version of the same experiment (the code is in Putting it all together), with 100 runs per setting, gives:

planning steps \(n\) median episodes until the optimal route runs on it after 10 episodes median real steps until the optimal route 0 (plain Q-learning) 32 0% about 840 5 10 34% 211 50 7 84% 129

What to notice

  • Planning is a trade. With \(n = 50\) the agent needs about 6× fewer real steps than plain Q-learning, but it does 50 extra updates per real step. Dyna pays with computation (cheap) to save experience (expensive).
  • Returns diminish. Going from 0 to 5 helps more than going from 5 to 50. Once the model has been replayed enough for the Q-values to settle, more planning adds little. Try your own \(n\) with the slider.
  • Look closely at n = 50 late on. Its curve flattens a little below 100%. In the Python runs, 5 of the 100 agents with \(n = 50\) were still on a 9-step route after 60 episodes. That's a real weakness of planning with a learned model, and Step 7 explains it.

Dyna and the replay buffer

The DQN replay buffer is close to Dyna: it stores real transitions and replays them for extra updates. A replay buffer is a non-parametric model that can only replay exactly what happened. A real model can also answer questions about state-action pairs in new combinations, and (if it is a network) generalise to states it has never seen.

docs.title: Step 5 — Planning at decision time: Monte Carlo Tree Search
docs.text:
Dyna plans in the background: it improves a Q-table for all states, whenever it has spare time. A different style is to plan at decision time: when you have to move now, focus all your thinking on the current state and the futures that can follow from it. That is what chess players do.

The obvious way is a search tree: the current state is the root, each legal move is a branch, each reply is a branch below that, and so on. For tic-tac-toe you could search the whole tree. For Go there are about \(10^{170}\) positions, so you must be selective. Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) grows the tree one path at a time, spending more effort on moves that look promising. Every node stores two numbers: a visit count \(N\) and a total value \(W\), so its average value is \(Q = W / N\).

Each simulation has four phases:

The selection rule is the heart of MCTS. At each node it treats the children like the arms of a multi-armed bandit and uses the UCB rule, which in a tree is called UCT (Upper Confidence bounds applied to Trees):

\[ \text{UCT}(\text{child}) = \underbrace{\frac{W}{N}}_{\text{exploit: average result}} + \underbrace{c \sqrt{\frac{\ln N_{\text{parent}}}{N}}}_{\text{explore: bonus for few visits}} \]

The first term favours moves that have worked well. The second is large for moves that have hardly been tried, and shrinks as \(N\) grows. With \(c = \sqrt 2\) this balances exploring and exploiting in the same way as UCB does for bandits.

Try it: X to move in the position at the top. One move wins by force; the others don't. Press Next phase a few times to watch single simulations, then +10 and +100 to see where the visits go.

🌳 Interactive: Monte Carlo Tree Search, step by step

What to notice

  • The winning move is "left". It makes two threats at once (the left column and the middle row), and O can only block one. Exact minimax search agrees: left is a win (+1), top-left, top and centre are draws (0), and bottom loses (−1).
  • Early on, random play-outs mislead. In our Python run with seed 0, after 25 simulations MCTS preferred top-left (7 visits) and even rated the losing move bottom at +0.25: random opponents don't punish mistakes. After 100 simulations it preferred centre.
  • Then the tree takes over. As the tree grows deeper below left, the search sees that every O reply loses. In the same run, left had 80% of the visits after 400 simulations (\(Q = +0.91\)) and 91% after 1000.
  • More thinking, better moves. Over 100 Python runs with different seeds, MCTS chose left in 23 runs with K = 25, 36 with K = 50, 67 with K = 100, 97 with K = 200 and all 100 with K = 400.
  • Watch the UCT column. Moves with few visits get a large bonus, so even bad moves are re-checked now and then. The bonus is why the search keeps looking at left long enough to discover it is winning.

docs.title: Step 6 — AlphaGo, AlphaZero and MuZero: search + deep learning
docs.text:
Random play-outs are a weak judge of a position, and in Go a game lasts 200+ moves, so a random play-out tells you almost nothing. The AlphaGo family made MCTS strong by adding a neural network \(f_\theta(s) = (\mathbf{p}, v)\) with two heads:

  • a policy head \(\mathbf{p}\): prior probabilities for each move, "which moves would a strong player consider?"
  • a value head \(v\): a prediction of the final result from this position, like the critic in actor-critic.

The network changes two phases of MCTS:

  1. Selection uses the prior \(P(s, a)\) from the policy head, so the search mostly looks at moves the network likes (the PUCT rule): $$ \text{score}(s, a) = Q(s, a) + c\, P(s, a)\, \frac{\sqrt{N(s)}}{1 + N(s, a)} $$
  2. Simulation is dropped. Instead of a random play-out, the new leaf is scored by the value head \(v\). One network call replaces hundreds of random moves.

How is the network trained? By self-play: the agent plays games against itself, choosing each move with MCTS. The search makes the agent stronger than its raw network, so the search results are better training targets than the network's own outputs:

This is a form of policy iteration (from the dynamic programming lesson): MCTS is the policy improvement step, and training the network to imitate it makes the improvement permanent.

The family in short:

System Model used for search Network trained from Games AlphaGo (2016) the game rules human expert games, then self-play Go AlphaGo Zero (2017) the game rules self-play only, no human data Go AlphaZero (2017) the game rules self-play only Go, chess, shogi MuZero (2019) a learned model self-play and real experience Go, chess, shogi, Atari

MuZero goes one step further. It doesn't get the rules. It learns three networks: a representation that turns the observation into a hidden state, a dynamics network that predicts the next hidden state and reward from a hidden state and an action (the learned model), and the same prediction network for \(\mathbf{p}\) and \(v\). MCTS then searches entirely inside the learned hidden space. The learned model never has to reconstruct the screen or the board; it only has to predict what matters for planning: rewards, values and policies.

What to notice

The network alone is like fast intuition; MCTS is slow deliberate thinking that checks the intuition. Training on the search results turns slow thinking into better intuition, and the loop repeats.

docs.title: Step 7 — When the model is wrong
docs.text:
A model is only useful if it is right where the planner looks. Three things go wrong in practice:

  • Errors compound. A one-step model that is a little off feeds its own prediction back in as the next state, so mistakes add up over a long imagined trajectory. If each predicted step is right with probability 0.95, a 10-step imagined rollout is entirely right with probability \(0.95^{10} \approx 0.60\), and a 50-step one only \(0.95^{50} \approx 0.08\). This is why methods such as MBPO (model-based policy optimisation) only imagine short rollouts branching off real states.
  • The planner exploits model errors. A planner searches for the action with the best predicted outcome. If the model is wrong somewhere in a flattering way, that is exactly where the planner will go, like the 10-try model in Step 2 that thought the cliff edge was perfectly safe.
  • The model only knows what you tried. Dyna-Q's planning only replays state-action pairs it has seen. In all 5 stuck runs from Step 4, the agent had never tried moving right from one or two cells near the end of the cliff edge, so its model knew nothing there and the planner kept polishing a 9-step detour that it did know. Dyna-Q+ fixes this with a small exploration bonus for state-action pairs not tried for a long time.

Model-based or model-free?

Model-based methods use data far more efficiently and can reuse a model for new goals. Model-free methods are simpler and don't suffer from model bias: their errors come only from noise. Many modern systems combine both, as Dyna does: plan where the model is trusted, learn directly from real experience everywhere.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Here is Dyna-Q on the cliff world in plain Python, with the model as a table of counts. Set n_planning = 0 and it is ordinary Q-learning:

import random
from statistics import mean, median

MAP = ["......",
       "..#...",
       "......",
       "SCCCCG"]
MOVES = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]          # up, right, down, left
START = (3, 0)


def env_step(s, a):
    """The real environment (the agent does NOT get to read this code)."""
    r, c = s[0] + MOVES[a][0], s[1] + MOVES[a][1]
    if not (0 <= r < 4 and 0 <= c < 6) or MAP[r][c] == "#":
        r, c = s                                      # bumped a wall or edge: stay put
    tile = MAP[r][c]
    if tile == "G":
        return (r, c), +10, True
    if tile == "C":
        return (r, c), -20, True
    return (r, c), -1, False


def greedy(Q, s, rng):
    best = max(Q[s])
    return rng.choice([a for a in range(4) if Q[s][a] == best])   # break ties at random


def dyna_q(n_planning, episodes=60, alpha=0.1, gamma=0.95, eps=0.1, seed=0):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    Q = {(r, c): [0.0] * 4 for r in range(4) for c in range(6)}
    model = {}                       # (s, a) -> {(s', r, done): how often we saw it}
    history = []                     # after each episode: is the greedy route the 7-step one?

    def q_update(s, a, r, s2, done):
        target = r if done else r + gamma * max(Q[s2])
        Q[s][a] += alpha * (target - Q[s][a])

    for _ in range(episodes):
        s, done, t = START, False, 0
        while not done and t < 1000:
            # 1. act in the REAL world (ε-greedy) and learn from it: plain Q-learning
            a = rng.randrange(4) if rng.random() < eps else greedy(Q, s, rng)
            s2, r, done = env_step(s, a)
            q_update(s, a, r, s2, done)
            # 2. learn the MODEL: count what happened
            counts = model.setdefault((s, a), {})
            counts[(s2, r, done)] = counts.get((s2, r, done), 0) + 1
            # 3. PLAN: n extra Q-learning updates on experience imagined by the model
            seen = list(model)
            for _ in range(n_planning):
                ps, pa = rng.choice(seen)                       # a state-action we have tried
                outcomes = model[(ps, pa)]
                (ps2, pr, pdone), = rng.choices(list(outcomes), weights=list(outcomes.values()))
                q_update(ps, pa, pr, ps2, pdone)
            s, t = s2, t + 1
        history.append(greedy_route_length(Q) == 7)
    return history


def greedy_route_length(Q):
    """Follow the greedy policy (no exploration) from the start; return its number of steps."""
    s = START
    for t in range(1, 30):
        s, r, done = env_step(s, Q[s].index(max(Q[s])))
        if done:
            return t if r > 0 else None
    return None


for n in [0, 5, 50]:
    runs = [dyna_q(n, seed=seed) for seed in range(100)]
    first = [h.index(True) + 1 if True in h else 61 for h in runs]
    print(f"n = {n:2d}: optimal route found after {median(first):4.1f} episodes (median of 100 runs); "
          f"runs on it after 10 episodes: {mean(h[9] for h in runs):.0%}, after 60: {mean(h[-1] for h in runs):.0%}")

n =  0: optimal route found after 32.0 episodes (median of 100 runs); runs on it after 10 episodes: 0%, after 60: 100%
n =  5: optimal route found after 10.0 episodes (median of 100 runs); runs on it after 10 episodes: 34%, after 60: 100%
n = 50: optimal route found after  7.0 episodes (median of 100 runs); runs on it after 10 episodes: 84%, after 60: 95%

And a compact MCTS for tic-tac-toe. The "model" is just the rules (play, moves, winner); minimax checks the answer by searching the whole game tree:

import math
import random

LINES = [(0, 1, 2), (3, 4, 5), (6, 7, 8), (0, 3, 6), (1, 4, 7), (2, 5, 8), (0, 4, 8), (2, 4, 6)]
NAMES = ["top-left", "top", "top-right", "left", "centre", "right", "bottom-left", "bottom", "bottom-right"]


# ---- The model: the rules of tic-tac-toe. A board is a 9-character string like "..O..XX.O".
def winner(b):
    for i, j, k in LINES:
        if b[i] != "." and b[i] == b[j] == b[k]:
            return b[i]
    return None

def to_move(b):
    return "X" if b.count("X") == b.count("O") else "O"

def moves(b):
    return [] if winner(b) else [i for i in range(9) if b[i] == "."]

def play(b, i):
    return b[:i] + to_move(b) + b[i + 1:]


class Node:
    def __init__(self, board, parent=None, move=None):
        self.board, self.parent, self.move = board, parent, move
        self.children, self.untried = [], moves(board)
        self.N, self.W = 0, 0.0          # visit count, total value (for the player who moved INTO this node)


def uct(child, c=math.sqrt(2)):
    return child.W / child.N + c * math.sqrt(math.log(child.parent.N) / child.N)


def mcts(board, simulations, rng):
    root = Node(board)
    for _ in range(simulations):
        node = root
        # 1. Selection: walk down the tree, always taking the child with the highest UCT score
        while not node.untried and node.children:
            node = max(node.children, key=uct)
        # 2. Expansion: add one new child for a move we have never tried here
        if node.untried:
            m = node.untried.pop(rng.randrange(len(node.untried)))
            child = Node(play(node.board, m), node, m)
            node.children.append(child)
            node = child
        # 3. Simulation: play random moves until the game ends
        b = node.board
        while moves(b):
            b = play(b, rng.choice(moves(b)))
        w = winner(b)
        # 4. Backup: every node on the path gets +1 / 0 / -1 from the view of the player who moved into it
        while node:
            mover = "O" if to_move(node.board) == "X" else "X"
            node.N += 1
            node.W += 0 if w is None else (1 if w == mover else -1)
            node = node.parent
    return root


def minimax(b):
    """Exact value for the player to move (+1 win, 0 draw, -1 loss). Fine for a game this small."""
    if winner(b):
        return -1                        # the previous player just won
    if not moves(b):
        return 0
    return max(-minimax(play(b, m)) for m in moves(b))


board = "..O..XX.O"                      # X to move
print("minimax:", {NAMES[m]: -minimax(play(board, m)) for m in moves(board)})
for K in [25, 100, 400, 1000]:
    root = mcts(board, K, random.Random(0))
    best = max(root.children, key=lambda ch: ch.N)
    stats = ", ".join(f"{NAMES[ch.move]} {ch.N} ({ch.W / ch.N:+.2f})"
                      for ch in sorted(root.children, key=lambda ch: ch.move))
    print(f"K={K:4d}: plays {NAMES[best.move]:7s} share {best.N / K:4.0%} | N (W/N): {stats}")

for K in [25, 50, 100, 200, 400]:
    right = sum(max(mcts(board, K, random.Random(s)).children, key=lambda ch: ch.N).move == 3
                for s in range(100))
    print(f"K={K:3d}: picks the winning move in {right}/100 runs")

K=  25: plays top-left share  28% | N (W/N): top-left 7 (+0.43), top 6 (+0.33), left 4 (+0.00), centre 4 (+0.00), bottom 4 (+0.25)
K= 100: plays centre  share  31% | N (W/N): top-left 21 (+0.33), top 16 (+0.25), left 20 (+0.40), centre 31 (+0.45), bottom 12 (+0.08)
K= 400: plays left    share  80% | N (W/N): top-left 21 (+0.33), top 17 (+0.24), left 319 (+0.91), centre 31 (+0.45), bottom 12 (+0.08)
K=1000: plays left    share  91% | N (W/N): top-left 23 (+0.30), top 23 (+0.26), left 907 (+0.96), centre 34 (+0.44), bottom 13 (+0.00)

To go from here to AlphaZero, replace the random play-out with a call to a value network, add the network's prior \(P(s, a)\) to the selection score (the PUCT rule), and train the network on the visit counts and game results from self-play. Open-source versions to read: alpha-zero-general (small and readable) and DeepMind's mctx (MCTS for AlphaZero and MuZero in JAX).

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"Model-based means the agent is given the rules.\"

Sometimes it is (MCTS and AlphaZero use the game rules), but often the model is learned from experience, as in Dyna and MuZero. "Model-based" only means the agent has some model of \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\) and uses it to plan.

\"More planning is always better.\"

Planning is only as good as the model. With a learned model, extra planning can make the agent more confident in the model's mistakes, as in the stuck Dyna runs and the "safe" cliff edge of Step 2. The gain from more planning also shrinks fast (0 → 5 steps helped more than 5 → 50).

\"MCTS picks the move with the highest average value.\"

The usual choice is the most-visited child. Visits are a more robust signal: a move can have a high average from only a few lucky play-outs, but it only collects many visits if it kept looking good as the search looked deeper.

\"AlphaZero is just a very good neural network.\"

The raw network is much weaker than network + search. The search improves on the network at every move, and the network is trained to imitate those improved choices. Take the search away and both the play and the training signal get worse.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. What does a model of the environment predict, and how would you learn one in a small grid world?

It predicts what happens after taking action \(a\) in state \(s\): the next state \(s'\) and the reward \(r\) (or their probabilities \(\hat p(s', r \mid s, a)\)). In a small grid world you count: every real transition adds 1 to \(n(s, a, s', r)\), and \(\hat p = n(s, a, s', r) / n(s, a)\).

2. Dyna-Q with n = 0 is which algorithm? What does n > 0 add, and what does it cost?

With \(n = 0\) it is plain Q-learning. With \(n > 0\) every real step is followed by \(n\) Q-learning updates on transitions imagined by the model. It costs extra computation per step, but it saves real experience: on the cliff world, \(n = 50\) found the optimal route after a median of 129 real steps versus about 840 for \(n = 0\).

3. In the UCT formula, what happens to a child that has been visited very few times? Why is that useful?

Its exploration bonus \(c\sqrt{\ln N_{\text{parent}} / N}\) is large, so it gets selected again even if its average looks poor. That stops the search from writing off a move after a few unlucky random play-outs. In the tic-tac-toe example, the winning move left had an average of 0.00 after 25 simulations and only became the favourite once the search kept revisiting it.

4. In AlphaZero, what are the training targets for the policy head and the value head?

The policy head is trained towards the MCTS visit-count distribution \(\pi\) at each position (what the search preferred). The value head is trained towards the final game result \(z\) (+1, 0 or −1 from the view of the player to move).

5. Why do errors in a learned model hurt more on long imagined rollouts than on short ones?

Each imagined step starts from the model's previous prediction, so errors compound. If each step is right with probability 0.95, a 10-step rollout is all correct with probability about 0.60 and a 50-step one only about 0.08. That's why methods like MBPO use short model rollouts that start from real states.
