docs.title: Monte Carlo and Temporal-Difference Learning
docs.text:
TL;DR

Dynamic programming needs a model of the world. Real agents usually don't have one, so they learn values from experience. Monte Carlo (MC) plays a whole episode, then moves each state's value toward the return it actually got. Temporal-difference (TD) learning doesn't wait: after every single step it moves \(V(s)\) toward \(r + \gamma V(s')\), a target that uses its own guess for the next state. TD learns "a guess from a guess", and that usually makes it learn faster.

Level: beginner–intermediate · Prerequisites: What is RL? (returns, policies, values) and Dynamic programming (policy evaluation with the Bellman equation)

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
In the dynamic programming lesson we computed the value of every state by sweeping over the Bellman equation. That worked because we knew the rules: for every state and action, the exact probability of every next state and reward, \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\).

Almost no real problem hands you that table. Nobody can write down the transition probabilities of a robot arm, a game of Go against an unknown opponent, or a user chatting with an assistant. What you can do is try things and watch what happens.

This lesson is about learning values from that raw experience. The two ideas in it, Monte Carlo and TD learning, are the foundation of almost everything that follows: Q-learning, SARSA and DQN are TD methods, and REINFORCE is a Monte Carlo method. In this lesson we only predict (estimate \(V^\pi\) for a fixed policy \(\pi\)). Using these estimates to improve the policy (control) is the next lesson.

docs.title: Step 1 — Learning without a model
docs.text:
Dynamic programming and the methods in this lesson want the same thing: the value function \(V^\pi(s)\) from lesson 1. They differ in what they need.

Remember the definition of value: \(V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t \mid s_t = s]\), the expected return from \(s\). An expectation is just an average over many tries. So if we can't compute the average from a model, we can estimate it from samples, exactly like the "Run 1000 episodes" button in lesson 1 did. This is what model-free means: the agent never learns or uses \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\).

What to notice

Both roads end at the same box. Model-free methods are not "worse DP". They answer the same question with a different ingredient: samples instead of probabilities.

docs.title: Step 2 — Monte Carlo: average the returns you actually got
docs.text:
Monte Carlo methods are named after the casino: they estimate an average by sampling. The recipe for estimating \(V^\pi(s)\):

  1. Follow \(\pi\) until the episode ends.
  2. For each state \(s\) you visited, compute the return \(G_t\) that followed (the discounted sum of rewards from that point to the end).
  3. \(V(s)\) is the average of all the returns you have seen from \(s\).

If a state is visited twice in one episode, first-visit MC only uses the return after the first visit. (Every-visit MC uses all of them; both work.)

Keeping a list of every return is wasteful. The same average can be updated one return at a time. If \(N(s)\) counts the returns seen so far from \(s\):

\[ V(s) \leftarrow V(s) + \frac{1}{N(s)}\,\big(G_t - V(s)\big) \]

Read it as: nudge the estimate toward the new sample, by a fraction of the gap. In practice we often use a constant step size \(\alpha\) (say 0.1) instead of \(1/N(s)\):

\[ V(s) \leftarrow V(s) + \alpha\,\big(G_t - V(s)\big) \]

A constant \(\alpha\) forgets old returns slowly, which helps when the policy (and so the true values) keep changing, as they will in the next lesson.

The test problem: a random walk. Five states A–E sit in a row. Every episode starts in C and steps left or right with probability ½ each. Leaving on the right gives reward +1; leaving on the left gives 0; every other step gives 0. With \(\gamma = 1\), the value of a state is just the probability of leaving on the right, which works out to \(V^\pi(A), \dots, V^\pi(E) = \tfrac16, \tfrac26, \tfrac36, \tfrac46, \tfrac56\). Knowing the true answer lets us measure exactly how well each method learns.

🎲 Interactive: Monte Carlo on the random walk

What to notice

  • While the episode is running, nothing changes. MC cannot update until it knows the return, and it only knows the return at the end.
  • When the episode ends, every state visited moves toward the same number (0 or 1 here). One lucky episode that leaves on the right drags A up toward 1, even though A's true value is only \(\tfrac16\).
  • Press Run 10 episodes a few times. The bars do approach the green dashes, but they keep jumping around: each return is a noisy sample.

docs.title: Step 3 — TD(0): learn a guess from a guess
docs.text:
Here is the key observation. The return obeys a one-step relation (the Bellman equation from the MDP lesson):

\[ G_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma\, G_{t+1} \qquad\text{so}\qquad V^\pi(s_t) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\big[\,r_{t+1} + \gamma\, V^\pi(s_{t+1})\,\big] \]

So instead of waiting for the real \(G_t\), we can plug in our current estimate of what comes after: \(r_{t+1} + \gamma V(s_{t+1})\). That gives TD(0), the simplest temporal-difference method:

\[ V(s_t) \leftarrow V(s_t) + \alpha\,\big[\underbrace{r_{t+1} + \gamma V(s_{t+1})}_{\text{TD target}} - V(s_t)\big] \]

The bracket has its own name, the TD error:

\[ \delta_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t) \]

\(\delta_t\) is the surprise of one step: how much better or worse things look one step later than they did a moment ago. Positive \(\delta_t\) → \(s_t\) was better than we thought, so raise \(V(s_t)\). A terminal state has value 0, so on the final step the target is just \(r_{t+1}\).

Updating an estimate from another estimate is called bootstrapping ("pulling yourself up by your own bootstraps"). DP bootstraps too: it also uses \(V(s')\) in its target. TD combines the two worlds: it samples like Monte Carlo and bootstraps like DP.

⏱️ Interactive: TD updates every step, MC waits for the end

What to notice

  • Reset values, then step through the first episode. Every TD error is \(0 + 0.5 - 0.5 = 0\) until the very last step: all states look equally good, so there is no surprise. Only the state next to the exit learns something in episode 1. MC, in contrast, moves every visited state.
  • In later episodes the information spreads backwards one step at a time: once E has a high value, a step from D into E produces a positive \(\delta\) and raises D.
  • TD updates use \(V(s')\), which is itself only a guess. Early on that guess is wrong, so TD's target is biased. But it depends on just one random step, so it jumps around much less than MC's target.

docs.title: Step 4 — MC vs TD: waiting for the truth vs trusting your guess
docs.text:
A small example makes the difference concrete. You drive home from work and keep predicting your total travel time:

Moment Minutes so far Predicted time still to go Predicted total Leave the office 0 30 30 Reach the car, it's raining 5 35 40 Leave the highway, traffic was light 20 15 35 Stuck behind a slow truck 30 10 40 Turn into your street 40 3 43 Arrive home 43 0 43
  • Monte Carlo says: wait until you are home. The real total was 43, so every earlier prediction (30, 40, 35, 40) should move toward 43.
  • TD says: don't wait. When you see the rain, your new prediction (40) already tells you that "30" was too optimistic, so update it toward 40 right then. Each prediction moves toward the next prediction.

TD is how people actually learn: you don't need to crash the car to learn that skidding was a bad sign. The trade-off, in one table:

Monte Carlo TD(0) Target the real return \(G_t\) \(r_{t+1} + \gamma V(s_{t+1})\) Bias none: \(G_t\) is a true sample of \(V^\pi(s_t)\) biased while \(V\) is still wrong Variance high: \(G_t\) depends on every random step until the end low: depends on one random step When it can update only at the end of an episode after every step (online) Needs episodes to end? yes no, works for never-ending tasks Uses the Markov property? no yes (it trusts \(V(s')\) to summarise the future)

Neither is always better. But because TD's targets are much less noisy, it usually learns faster in practice, as the next step shows.

What to notice

"Bias" and "variance" here mean the same thing as in supervised learning. MC is an unbiased but noisy estimator; TD trades a little bias (which disappears as \(V\) improves) for a big cut in noise.

docs.title: Step 5 — The race: MC vs TD on the random walk
docs.text:
Let's measure. Both methods start every value at 0.5 and see the same kind of episodes. After each episode we compute the RMS error between the estimates and the true values \(\tfrac16, \dots, \tfrac56\) (the square root of the average squared error over the five states). One run is noisy, so the curves below average 100 runs with fixed random seeds. At the start the RMS error is 0.236.

🏁 Interactive: learning curves for MC and TD

What to notice

  • TD learns much faster at first. With the default settings (MC \(\alpha = 0.02\), TD \(\alpha = 0.1\)), after 25 episodes TD's error is 0.056 while MC's is still 0.174.
  • Click "MC 0.03 · TD 0.05". TD with a small step size ends lowest of all: 0.035 after 100 episodes, against 0.056 for MC.
  • The step size is a trade-off. A large \(\alpha\) learns fast but never settles: TD with \(\alpha = 0.15\) reaches its lowest error, 0.055, around episode 25, then drifts back up to 0.069. With "both large" (MC 0.1, TD 0.3) TD's error is lowest early (0.073 after 10 episodes) and then rises to 0.108. With a constant \(\alpha\), the estimates keep chasing each new noisy sample.
  • Compare the two at the same step size, \(\alpha = 0.1\): TD's error bottoms out at 0.047 (around episode 45), MC's only at 0.081 (around episode 54). MC's targets are noisier, so its floor is higher.

docs.title: Step 6 — TD on the cliff world
docs.text:
The random walk is tiny. Now let TD estimate the values of a policy on the cliff world from lesson 1, with \(\gamma = 0.95\). The policy is fixed (the arrows); TD only evaluates it. In the DP lesson we computed these values with the model. Here TD never sees the model, only episodes, and we can check whether it lands on the same numbers.

🧗 Interactive: TD(0) evaluates a policy on the cliff world

What to notice

  • TD finds the DP values without the model. With Edge of the cliff and no slip, after 1000 episodes (\(\alpha = 0.1\)) TD's \(V(\text{start})\) is 2.03, against the DP value of 2.05. After 2000 episodes the two agree to two decimals.
  • Values spread backwards from the goal. Press Reset, then +100 episodes: the two cells nearest the goal already match DP (10.0 and 8.5), while the top-left cells are still stuck near 0 or below. Each update only passes information one step back.
  • On a slippery floor, a constant \(\alpha\) keeps jittering. Tick slippery floor (DP: \(V(\text{start}) = -9.08\)). After 1000 episodes TD says −9.12, but after 2000 it says −9.84: each slip is a random surprise, and with a fixed step size the estimate keeps reacting to it. Checked every 250 episodes between 1000 and 5000, the RMS error over all cells bounces between 0.59 and 2.05 and never settles to 0. The usual fix is a step size that shrinks over time.
  • The random walk and the cliff world tell the same story: TD learns quickly, and \(\alpha\) decides how fast versus how precisely.

docs.title: Step 7 — Between the two: n-step TD and backup diagrams
docs.text:
MC and TD(0) are two ends of a dial. n-step TD looks \(n\) real rewards ahead, then bootstraps:

\[ G_{t:t+n} = r_{t+1} + \gamma r_{t+2} + \dots + \gamma^{n-1} r_{t+n} + \gamma^n V(s_{t+n}) \] \[ V(s_t) \leftarrow V(s_t) + \alpha\,\big[G_{t:t+n} - V(s_t)\big] \]

With \(n = 1\) this is TD(0). If \(n\) reaches past the end of the episode, there is nothing left to bootstrap from and it becomes Monte Carlo. Values in between often work best. (TD(λ) averages over all \(n\) at once; Sutton & Barto, Chapter 12, covers it.)

A backup diagram shows what an update looks at: how deep (one step, or all the way to the end) and how wide (every possible next state, or one sample).

What to notice

Two questions classify every method in this course: does it bootstrap (use \(V(s')\) in its target)? and does it sample (use real experience instead of a model)? DP: bootstraps, doesn't sample. MC: samples, doesn't bootstrap. TD: both.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Here is TD(0) prediction as a loop. Compare it with the agent loop from lesson 1: the "Learn" box is now one concrete line.

Here are both methods on the random walk in plain Python, with the same experiment as the learning-curve widget (100 runs of 100 episodes, values starting at 0.5):

import random

# The random walk: states 1..5 are A..E, 0 and 6 are the two ends (terminal, V = 0).
TRUE_V = [None, 1/6, 2/6, 3/6, 4/6, 5/6]


def play_episode():
    """Start in C, step left or right at random. Returns a list of (s, r, s_next)."""
    s, steps = 3, []
    while 0 < s < 6:
        s_next = s + random.choice([-1, +1])
        r = 1.0 if s_next == 6 else 0.0          # +1 only for leaving on the right
        steps.append((s, r, s_next))
        s = s_next
    return steps


def mc_update(V, steps, alpha, gamma=1.0):
    """First-visit Monte Carlo: wait for the end, then move V(s) toward the real return G."""
    G, returns = 0.0, []
    for s, r, _ in reversed(steps):              # walk backwards: G_t = r_{t+1} + γ G_{t+1}
        G = r + gamma * G
        returns.append((s, G))
    returns.reverse()
    seen = set()
    for s, G in returns:
        if s not in seen:                        # only the first visit to s counts
            seen.add(s)
            V[s] += alpha * (G - V[s])


def td_update(V, steps, alpha, gamma=1.0):
    """TD(0): update after every step, toward r + γ V(s')."""
    for s, r, s_next in steps:                   # (in a live agent this runs inside the episode)
        delta = r + gamma * V[s_next] - V[s]     # the TD error
        V[s] += alpha * delta


def rms_error(V):
    return (sum((V[s] - TRUE_V[s]) ** 2 for s in range(1, 6)) / 5) ** 0.5


def experiment(update, alpha, runs=100, episodes=100):
    curve = [0.0] * (episodes + 1)               # average RMS error after each episode
    for _ in range(runs):
        V = [0.0] + [0.5] * 5 + [0.0]            # guesses start at 0.5; the ends stay 0
        curve[0] += rms_error(V) / runs
        for ep in range(1, episodes + 1):
            update(V, play_episode(), alpha)
            curve[ep] += rms_error(V) / runs
    return curve


random.seed(0)
for name, update, alpha in [("MC", mc_update, 0.02), ("MC", mc_update, 0.03),
                            ("TD", td_update, 0.05), ("TD", td_update, 0.1)]:
    c = experiment(update, alpha)
    print(f"{name} α={alpha:<4}  RMS error after 10 episodes: {c[10]:.3f}   25: {c[25]:.3f}   100: {c[100]:.3f}")

MC α=0.02  RMS error after 10 episodes: 0.210   25: 0.176   100: 0.079
MC α=0.03  RMS error after 10 episodes: 0.197   25: 0.151   100: 0.059
TD α=0.05  RMS error after 10 episodes: 0.174   25: 0.110   100: 0.038
TD α=0.1   RMS error after 10 episodes: 0.128   25: 0.060   100: 0.056

Python's random numbers differ from the widget's, so the numbers differ slightly in the third decimal, but the story is the same: TD gets ahead early and ends lower. Notice how little separates the two functions: mc_update uses the return G, td_update uses r + gamma * V[s_next]. Everything else in this course (SARSA, Q-learning, DQN, actor-critic) keeps that delta line and changes what goes around it.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"TD uses its own guesses, so it converges to the wrong answer.\"

The guesses are wrong at first, but they are corrected by real rewards at every step. For a fixed policy, tabular TD(0) converges to \(V^\pi\) (with a step size that shrinks appropriately; with a small constant \(\alpha\) it hovers close to it). The bias is temporary; the lower variance is what you keep.

\"Monte Carlo is unbiased, so it must be more accurate.\"

Unbiased only means right on average. Each MC target carries the randomness of an entire episode, so with limited experience MC estimates are often further from the truth than TD's, as the learning curves show.

\"Model-free means the agent doesn't need an environment.\"

The opposite: model-free methods need lots of interaction with the environment, because experience is their only source of information. What they don't need is a written-down model \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\).

\"MC and TD need the agent to know the transition probabilities to compute the expectation.\"

They never compute an expectation explicitly. Averaging many sampled updates does the same job: states that are reached more often simply get more updates.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. \(V(C) = 0.5\), you run an episode from C that ends on the right (return \(G = 1\)), and \(\alpha = 0.1\). What is the Monte Carlo update for \(V(C)\)?

$V(C) \leftarrow 0.5 + 0.1 \cdot (1 - 0.5) = $ 0.55.

2. \(V(C) = 0.5\), \(V(D) = 0.6\). The agent steps from C to D with reward 0, \(\gamma = 1\), \(\alpha = 0.1\). What are the TD error and the new \(V(C)\)?

\(\delta = 0 + 1 \cdot 0.6 - 0.5 = 0.1\), so $V(C) \leftarrow 0.5 + 0.1 \cdot 0.1 = $ 0.51.

3. In the random walk with every value starting at 0.5, why does TD change only one state during the first episode?

Every step that doesn't end the episode has reward 0 and goes between two states that both have value 0.5, so \(\delta = 0 + 0.5 - 0.5 = 0\). Only the final step has a target that differs from 0.5: the real reward (0 or 1) with \(V(\text{end}) = 0\). So only the state next to the exit (A or E) moves.

4. Your task never ends (a thermostat controlling a building forever). Can you use Monte Carlo? Can you use TD?

Plain Monte Carlo needs complete episodes to compute returns, so it can't be used directly. TD only needs one step \((s, r, s')\) at a time, so it works on continuing tasks. (Discounting with \(\gamma < 1\) keeps the values finite.)

5. In the learning-curve widget, TD with a large \(\alpha\) gets lower error early but higher error later. Why?

A large step size moves each estimate a long way toward each new target. That learns fast, but every target is noisy, so the estimates keep bouncing around the true values instead of settling. A small \(\alpha\) averages over more experience: slower at first, more precise in the end.

docs.text:
• Richard Sutton & Andrew Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.), Chapter 5 (Monte Carlo), Chapter 6 (TD learning, including the random walk and driving-home examples) and Chapter 7 (n-step methods)
  • Richard Sutton, Learning to Predict by the Methods of Temporal Differences (1988), the paper that introduced TD learning
  • David Silver, UCL Course on RL, Lecture 4: Model-Free Prediction
  • Gerald Tesauro, Temporal Difference Learning and TD-Gammon (1995), TD learning that reached world-class backgammon

docs.title: Multi-Armed Bandits
docs.text:
TL;DR

A multi-armed bandit is the simplest reinforcement-learning problem: there is only one situation, and you repeatedly choose one of \(k\) actions ("arms"), each paying a random reward from its own hidden distribution. To do well you must explore (try arms to learn what they are worth) and exploit (pull the arm that looks best). This lesson builds the tools for that trade-off: running value estimates, the update rule new estimate = old + step × error, and four ways to explore (ε-greedy, optimistic initial values, UCB and Thompson sampling), compared by their regret.

Level: beginner · Prerequisites: What is RL? (agent, action, reward, ε-greedy). Knowing what an average and a square root are is enough for the math.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
Many real decisions are bandit problems:

  • A/B testing on websites. Which of three headlines gets the most clicks? Every visitor you show a weak headline to is a lost click.
  • Clinical trials. Which of several treatments works best? Every patient given the worse treatment pays a real price, so you want to shift patients to the better one as soon as the evidence allows.
  • Recommendations and ads. Which song, article or ad should you show next? You learn from every click, while still trying new items.

Bandits are also the cleanest place to study exploration versus exploitation, which lesson 1 only teased. In a bandit there are no states that change and no delayed rewards, so exploration is the only hard part. The tools you build here (value estimates, the incremental update, ε-greedy, optimism) are reused in every later lesson of this series.

docs.title: Step 1 — The k-armed bandit: one state, k actions
docs.text:
Picture a row of slot machines (old slang: "one-armed bandits", because they take your money). Each machine pays out a random amount when you pull its arm. Some machines are better on average than others, but you don't know which. You have a fixed number of pulls. How do you collect the most money?

That is the k-armed bandit problem:

  • You have \(k\) possible actions (arms).
  • Each time step \(t\), you pick one arm \(a_t\) and receive a reward \(r_{t+1}\).
  • Each arm's reward is random, drawn from that arm's own distribution, which never changes and which you cannot see.
  • Your goal: the largest total reward over many pulls.

In the language of lesson 1, the agent–environment loop still runs, but the state never changes. Your action affects only the reward you get right now, not the situation you will be in next. That removes the credit-assignment problem completely and leaves the pure question: which arm is best, and how much should I spend finding out?

Problem Arms Reward Slot machines the machines the payout A/B test page variants A, B, C 1 if the visitor clicks, else 0 Clinical trial treatments 1 if the patient recovers, else 0 News site candidate headlines 1 if clicked, else 0

Try it: five slot machines, 25 pulls. Each pull pays the arm's hidden value plus random noise, so one lucky or unlucky pull can mislead you. When your pulls run out, the true values are revealed.

🎰 Interactive: play a 5-armed bandit

What to notice

  • One pull tells you little. The noise is as large as the differences between arms, so a single good reward can make a mediocre arm look great.
  • You felt the dilemma. Every pull spent testing a new arm is a pull not spent on your current favourite. Stick with your favourite too early and you may never find the real best arm.
  • Play a few games. Did you always find the best arm (★ after the reveal)? The regret in the readout counts how much expected reward your choices cost you compared with always pulling the best arm. Step 7 makes this the yardstick for every method.

docs.title: Step 2 — Action values: what is each arm worth?
docs.text:
The true value of an arm is the reward it pays on average:

\[ q_*(a) = \mathbb{E}\left[\, r_{t+1} \mid a_t = a \,\right] \]

This is the bandit version of the Q-value from lesson 1. With only one state, "how good is action \(a\)" doesn't depend on where you are. If you knew \(q_*(a)\) for every arm, the problem would be trivial: always pull the arm with the largest \(q_*\). But you don't, so you estimate it.

The most natural estimate is the sample average: add up the rewards you have received from arm \(a\) and divide by the number of times you pulled it.

\[ Q_t(a) = \frac{\text{sum of rewards from } a \text{ so far}}{N_t(a)} \]

where \(N_t(a)\) is how many times arm \(a\) has been pulled before step \(t\). This is exactly the orange bar in the widget above. By the law of large numbers, \(Q_t(a) \to q_*(a)\) as \(N_t(a)\) grows: more pulls, better estimate.

The greedy action is the arm with the highest estimate right now, \(\arg\max_a Q_t(a)\). Choosing it is exploiting; choosing anything else is exploring.

What to notice

  • The estimate of an arm only improves when you pull that arm. An arm you ignore keeps whatever estimate (good or bad) it had.
  • So a greedy agent can get stuck: if the best arm happens to give a poor first reward, its estimate stays low, and the agent never comes back to correct it.

docs.title: Step 3 — Learning incrementally: new estimate = old estimate + step × error
docs.text:
Storing every reward to recompute the average is wasteful. There is a neater way. Say arm \(a\) has given rewards \(r_1, \dots, r_n\) (numbered by pulls of this arm), and \(Q_n\) is the average of the first \(n-1\) of them. Then the average of all \(n\) is

\[ Q_{n+1} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i = \frac{1}{n}\Big(r_n + (n-1)\,Q_n\Big) = Q_n + \frac{1}{n}\Big(r_n - Q_n\Big) \]

Read the last form out loud:

\[ \text{new estimate} \;=\; \text{old estimate} \;+\; \text{step size} \times \underbrace{(\text{target} - \text{old estimate})}_{\text{error}} \]

You only need to remember \(Q\) and \(N\) for each arm. Each new reward nudges the estimate towards itself, by a step that shrinks as evidence accumulates.

This pattern is everywhere in machine learning. Gradient descent (lesson) has the same shape, \(w \leftarrow w - \eta \nabla L\): old value plus a step in the direction that reduces the error. In fact, \(Q \leftarrow Q + \alpha (r - Q)\) is one gradient-descent step on the squared error \(\tfrac{1}{2}(r - Q)^2\). In later lessons the target will change (it becomes "reward plus the value of the next state"), but the update keeps this form.

When the world changes: a constant step size

With step \(\tfrac{1}{n}\), the 1000th reward counts as much as the first. That is right if the arms never change. If they drift (a headline goes stale, a market moves), use a constant step size \(\alpha\), say 0.1: \(Q \leftarrow Q + \alpha (r - Q)\). Then recent rewards count more and old ones fade away exponentially, so the estimate keeps tracking the moving target. Most of deep RL uses a constant step size (the learning rate).

What to notice

  • The update needs only two numbers per arm, \(Q(a)\) and \(N(a)\), however many pulls you make.
  • The error \(r - Q\) is the learning signal. If rewards match expectations, the estimate stops moving.

docs.title: Step 4 — Greedy vs ε-greedy
docs.text:
Now we can build agents. The simplest is greedy: always pull the arm with the highest \(Q\) (break ties at random). ε-greedy (from lesson 1) adds a little exploration: with probability \(\varepsilon\) pick a random arm, otherwise act greedily.

To compare them fairly we use the classic 10-armed testbed from Sutton & Barto's textbook:

  1. Make a random bandit with 10 arms. Each arm's true value \(q_*(a)\) is drawn from a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
  2. Each pull of arm \(a\) pays \(q_*(a)\) plus normal noise (standard deviation 1).
  3. Let the agent play 1000 pulls, learning with sample averages.
  4. Repeat on 2000 different random bandits and average, so the curves show typical behaviour rather than luck.

The widget runs all of this in your browser (with a fixed random seed, so everyone sees the same curves). Move the slider to try your own \(\varepsilon\).

📈 Interactive: greedy vs ε-greedy on the 10-armed testbed

What to notice

  • Greedy gets stuck. It improves fast at first, then flattens: over the last 100 steps it picks the best arm only 34.4% of the time (average reward 1.004). In most runs it locked onto a decent-looking arm early and never checked the others again.
  • A little exploration pays off. ε = 0.1 reaches 80.0% optimal (reward 1.361), and ε = 0.01 reaches 59.1% (reward 1.299). For comparison, always pulling the best arm would earn 1.532 on average on these bandits.
  • ε = 0.1 has a ceiling. Even with perfect estimates it still explores 10% of the time, so it can pick the best arm at most \(90\% + 10\% \times \tfrac{1}{10} = 91\%\) of the time.
  • ε = 0.01 is slower but ends higher. Run both for 10,000 steps (we did, in Python) and ε = 0.01 overtakes: average reward 1.501 vs 1.378 over the last 100 steps. Try ε = 0.3 or 0.5 with the slider: too much exploration wastes pulls on arms you already know are bad.

docs.title: Step 5 — Optimistic initial values
docs.text:
Here is a trick that makes even a greedy agent explore. Instead of starting every estimate at 0, start it way too high, say \(Q_1(a) = 5\), when real values are around 0 to 2.

Now every arm looks wonderful until it is tried. The greedy agent pulls the arm with the highest estimate, gets a reward around 1, and its estimate drops: disappointing! So the agent moves on to another arm that still looks wonderful. It ends up trying every arm, several times, before settling down. The exploration comes from optimism, not randomness.

Like Sutton & Barto, this agent uses a constant step size \(\alpha = 0.1\). (With step \(\tfrac{1}{n}\), the very first reward would replace the 5 completely, so each arm would be tried only once. In our Python check that version reached only 69.2% optimal.)

🌈 Interactive: optimistic initial values

What to notice

  • The early spike. For the first 10 pulls the optimistic agent tries the 10 arms one after another, so it picks the best arm only about 10% of the time. At step 11 it returns to the arm whose estimate fell the least, often the best one, and jumps to 41.3% optimal. The next pulls wobble as the optimism wears off.
  • Then it beats ε-greedy. Over the last 100 steps it picks the best arm 85.9% of the time (reward 1.495), without ever acting randomly.
  • Turn the dial. With \(Q_1 = 0\) it is just the greedy agent again (with α = 0.1). Bigger values explore for longer before settling.
  • The catch: optimism only drives exploration at the start. If the arms change later, the agent has no reason to explore again.

docs.title: Step 6 — Upper confidence bounds (UCB): explore where you are unsure
docs.text:
ε-greedy explores blindly: when it explores, a hopeless arm it has tried 300 times is as likely as a promising arm it has tried twice. Smarter: explore the arms you are unsure about, because they might be better than they look.

Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) action selection gives each arm a bonus that is large when the arm has been tried rarely:

\[ a_t = \arg\max_a \left[\, Q_t(a) + c \sqrt{\frac{\ln t}{N_t(a)}} \,\right] \]
  • \(Q_t(a)\): what the arm seems to be worth (exploitation).
  • \(c\sqrt{\ln t / N_t(a)}\): an uncertainty bonus (exploration). It shrinks as you pull the arm more (\(N_t(a)\) grows) and grows slowly for arms you neglect (\(\ln t\) keeps rising).
  • \(c\): how optimistic to be. \(c = 0\) is plain greedy.
  • An arm never tried has \(N_t(a) = 0\) and an infinite bonus, so UCB tries every arm once first.

The idea is called optimism in the face of uncertainty: act as if each arm is as good as it plausibly could be. Either the arm really is good (you win), or it isn't and pulling it shrinks its bonus (you learn).

🎯 Interactive: watch UCB choose

What to notice

  • Bars shrink with pulls. After a few dozen steps, the arm you pull most has a short bar (you are sure about it), while rarely pulled arms keep tall bars.
  • Neglected arms come back. Watch an arm with a low estimate: its top slowly rises (the \(\ln t\) term) until it is checked again. UCB never stops exploring completely, but it explores less and less often.
  • c sets the balance. With \(c = 0\) the bars vanish and UCB is greedy. With \(c = 3\) it keeps re-checking bad arms for a long time.

On the testbed, UCB with \(c = 2\) picks the best arm 84.9% of the time over the last 100 steps (reward 1.479), and like the optimistic agent it jumps to 43.6% at step 11, right after its round of trying each arm once.

Thompson sampling: explore by sampling your beliefs

A third idea, from 1933 and very popular in industry: keep a belief about each arm's value, a probability distribution that is wide when you have few pulls and narrow when you have many. Each step, draw one random sample from each arm's belief and pull the arm with the highest sample. An uncertain arm sometimes draws a high sample and gets tried; a well-known bad arm almost never does. As the beliefs narrow, the agent naturally shifts to exploiting.

In our testbed the belief for an arm is a normal distribution with mean \(\frac{\text{sum of rewards}}{N(a) + 1}\) and standard deviation \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N(a)+1}}\) (Bayes' rule, starting from the belief that values look like \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\)). It reaches 91.3% optimal over the last 100 steps. It has a head start here, because that starting belief matches exactly how the testbed creates its arms.

docs.title: Step 7 — Regret: the yardstick for exploration
docs.text:
How should we compare these agents? "Average reward at the end" ignores how much the agent lost while learning. The standard yardstick is regret: the reward you expect to lose compared with someone who knew the best arm \(a^*\) from the start.

\[ \text{Regret}_T = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \Big( q_*(a^*) - q_*(a_t) \Big) \]

Each step you pick the best arm costs nothing; each step you pick another arm costs the gap between their true values. Lower is better, and zero is impossible (you have to try arms to learn which is best).

How regret grows tells you the most:

  • Greedy: if it locks onto the wrong arm, it pays the same gap every step forever. Regret grows linearly in \(T\).
  • ε-greedy (fixed ε): it keeps exploring at the same rate forever, so it also grows linearly, just with a smaller slope.
  • UCB and Thompson sampling: they explore less and less as they become sure, so regret grows only like \(\log T\). A classic result by Lai and Robbins (1985) shows that, up to a constant, \(\log T\) is the best any method can do.
🏁 Interactive: every method, measured by regret

What to notice

  • Total regret after 1000 pulls (2000 runs, seed 1): greedy 535.1, ε-greedy 0.1 229.8, optimistic 242.3, UCB (c = 2) 148.2, Thompson 69.7. For scale, a perfect agent would collect about 1532 in total.
  • Look at the slopes on the right. Greedy and ε-greedy keep climbing in a straight line: over the last 100 steps they still lose 0.527 and 0.169 per step. UCB and Thompson bend over and flatten: by then they lose only 0.050 and 0.017 per step.
  • Optimistic vs ε-greedy: the optimistic agent's early exploration is expensive (it loses 0.581 per step during steps 100–200, against 0.287 for ε-greedy), so its total regret ends slightly higher. But its curve flattens (0.036 per step at the end), so it would pull ahead in a longer run.
  • Tune c. Set UCB's \(c\) to 1: its regret drops to 59.1 and it picks the best arm 91.7% of the time. The best knob setting depends on the problem, which is why theory-backed defaults matter.
  • Change the seed or the number of runs. With 200 runs the curves get noisier, but the ranking stays the same (we checked seeds 2, 3 and 7 in Python).

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Every bandit agent is the same loop. They differ only in one box: how to choose the arm.

Method How it explores Knob Regret on our testbed (1000 pulls) Greedy never none 535.1 ε-greedy at random, at a fixed rate ε 229.8 (ε = 0.1) Optimistic greedy every arm looks great until tried starting value \(Q_1\) 242.3 (\(Q_1 = 5\)) UCB arms with few pulls get a bonus c 148.2 (c = 2) Thompson sampling sample from beliefs, pick the best sample prior belief 69.7

Here is the whole testbed in numpy. To keep it fast it plays all 2000 bandits at once: each row of Q is one bandit.

import numpy as np


def run_testbed(choose, runs=2000, steps=1000, k=10, q0=0.0, alpha=None, seed=0):
    """Play `runs` random k-armed bandits at once (one per row). Returns % optimal and total regret."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    q_star = rng.normal(0, 1, (runs, k))            # true action values, hidden from the agent
    best = q_star.argmax(axis=1)
    Q = np.full((runs, k), q0)                       # estimates
    N = np.zeros((runs, k))                          # how often each arm was pulled
    rows = np.arange(runs)
    optimal, regret = [], 0.0
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        a = choose(Q, N, t, rng)                     # 1. pick an arm in every run
        r = rng.normal(q_star[rows, a], 1)           # 2. pull it: noisy reward
        N[rows, a] += 1                              # 3. update the estimate:
        step = alpha if alpha else 1 / N[rows, a]    #    new = old + step × (reward − old)
        Q[rows, a] += step * (r - Q[rows, a])
        optimal.append(np.mean(a == best))
        regret += np.mean(q_star[rows, best] - q_star[rows, a])
    return 100 * np.mean(optimal[-100:]), regret


def argmax_random_ties(values, rng):
    noise = rng.random(values.shape) * 1e-9          # tiny noise breaks ties at random
    return np.argmax(values + noise, axis=1)


def epsilon_greedy(eps):
    def choose(Q, N, t, rng):
        greedy = argmax_random_ties(Q, rng)
        random = rng.integers(0, Q.shape[1], len(Q))
        return np.where(rng.random(len(Q)) < eps, random, greedy)
    return choose


def ucb(c):
    def choose(Q, N, t, rng):
        tried = N > 0
        bonus = np.where(tried, c * np.sqrt(np.log(t) / np.maximum(N, 1)), np.inf)  # untried arms first
        return argmax_random_ties(Q + bonus, rng)
    return choose


for name, kwargs in [("greedy", dict(choose=epsilon_greedy(0.0))),
                     ("ε-greedy 0.01", dict(choose=epsilon_greedy(0.01))),
                     ("ε-greedy 0.1", dict(choose=epsilon_greedy(0.1))),
                     ("optimistic Q0=5", dict(choose=epsilon_greedy(0.0), q0=5.0, alpha=0.1)),
                     ("UCB c=2", dict(choose=ucb(2.0)))]:
    pct, regret = run_testbed(**kwargs)
    print(f"{name:16s} optimal action (last 100 steps) {pct:5.1f}%   total regret {regret:6.1f}")

greedy           optimal action (last 100 steps)  34.7%   total regret  521.5
ε-greedy 0.01    optimal action (last 100 steps)  58.4%   total regret  357.8
ε-greedy 0.1     optimal action (last 100 steps)  80.0%   total regret  233.4
optimistic Q0=5  optimal action (last 100 steps)  85.6%   total regret  240.9
UCB c=2          optimal action (last 100 steps)  85.4%   total regret  148.3

The numbers differ a little from the widgets because numpy draws different random bandits, but the ranking and the sizes are the same.

From bandits to full reinforcement learning

  • In a contextual bandit, the agent also sees a context before choosing (the user's profile, the patient's symptoms), and the best arm depends on it. This is how most real recommendation and ad systems work.
  • In full RL, the action also changes what happens next: the next state, and so the future rewards. Then "how good is this action" must include everything that follows. Describing that properly is the job of the next lesson, Markov decision processes and the Bellman equations.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"Exploration is wasted reward.\"

Exploration is an investment. Greedy never "wastes" a pull, yet it had by far the worst regret on the testbed (535.1, against 229.8 for ε = 0.1), because it never found the best arm in most runs.

\"More exploration is always safer.\"

Exploring costs reward every time. On the testbed, ε = 0.2 picked the best arm less often than ε = 0.1 (73.8% vs 80.0% over the last 100 steps) and had higher regret (352.6 vs 229.8), because it kept pulling arms it already knew were bad.

\"The arm with the highest average so far is the best arm.\"

Only if you have pulled every arm often enough. After a few pulls, averages are dominated by noise. That is exactly why UCB adds a bonus that depends on the number of pulls, not just the average.

\"UCB prefers risky arms.\"

UCB's bonus is about how little you know (few pulls), not about how variable an arm's payouts are. An arm with wildly varying rewards that you have pulled 500 times gets a small bonus.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. An arm's estimate is Q = 2.0 after 4 pulls. The 5th pull pays 4.5. What is the new sample-average estimate?

$Q \leftarrow 2.0 + \tfrac{1}{5}(4.5 - 2.0) = 2.0 + 0.5 = $ 2.5. (Check: the 4 earlier rewards sum to 8.0; \((8.0 + 4.5)/5 = 2.5\).)

2. With ε = 0.1 and 10 arms, what is the highest possible % of optimal actions, even with perfect estimates?

With probability 0.9 it acts greedily (the best arm, once the estimates are right). With probability 0.1 it picks a random arm, which is the best one with probability \(\tfrac{1}{10}\). Total: \(0.9 + 0.1 \times 0.1 = 0.91\), so 91%.

3. UCB with c = 2 at step t = 200. Arm A: Q = 1.0 after 100 pulls. Arm B: Q = 0.8 after 4 pulls. Which does it pick?

\(\ln 200 \approx 5.30\). Arm A: \(1.0 + 2\sqrt{5.30/100} \approx 1.0 + 0.46 = 1.46\). Arm B: \(0.8 + 2\sqrt{5.30/4} \approx 0.8 + 2.30 = 3.10\). UCB picks arm B: its estimate is lower, but it is so uncertain that it might well be better.

4. Why do optimistic initial values not help when the arms' values change over time?

Optimism makes the agent explore only at the beginning, until the inflated estimates have come down. After that the agent is plain greedy. If an arm later becomes better, nothing pushes the agent to try it again. ε-greedy (with a constant step size) or UCB keep exploring and can notice the change.

5. A clinical trial gives half the patients treatment A and half treatment B, then picks the winner. A bandit algorithm shifts patients towards the better-looking treatment as results arrive. Which has lower regret, and why?

Usually the bandit. The fixed 50/50 split keeps giving the worse treatment to half the patients until the trial ends, so its regret grows linearly during the trial. A bandit (UCB, Thompson) gives the worse treatment less and less often as the evidence accumulates. The price is that the final comparison is less balanced, which is why medical trials use bandits only with careful statistical design.

docs.text:
• Richard Sutton & Andrew Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed., free online), Chapter 2. The 10-armed testbed comes from here.
  • Tor Lattimore & Csaba Szepesvári, Bandit Algorithms (free online). The thorough, mathematical treatment, including regret bounds.
  • Daniel Russo et al., A Tutorial on Thompson Sampling (2018). Clear and practical.
  • Peter Auer, Nicolò Cesa-Bianchi & Paul Fischer, Finite-time Analysis of the Multiarmed Bandit Problem (2002). The paper that introduced UCB1.

docs.title: Offline RL and Imitation Learning
docs.text:
TL;DR

Sometimes trial and error is too dangerous or too expensive: you can't let a robot crash a car or let an algorithm experiment on patients. Instead you learn from a fixed dataset of what others did. Imitation learning copies an expert (behaviour cloning), but small mistakes snowball because the copy ends up in situations the expert never showed it; DAgger fixes this by asking the expert about the learner's own mistakes. Offline RL uses the rewards in the data to do better than the data, but plain Q-learning breaks offline: it trusts made-up values for actions nobody ever tried. The fix is pessimism: only trust what the data supports (BCQ, CQL, IQL).

Level: intermediate · Prerequisites: Q-learning & SARSA, Deep Q-Networks

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
Every RL method so far learns by trying things: an ε-greedy agent in the cliff world falls off the cliff hundreds of times before it learns not to. That is fine in a simulator. It is not fine when:

  • Healthcare: you want a policy for dosing fluids and vasopressors in sepsis. You cannot give random doses to see what happens. But hospitals have years of electronic health records showing what clinicians did and how patients fared.
  • Driving: you have millions of kilometres of human driving logs, but you cannot let a learning car explore by swerving into traffic.
  • Robotics: real robots are slow, break, and need a person to reset them. Logs of past runs and human tele-operation are cheap by comparison.

In all three cases there is a lot of logged data and very little room for new trial and error. This lesson is about squeezing a good policy out of that data, and about the traps that make it much harder than it looks.

A word of caution for clinical data

Learning treatment policies from records is an active research area (for example the "AI Clinician" for sepsis, see Further reading), and also a heavily debated one. Records hide things: doctors act on information that never made it into the data, so "patients who got drug X did worse" can simply mean "sicker patients got drug X". Everything in this lesson assumes the state you see contains what the decision-maker saw. In medicine that is rarely fully true, so treat any learned policy as a hypothesis to test carefully, not a treatment recommendation.

docs.title: Step 1 — Three ways to get experience: online, off-policy, offline
docs.text:
So far the agent has always been able to collect its own data. RL methods differ in how they use that data:

  • Online, on-policy (SARSA, policy gradients, PPO): act with the current policy, learn from what just happened, throw the experience away, repeat.
  • Off-policy (Q-learning, DQN): keep experience in a replay buffer and reuse it, even data collected by older versions of the policy. But the agent still keeps acting and adding fresh data.
  • Offline (also called batch RL): someone else, the behaviour policy \(\pi_\beta\), collected a dataset \(\mathcal{D} = \{(s, a, r, s')\}\) in the past. The learner gets that dataset and nothing else. It never acts in the environment until training is over.

There are two very different things you can do with a fixed dataset:

Imitation learning Offline RL Data needed states and the expert's actions \((s, a)\) states, actions and rewards \((s, a, r, s')\) Goal act like the expert act better than the data, if possible Main tool supervised learning Q-learning, made pessimistic

What to notice

Off-policy and offline sound alike, but the difference is huge. Q-learning is off-policy, yet in Step 5 you will see it fail badly offline. Off-policy learners can still try an action to find out that it is bad. Offline learners can't.

docs.title: Step 2 — Imitation learning: behaviour cloning is supervised learning
docs.text:
The simplest idea: you have recordings of an expert. In each recorded state \(s_i\) the expert took action \(a_i\). Treat this as an ordinary supervised learning problem: the state is the input, the expert's action is the label. This is behaviour cloning (BC).

For discrete actions, train a classifier \(\pi_\theta(a \mid s)\) with the usual cross-entropy loss. For continuous actions (a steering angle, a drug dose), train a regressor with squared error:

\[ \theta^* = \arg\max_\theta \sum_i \log \pi_\theta(a_i \mid s_i) \qquad\text{or}\qquad \theta^* = \arg\min_\theta \sum_i \big\| \pi_\theta(s_i) - a_i \big\|^2 \]

No rewards, no Bellman equation, no exploration. That is why BC is the first thing to try when you have expert data: it is just a neural network trained on labelled data, which you already know how to do. It has worked surprisingly well in practice, from NVIDIA's 2016 end-to-end car that learned to steer from 72 hours of human driving to modern robot manipulation policies trained on tele-operation data.

The running example for the next two steps is a car following a winding lane. The state is three numbers: how much the road bends here (\(\kappa\)), how far the car is from the lane centre (\(e\)), and how far its heading points away from the road (\(h\)). The expert steers with the bend and gently back towards the centre:

\[ a^{\text{expert}} = \kappa - 0.1\, e - 0.5\, h \]

We record one perfect drive by this expert and fit a linear policy \(a = w_1 \kappa + w_2 e + w_3 h\) to it by least squares. The fit is perfect: on the recorded states, the clone's action differs from the expert's by less than \(10^{-6}\). The training loss is essentially zero.

What to notice

"Zero training error" sounds like success. Hold on to that thought: in the next step this perfect student drives off the road in 94% of drives.

docs.title: Step 3 — Why copying drifts: compounding errors
docs.text:
Here is the catch. Look at the expert's recording: the expert drove perfectly, so \(e\) and \(h\) were always zero. The data shows how to follow the bend. It never shows what to do when you are off-centre, because the expert never was. The clone learns \(w = (1, 0, 0)\): "steer with the bend" and nothing else.

Now let the clone drive with a tiny bit of steering noise (a gust of wind, a bump, a small modelling error). After the first small mistake it is in a state the expert never visited. It has no idea how to recover, so it makes another error, which takes it even further from familiar territory, and so on.

Try it: the red line is the behaviour-cloned car, the green line is the expert, both with exactly the same random noise. The chart averages 200 drives.

🚗 Interactive: a perfect copy that drives off the road

What to notice

  • With the default noise (\(\sigma = 0.01\)), the expert stays within about 0.03 of the centre. The clone, with zero training error, is on average 0.55 off at \(t = 25\), 1.60 at \(t = 50\) and 4.69 at \(t = 100\), and leaves the lane in 94% of drives.
  • The error doesn't just grow, it speeds up: each doubling of time multiplies the offset by about 2.9. Mistakes compound.
  • Set \(\sigma = 0\). Now the clone is perfect too: with no mistakes, it never leaves the expert's states. The problem is not the copy itself but the distribution shift: at test time the learner visits states that were not in its training data.
  • Double the noise to \(\sigma = 0.02\) and the clone's offset at \(t = 100\) doubles to 9.37.

Why "errors grow like \(T^2\)"? A simple counting argument (Ross & Bagnell, 2010): suppose the learner makes a mistake with a small probability \(\varepsilon\) per step on the expert's states, and once it is off the expert's path it never gets back. The chance of being off-track by step \(t\) is \(1 - (1-\varepsilon)^t \approx \varepsilon t\). Adding these up over an episode of length \(T\):

\[ \text{expected steps off-track} \;=\; \sum_{t=1}^{T} \big(1 - (1-\varepsilon)^t\big) \;\approx\; \frac{\varepsilon\, T^2}{2} \]

With \(\varepsilon = 0.01\) and \(T = 100\) that is 37.2 bad steps; with \(T = 200\) it is 114.3. A learner that could recover after each mistake would only lose about \(\varepsilon T\) steps: 1.0 and 2.0. Supervised learning assumes that test inputs come from the same distribution as training inputs. In sequential decision-making, your own actions choose your next input, so that assumption breaks.

docs.title: Step 4 — DAgger: ask the expert about your own mistakes
docs.text:
If the problem is "the training data has no off-track states", the fix is to put them in. DAgger (Dataset Aggregation, Ross, Gordon & Bagnell, 2011) does exactly this:

  1. Train a policy on the expert's demonstrations (plain BC).
  2. Let the learner drive, and record the states it visits, including its mistakes.
  3. Ask the expert: "what would you have done here?" Label those states with the expert's actions.
  4. Add them to the dataset (keep everything old), retrain, and repeat.

The key change: the training states now come from the learner's own distribution, not the expert's. That gives the guarantee the counting argument wanted: mistakes cost about \(\varepsilon T\), not \(\varepsilon T^2\).

Try it: same road, same noise, now with a DAgger learner (orange). Each DAgger round adds 5 drives by the learner, labelled by the expert.

🧑‍🏫 Interactive: behaviour cloning vs DAgger

What to notice

  • After one round, DAgger learns the weights \((1.00, -0.10, -0.50)\): exactly the expert's rule, including how to steer back. Its average offset at \(t = 100\) is 0.03 and it leaves the lane in 0% of drives, like the expert.
  • Set DAgger rounds to 0: the orange line becomes the red one. DAgger starts as behaviour cloning.
  • One round is enough here because the learner (a linear rule) can represent the expert exactly. Real policies are neural networks that can't, and usually need several rounds.
  • Set \(\sigma = 0\) and look at the DAgger weights: with no mistakes there are no off-track states to learn from, so the offset and heading weights are poorly pinned down. DAgger needs the learner's mistakes to learn from them.

The catch: DAgger needs an expert you can query on new states. A driving instructor in the passenger seat, a slow planning algorithm, or a simulator with a known-good controller can do this. A ten-year-old hospital database cannot: nobody can go back and ask what the doctor would have done for a patient state that never happened. Practical workarounds include adding noise to the expert's demonstrations so they contain small recoveries (the DART idea) and training on lots of diverse data.

docs.title: Step 5 — Offline RL, and why plain Q-learning breaks
docs.text:
Imitation learning has a ceiling: at best it is as good as the expert. Often the data is not expert data. Hospital records mix good and bad decisions; driving logs mix careful and careless drivers. If the data also contains rewards (patient survived, trip completed safely), we could hope to do better than the average decision in the data: keep the good choices, avoid the bad ones. That is offline RL.

The obvious first attempt: Q-learning is off-policy, so just run it on the fixed dataset. Sweep over the logged transitions again and again with the familiar update:

\[ Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha \Big[\, r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a) \Big] \]

Look at the \(\max_{a'}\). It considers every action in the next state, including actions that never appear in the data. Their \(Q\)-values were never trained. In a table they keep whatever value they started with; in a neural network they are whatever the network happens to extrapolate. Either way, nothing in the data ever corrects them. And because the max seeks out the largest value, it picks exactly these made-up numbers whenever they are too high. This is called extrapolation error, and the result is overestimation: the agent believes unseen actions are wonderful.

Online, this would fix itself: the agent would try the "wonderful" action, get a bad reward, and update. Offline, it never gets the chance.

Try it: this is the cliff world from lesson 1 (no slipping, \(\gamma = 0.95\)). The data was logged by someone following the safe detour policy, who takes a random action a fraction \(\varepsilon\) of the time. Naive Q-learning sweeps that dataset 200 times. The blue wedges show which actions appear in the data.

🗄️ Interactive: naive Q-learning on a fixed dataset

What to notice

  • The agent is confidently wrong. With the default data (ε = 0.1, 20 episodes, 239 transitions), the data covers only 26 of the 72 state-action pairs. In the start cell the data shows only "up" and "left", each worth \(-1.0\) (one step cost). "Right" and "down" were never tried and keep their starting guess of 0, which looks better. So the agent believes \(V(\text{start}) = 0.00\), picks "right", and really gets \(-20.00\): straight off the cliff.
  • Red arrows are actions the agent has never seen in the data, chosen because nothing ever corrected their values.
  • Set ε = 0 (the logger always follows the detour): only 11 of 72 pairs are covered, and the result is the same cliff dive. The logging policy itself is worth \(-2.04\), so the "learned" policy is far worse than simply copying the data.
  • Now give it coverage: ε = 0.5 and 100 episodes (71 of 72 pairs). Naive Q-learning now finds the best route along the cliff edge and gets \(2.05\), the optimal value. Offline Q-learning is fine when the data covers the actions it wants to take. The trouble is that real datasets almost never do.

Why this is worse with neural networks

In a table, an unseen action keeps one stale value. A deep Q-network (lesson 7) is trained on the dataset's actions, and its outputs for other actions are an unconstrained extrapolation. Some of those extrapolations are too high by chance, the max picks them, and bootstrapping copies the inflated value backwards to earlier states. In practice offline DQN's value estimates can grow without limit while the actual policy gets worse.

docs.title: Step 6 — The fix: be pessimistic about what you have not seen
docs.text:
All modern offline RL methods share one principle: don't trust values for actions the data doesn't support. They differ in how they enforce it.

1. Stay close to the data (policy constraints, e.g. BCQ). Batch-Constrained Q-learning (Fujimoto, Meger & Precup, 2019) only allows the max to look at actions that the behaviour policy would plausibly take. In a table this is easy: take the max only over actions that appear in the data,

\[ r + \gamma \max_{a' \,:\, (s', a') \in \mathcal{D}} Q(s', a'). \]

With neural networks, BCQ trains a generative model of the data's actions and only considers actions it would produce. Related methods (BEAR, TD3+BC) add a penalty that keeps the learned policy close to the data's actions.

2. Push unseen values down (pessimism, e.g. CQL). Conservative Q-Learning (Kumar et al., 2020) keeps the network free, but adds a term to the loss that pushes \(Q\) down on all actions (mostly on the ones it currently rates highly) and up on the actions that are actually in the data:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{CQL}}(\theta) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{(s,a,r,s') \sim \mathcal{D}}\Big[\big(Q_\theta(s,a) - y\big)^2\Big]}_{\text{the usual TD loss}} \;+\; \lambda \, \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathcal{D}}\Big[\, \underbrace{\log \sum_{a} e^{Q_\theta(s,a)}}_{\text{push all actions down}} \;-\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \mathcal{D}}\, Q_\theta(s,a)}_{\text{push data actions up}} \Big] \]

The net effect: an action the data never shows gets pushed down until it no longer wins the max. The learned values become a lower bound on the true values, so when the agent is wrong, it errs on the side of caution.

3. Never ask about unseen actions at all (IQL). Implicit Q-Learning (Kostrikov, Nair & Levine, 2021) avoids the max entirely. It learns \(Q\) only on the dataset's own actions, estimates "how good is the best action the data shows here" with a trick called expectile regression, and then extracts a policy by weighted behaviour cloning: copy the data's actions, but copy the ones with a high advantage \(Q(s,a) - V(s)\) much more strongly. It is simple, stable, and a common default today.

Our widget uses a tabular version of the same idea, a pessimistic Q-learning: actions that never appear in the data get value \(-\infty\) (so they are never chosen), and actions seen only a few times pay a penalty \(\beta / \sqrt{n(s,a)}\), where \(n(s,a)\) is how often they appear. The fewer times we have seen something, the less we trust it. (The \(-\infty\) part is BCQ's constraint; the penalty is CQL's spirit, in its simplest form.)

Try it: switch between the three learners on the same dataset.

🛡️ Interactive: naive vs pessimistic offline learning

What to notice

  • On the default data (ε = 0.1, 20 episodes), pessimistic Q-learning follows the detour to the goal and really gets \(-2.04\). It believes \(V(\text{start}) = -3.00\): a little lower than the truth, which is exactly the point of pessimism. No red arrows: it never picks an action it hasn't seen.
  • Naive Q-learning on the same data believes \(0.00\) and gets \(-20.00\). Same data, same algorithm family; the only change is refusing to trust the unknown.
  • Pessimism also helps when the data is good. With ε = 0.5 and 100 episodes, pessimistic Q-learning finds the optimal edge route (\(2.05\)), even though the logging policy itself is only worth \(-12.57\). It stitches together the good pieces of many imperfect episodes.
  • Pessimism is not magic. With ε = 1 (purely random logging) and only 20 episodes, the data is mostly aimless wandering and every learner fails: naive \(-19.88\), pessimistic \(-20.00\), behaviour cloning \(-19.88\). No algorithm can find a good route the data never shows.

docs.title: Step 7 — Behaviour cloning or offline RL?
docs.text:
Use the third button in the widget above, Behaviour cloning (in each cell, copy the most common action in the data):

Logged data Logging policy is worth Behaviour cloning Pessimistic Q-learning expert-like: ε = 0, 20 episodes \(-2.04\) \(-2.04\) \(-2.04\) mostly good: ε = 0.1, 20 episodes \(-3.70\) \(-2.04\) \(-2.04\) mixed: ε = 0.5, 100 episodes \(-12.57\) \(-2.04\) \(2.05\) random: ε = 1, 100 episodes \(-19.88\) \(-19.88\) \(2.05\)

The pattern matches what researchers find on real benchmarks:

  • Expert (or near-expert) data → behaviour cloning. It is simple and stable, and needs no rewards. Offline RL can't beat the expert's actions if those are the only actions in the data, and its extra machinery adds ways to go wrong. In the clean-data rows, BC already gets everything there is to get.
  • Mixed-quality data with rewards → offline RL. BC faithfully copies the average behaviour, mistakes included (it even filters out some noise by taking the most common action, which is why it beats the logging policy). Offline RL uses the rewards to tell good decisions from bad ones and can beat every policy in the data, as in the last two rows.
  • In between there are hybrids: filtered BC (clone only the best episodes), advantage-weighted BC (IQL's last step), and TD3+BC (Q-learning plus a BC term).

And whatever you train, evaluate before you deploy. Offline, you can't simply run the policy to see how good it is. Off-policy evaluation (OPE) methods estimate a new policy's value from the logged data, using importance sampling or a learned Q-function, but they are noisy and share the same blind spots as the data. In healthcare, the realistic path is: offline RL → off-policy evaluation → clinician review → a prospective, carefully monitored study.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Here is behaviour cloning and DAgger on the lane-following task, in NumPy. The learner is a linear policy fitted with least squares:

import numpy as np

T, K1, K2 = 100, 0.1, 0.5
kappa = 0.03 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * np.arange(T) / 60)     # how much the road bends at each step


def expert(k, e, h):                     # steer with the bend, and back towards the lane centre
    return k - K1 * e - K2 * h


def drive(policy, sigma, rng):
    """Drive one lap. e = distance from the lane centre, h = heading error."""
    e = h = 0.0
    states, offsets = [], []
    for t in range(T):
        states.append((kappa[t], e, h))
        a = policy(kappa[t], e, h)
        h += a - kappa[t] + sigma * rng.normal()          # steering noise: small mistakes
        e += h
        offsets.append(abs(e))
    return states, offsets


def fit(states):                                           # supervised learning: state -> expert action
    X = np.array(states)
    y = np.array([expert(*s) for s in states])
    w = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
    return lambda k, e, h: w @ (k, e, h), w


rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
sigma = 0.01

# Behaviour cloning: copy a perfect demonstration
demo, _ = drive(expert, 0.0, rng)
bc, w_bc = fit(demo)

# DAgger: let the learner drive, ask the expert what it should have done, retrain on everything
data, dagger, w_dag = list(demo), bc, w_bc
for round_ in range(3):
    for _ in range(5):
        visited, _ = drive(dagger, sigma, rng)
        data += visited
    dagger, w_dag = fit(data)

for name, pol, w in [("BC", bc, w_bc), ("DAgger", dagger, w_dag)]:
    runs = np.array([drive(pol, sigma, rng)[1] for _ in range(200)])
    print(f"{name:6s} weights (bend, offset, heading) = {np.round(w, 3)}   "
          f"mean |offset| at t=100: {runs[:, -1].mean():.2f}   left the lane: {(runs.max(1) > 1).mean():.0%}")

BC     weights (bend, offset, heading) = [1. 0. 0.]   mean |offset| at t=100: 4.82   left the lane: 95%
DAgger weights (bend, offset, heading) = [ 1.  -0.1 -0.5]   mean |offset| at t=100: 0.03   left the lane: 0%

(The random noise differs from the widget's, so the numbers differ slightly: 4.82 and 95% here, 4.69 and 94% in the widget.)

And here is offline learning on the cliff world: a logged dataset, naive Q-learning, the pessimistic version from Step 6, and behaviour cloning, each evaluated by actually running its greedy policy:

import numpy as np

MAP = ["......",
       "..#...",
       "......",
       "SCCCCG"]
MOVES = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]                  # up, right, down, left
SAFE = ["→→→→→↓",                                           # the "safe detour" policy from lesson 1
        "↑↑.↑↑↓",
        "↑↑←↑↑↓",
        "↑....."]
GAMMA = 0.95


def step(s, a):
    r, c = s[0] + MOVES[a][0], s[1] + MOVES[a][1]
    if not (0 <= r < 4 and 0 <= c < 6) or MAP[r][c] == "#":
        r, c = s                                            # bumped into a wall or edge
    tile = MAP[r][c]
    return (r, c), {"G": 10, "C": -20}.get(tile, -1), tile in "GC"


def log_data(eps, episodes, rng):
    """Someone else's behaviour: the safe detour, with a random action a fraction eps of the time."""
    data = []
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s = (3, 0)
        for t in range(100):
            a = rng.integers(4) if rng.random() < eps else "↑→↓←".index(SAFE[s[0]][s[1]])
            s2, r, done = step(s, a)
            data.append((s, a, r, s2, done))
            s = s2
            if done:
                break
    return data


def offline_q_learning(data, pessimism=None, epochs=200, lr=0.5):
    n = np.zeros((4, 6, 4))                                 # how often each (s, a) appears in the data
    for s, a, *_ in data:
        n[s][a] += 1
    if pessimism is None:
        Q = np.zeros((4, 6, 4))                             # naive: unseen actions keep the guess 0
    else:
        Q = np.where(n > 0, 0.0, -np.inf)                   # pessimistic: never trust an unseen action
    for _ in range(epochs):                                 # sweep the SAME fixed dataset again and again
        for s, a, r, s2, done in data:
            nxt = 0.0 if done else Q[s2].max()
            if nxt == -np.inf:
                nxt = 0.0                                   # s2 never left in the data (cut-off episode)
            penalty = 0.0 if pessimism is None else pessimism / np.sqrt(n[s][a])
            Q[s][a] += lr * (r - penalty + GAMMA * nxt - Q[s][a])
    return Q


def behaviour_cloning(data):
    counts = np.zeros((4, 6, 4))
    for s, a, *_ in data:
        counts[s][a] += 1
    return counts                                           # act = most common action in each state


def evaluate(table):                                        # run the greedy policy once in the real world
    s, G, disc = (3, 0), 0.0, 1.0
    for t in range(100):
        s, r, done = step(s, int(np.argmax(table[s])))
        G += disc * r
        disc *= GAMMA
        if done:
            break
    return G


rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for eps, episodes in [(0.1, 20), (0.5, 100)]:
    data = log_data(eps, episodes, rng)
    naive = offline_q_learning(data)
    pess = offline_q_learning(data, pessimism=0.5)
    print(f"data: eps={eps}, {episodes} episodes, {len(data)} transitions")
    print(f"  naive Q-learning   believes {naive[3, 0].max():6.2f}   really gets {evaluate(naive):6.2f}")
    print(f"  pessimistic        believes {pess[3, 0].max():6.2f}   really gets {evaluate(pess):6.2f}")
    print(f"  behaviour cloning                     really gets {evaluate(behaviour_cloning(data)):6.2f}")

data: eps=0.1, 20 episodes, 261 transitions
  naive Q-learning   believes   0.00   really gets -20.00
  pessimistic        believes  -2.99   really gets  -2.04
  behaviour cloning                     really gets  -2.04
data: eps=0.5, 100 episodes, 2049 transitions
  naive Q-learning   believes   2.05   really gets   2.05
  pessimistic        believes   0.53   really gets   2.05
  behaviour cloning                     really gets  -2.04

The pessimistic learner's beliefs are always below what it really gets (\(-2.99\) vs \(-2.04\), \(0.53\) vs \(2.05\)). The naive learner's belief of \(0.00\) hides a cliff dive. When you can't test a policy before deploying it, an under-estimate is a much safer mistake than an over-estimate.

For real problems, libraries such as d3rlpy and CORL implement BC, CQL, IQL and friends, and Minari (the successor of D4RL) provides standard offline datasets.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"Q-learning is off-policy, so it works on any fixed dataset.\"

Off-policy means it can learn from data collected by another policy, as long as it can keep collecting. Offline, the max in the target picks up values for actions the data never shows, and nothing ever corrects them. In the widget, naive Q-learning believes the start is worth 0.00 and walks off the cliff.

\"If behaviour cloning fits the expert data perfectly, it will behave like the expert.\"

The fit is only measured on the expert's states. The clone's own small mistakes take it to states the expert never visited, where it has no idea what to do, and the errors compound. Our clone had essentially zero training error and still left the lane in 94% of drives.

\"Offline RL can learn any policy if you have enough data.\"

It can only learn about actions the data contains. A million records of a single treatment protocol say nothing about the alternative. Coverage matters more than size: in the widget, 100 episodes of the plain detour cover just 11 of 72 state-action pairs.

\"Pessimism just makes the agent copy the data.\"

It only stops the agent from relying on actions the data doesn't support. Among the supported ones it still picks the best, so it can combine good pieces of different episodes and beat the logging policy (\(2.05\) vs \(-12.57\) in the mixed-data example).

\"A policy learned from hospital records tells us the best treatment.\"

Only if the records capture everything the clinicians based their decisions on, and the reward really measures what matters to patients. Hidden confounders, missing data and rare actions can make an offline policy look good on paper and be harmful in practice. It is a hypothesis to test, not a recommendation.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between off-policy and offline RL?

An off-policy learner (Q-learning, DQN) can learn from data collected by a different policy, but it keeps interacting with the environment and adding new data. An offline learner gets one fixed dataset and never interacts during training, so it can never test what happens when it tries an action the data doesn't show.

2. Why does behaviour cloning suffer from compounding errors, and why does DAgger help?

BC is trained only on the states the expert visited. A small mistake moves the learner to a state outside that distribution, where its actions are unreliable, so it makes more mistakes and drifts further: errors can add up to roughly \(\varepsilon T^2\) over an episode. DAgger runs the learner, has the expert label the states the learner actually visits, and retrains on them, so the learner learns how to recover. Errors then grow only like \(\varepsilon T\).

3. In the offline cliff-world widget, why does naive Q-learning pick \"right\" from the start cell?

In the default dataset, the start cell only shows "up" (the detour) and, once, "left". Both cost a −1 step, so their learned values are negative. "Right" and "down" never appear, so their values stay at the starting guess of 0, which is higher. The max picks "right" for a value that nothing ever checked, and "right" leads straight into the cliff (−20).

4. How does CQL prevent the problem in question 3?

It adds a term to the loss that pushes Q-values down for all actions (weighted towards the ones currently rated highest) and up for actions that actually appear in the data. Unseen actions only ever get pushed down, so they stop winning the max, and the learned values become a lower bound on the true ones. The widget's pessimistic learner gets the same effect in a table by giving unseen actions \(-\infty\) and penalising rarely seen ones.

5. You have ICU records from many clinicians with very different habits, and a recorded outcome for each patient. Behaviour cloning or offline RL? What would make you cautious?

The data is mixed quality and has rewards (outcomes), so offline RL with pessimism (CQL, IQL) is the natural choice: BC would copy the average habit, good and bad. Reasons for caution: unrecorded information that influenced treatment (confounding), treatments that were rarely or never given in some situations (poor coverage), whether the outcome is the right reward, and the difficulty of evaluating the policy without trying it. Any result needs off-policy evaluation, clinical review and a careful prospective study before it touches patients.
