docs.title: Policy Gradients and REINFORCE
docs.text:
TL;DR

Instead of learning how good each action is and then picking the best one, a policy-gradient method learns the policy itself: a network with weights \(\theta\) that outputs action probabilities \(\pi_\theta(a \mid s)\). It plays episodes and then nudges \(\theta\) by gradient ascent so that actions followed by a high return become more likely, and actions followed by a low return become less likely. REINFORCE is the simplest version. Subtracting a baseline (the return you expected anyway) keeps it correct and makes it far less noisy.

Level: intermediate · Prerequisites: Deep Q-Networks, Gradient Descent

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
Value-based methods like Q-learning and DQN answer "how good is each action?" and then act greedily. That works brilliantly for Atari, where there are a handful of buttons. But:

  • A robot arm has continuous actions (a torque for every joint). You can't take an \(\arg\max\) over infinitely many actions at every step.
  • Sometimes the best policy is random. In rock–paper–scissors any predictable strategy loses. Greedy action selection can only ever produce deterministic policies.
  • RLHF fine-tunes language models with policy gradients. The "policy" is the chatbot, the "action" is the next word, and PPO (the next lesson) is a policy-gradient method. Everything in that pipeline starts with the idea in this lesson.

Policy gradients are the foundation of almost every modern deep-RL algorithm for control and for language models: A2C, PPO, SAC, and the RL step of RLHF.

docs.title: Step 1 — Why learn the policy directly?
docs.text:
Recall from lesson 1 that a policy can be deterministic (one action per state) or stochastic (a probability for each action). A value-based agent like DQN learns \(Q(s, a)\) and then picks \(\arg\max_a Q(s, a)\), plus some \(\varepsilon\)-greedy randomness for exploration. Its policy is a by-product of the values.

A policy-based agent skips the middleman. It has a policy with adjustable knobs and tunes those knobs directly to get more reward.

Value-based (Q-learning, DQN) Policy-based (REINFORCE) What is learned \(Q(s,a)\), then act greedily \(\pi_\theta(a \mid s)\) directly Kind of policy deterministic (+ ε for exploring) naturally stochastic Continuous actions hard: needs \(\arg\max\) over all actions easy: output a distribution (e.g. a Gaussian) Small change in parameters can flip the \(\arg\max\) and change behaviour abruptly changes probabilities smoothly Data can reuse old experience (replay buffer) needs fresh episodes from the current policy

Here is a tiny world where the value-based approach gets stuck. In Sutton & Barto's short corridor, every step costs −1 and the episode ends at the goal on the right. The catch: in the second cell the actions are reversed ("right" moves left), and the agent can't tell the cells apart (it sees the same observation in all three). So its only choice is one number: \(p\), the probability of pressing "right".

Try it: drag \(p\) and watch the value \(J(p)\) of the policy (the average total reward from the start). Play a few episodes at different \(p\).

🚪 Interactive: the short corridor, where the best policy is random

What to notice

  • Both deterministic policies fail forever. Always "right" bounces between the first two cells; always "left" never leaves the start. \(J = -\infty\).
  • ε-greedy is not much better. With \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and two actions, the greedy action gets probability 0.95. That gives \(J = -82.1\) (greedy = left) or \(J = -44.2\) (greedy = right).
  • The best policy flips a biased coin: \(p = 2 - \sqrt{2} \approx 0.59\), worth \(J \approx -11.66\). Only a method that can learn probabilities can find it.
  • The purple curve is smooth. If we could compute its slope, we could simply climb it. That is exactly what a policy gradient does.
Where does the curve come from?

Write \(V_0, V_1, V_2\) for the values of the three cells under the policy. Each is "−1 for this step, plus the value of where you land": \(V_0 = -1 + pV_1 + (1-p)V_0\), \(\;V_1 = -1 + pV_0 + (1-p)V_2\), \(\;V_2 = -1 + (1-p)V_1\) (the goal is worth 0). Solving these three equations gives

\[J(p) = V_0 = -\frac{2(2-p)}{p(1-p)},\]

which is largest at \(p = 2-\sqrt{2}\), where \(J = -(6+4\sqrt{2}) \approx -11.66\). We checked this by solving the equations numerically on a fine grid of \(p\) values: the best grid point is \(p = 0.58579\) with \(J = -11.6569\).

docs.title: Step 2 — A policy with knobs
docs.text:
A parameterised policy is a function with weights \(\theta\) that takes a state and returns a probability for every action. For discrete actions the standard recipe is:

  1. A network (any network) turns the state into one score per action, called an action preference \(h_\theta(s, a)\).
  2. A softmax turns the scores into probabilities:
\[ \pi_\theta(a \mid s) = \frac{e^{h_\theta(s,a)}}{\sum_{b} e^{h_\theta(s,b)}} \]

Higher preference → higher probability, all probabilities are positive, and they add up to 1. The agent then samples its action from these probabilities, so it explores automatically.

For continuous actions (a torque, a steering angle) the network instead outputs the mean \(\mu_\theta(s)\) (and often the spread \(\sigma\)) of a Gaussian, and the action is sampled from it: \(a \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_\theta(s), \sigma^2)\). Everything below works the same way; only the formula for \(\ln \pi\) changes.

What to notice

  • The policy is stochastic by design: even with fixed \(\theta\), the same state can lead to different actions. Exploration is built in, no \(\varepsilon\) needed.
  • The probabilities are a smooth function of \(\theta\). That is what will let us use gradients.
  • In the short corridor, the "network" is just two numbers, \(h(\text{right})\) and \(h(\text{left})\), and \(p = \pi(\text{right})\) is their softmax.

docs.title: Step 3 — The goal: climb the expected return
docs.text:
We want the policy whose episodes collect the most reward on average. So the objective is the expected return from the start:

\[ J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}\left[\, G_0 \,\right] \]

This is the value of the start state, \(V^{\pi_\theta}(s_0)\), seen as a function of the weights. In the short corridor it was the purple curve in Step 1.

To make \(J\) bigger, use the update from the Gradient Descent lesson with the sign flipped. This is gradient ascent: walk uphill.

\[ \theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha\, \nabla_\theta J(\theta) \]

The problem: how do we compute \(\nabla_\theta J\)? \(J\) depends on \(\theta\) through the actions the policy picks, and on the environment through what happens next. We don't know the environment's rules (they might be a physics engine or the real world), so we can't differentiate through them. We can only play episodes and look at the returns. The next step shows that this is enough.

docs.title: Step 4 — The policy gradient: make good actions more likely
docs.text:
Here is the key result, the policy gradient theorem:

\[ abla_ heta J( heta) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_ heta}\left[\, \sum_{t} G_t \, abla_ heta \ln \pi_ heta(a_t \mid s_t) ight] \]

Read it in words, piece by piece:

  • \( abla_ heta \ln \pi_ heta(a_t \mid s_t)\) is the direction in weight space that makes the action we actually took, \(a_t\), more likely in state \(s_t\).
  • \(G_t\) is the return that followed that action: how well things went from then on.
  • So the gradient says: push up the log-probability of each action in proportion to the return that followed it. Good outcome: take a big step towards repeating it. Bad outcome: a smaller step, or (if \(G_t\) is negative) a step away from it.
  • The expectation means we can estimate it by sampling: play an episode with the current policy and compute the sum. No model of the environment needed.

Why the log? The log-derivative trick: \( abla_ heta \pi = \pi\, abla_ heta \ln \pi\). Dividing by \(\pi\) means that actions the policy already picks often (which therefore show up often in our samples) don't get an unfair head start; rare actions that turn out well get a bigger push per sample.

For a softmax policy the gradient with respect to the preferences is very simple:

\[ rac{\partial \ln \pi(a \mid s)}{\partial h(s, b)} = \mathbb{1}[a = b] - \pi(b \mid s) \]

The sampled action's preference goes up by \(1 - \pi(a)\); every other action's goes down by its probability. Example: \(\pi = (0.2, 0.5, 0.3)\), we sampled the middle action and got return \(G = +2\), with \(\alpha = 0.1\). The update is \(\Delta h = 0.1 \cdot 2 \cdot (-0.2,\, 0.5,\, -0.3) = (-0.04,\, +0.10,\, -0.06)\). (PyTorch's autograd gives the same gradient, \((-0.2, 0.5, -0.3)\).)

Where does the theorem come from? (a short derivation)

Write \( au = (s_0, a_0, r_1, s_1, a_1, \dots)\) for a whole episode and \(R( au)\) for its return. Then \(J( heta) = \sum_ au P_ heta( au)\, R( au)\), and

\[ abla_ heta J = \sum_ au abla_ heta P_ heta( au)\, R( au) = \sum_ au P_ heta( au)\, abla_ heta \ln P_ heta( au)\, R( au) = \mathbb{E}\left[ R( au)\, abla_ heta \ln P_ heta( au) ight]. \]

The probability of an episode is a product: start state × policy choices × environment transitions, so its log is a sum:

\[ \ln P_ heta( au) = \ln p(s_0) + \sum_t \Big[ \ln \pi_ heta(a_t \mid s_t) + \ln p(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t) \Big]. \]

Only the policy terms depend on \( heta\), so the unknown environment drops out of the gradient. Finally, an action can't affect rewards that came before it, so \(R( au)\) can be replaced by the reward-to-go \(G_t\) for each term (this removes noise without changing the expectation). With discounting, the exact theorem has an extra factor \(\gamma^t\); practical code almost always drops it.

Try it: here is a softmax policy over three actions (a one-state problem, like a bandit). Each action pays its mean reward plus a little noise, so every reward is positive (around 4 to 6). Press Sample an action & update a few times and read the update in the readout. Then run 100 updates.

🎰 Interactive: a REINFORCE update, one sample at a time

What to notice

  • One update, by hand. On run 1 the first sample is B with reward 6.60. All three probabilities start at \( frac13\), so the update is \(\Delta h = 0.1 \cdot 6.60 \cdot (- frac13, frac23, - frac13) = (-0.220, +0.440, -0.220)\): B goes up, the others go down.
  • Without a baseline, every sampled action is reinforced, because every reward is positive. Learning still works on average (better actions get pushed harder), but it is a lottery. Click New run (run 2) and then Run 100 updates: the policy settles on C, not the best action B (\(\pi(C) = 0.89\)).
  • Now tick subtract a baseline (it replays the same run). The weight becomes \(r - b\): positive for better-than-average rewards, negative for worse ones. Run 100 updates again: run 2 now ends with \(\pi(B) = 0.92\).
  • Test 1000 runs at \(\alpha = 0.1\): \(\pi(B)\) ends above 0.5 in 68.9% of runs without a baseline and 99.8% with one. Step 6 explains why.

docs.title: Step 5 — REINFORCE: the algorithm
docs.text:
REINFORCE (Williams, 1992) turns the theorem into an algorithm. It is a Monte Carlo method, like the Monte Carlo prediction from the earlier lessons: it waits until the episode is over, so that every return \(G_t\) is known exactly, and then updates.

REINFORCE

Repeat for many episodes:

  1. Play one episode with the current policy \(\pi_\theta\): \(s_0, a_0, r_1, s_1, a_1, r_2, \dots, s_T\).
  2. For every time step, compute the return that followed it: \(G_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma\, r_{t+2} + \dots\)
  3. Update the weights with one gradient-ascent step (the formula below).
  4. Throw the episode away and start again.
\[ \theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} G_t\, \nabla_\theta \ln \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) \]

That's all. No value table, no replay buffer, no target network. In PyTorch you write the sum as a "loss" \(-\sum_t G_t \ln \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\) and let the optimiser minimise it, which is the same as gradient ascent on \(J\).

Try it: run REINFORCE on the short corridor, starting from the bad policy \(p = 0.05\). Focus on the red curve for now (the green one is Step 6). Each curve is the average of 50 seeded runs. Change the step size \(\alpha\).

📈 Interactive: REINFORCE learns the short corridor

What to notice

  • It finds the random policy. At \(\alpha = 2^{-10}\) the red curve climbs from about \(-80\) to the dashed line, the best possible \(-11.66\). The runs end with an average return of \(-12.2\) over their last 100 episodes. A value-based method with ε-greedy could never do better than \(-44.2\) here.
  • Small steps are slow. At \(2^{-13}\) it still gets there, but only towards the end of the 1000 episodes.
  • Big steps are dangerous. At \(2^{-8}\), 2 of the 50 runs get stuck off the chart, and at \(2^{-7}\), 32 of 50 do. One unlucky, very long episode produces a huge update that pushes \(p\) almost to 0 or 1, and from there episodes become endless. The strip plot on the right shows every run's final score, so you can see the stragglers.
  • This sensitivity is a symptom of noise: each update is based on a single episode, and the returns vary wildly from episode to episode.

docs.title: Step 6 — Taming the noise: baselines
docs.text:
REINFORCE is unbiased: on average, its update points exactly along the true gradient. But each single estimate is very noisy (high variance). Look at the update again: every action is weighted by \(G_t\). In the short corridor every return is negative, so every action gets pushed down, and only the difference between big and small pushes carries information. In the bandit above every reward was positive, so every action got pushed up. Most of each update is noise that has to cancel out over many episodes.

The fix is to compare each return with what you expected to get, and only react to the surprise. Subtract a baseline \(b(s_t)\):

\[ heta \leftarrow heta + \alpha \sum_{t} ig(G_t - b(s_t) ig)\, abla_ heta \ln \pi_ heta(a_t \mid s_t) \]

Better than expected → positive weight → make the action more likely. Worse than expected → negative weight → make it less likely.

Why it doesn't break anything: the baseline does not depend on the action, so its contribution averages to zero:

\[ \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi} ig[\, b(s)\, abla_ heta \ln \pi_ heta(a \mid s) ig] = b(s) \sum_a abla_ heta \pi_ heta(a \mid s) = b(s)\, abla_ heta \underbrace{\sum_a \pi_ heta(a \mid s)}_{=\,1} = 0 \]

So the update is still unbiased, whatever baseline you choose. A good baseline just makes it much less noisy. The natural choice is the state value, \(b(s) = V^\pi(s)\), learned by a second network (that's what the code below does).

Try it: each histogram shows 2000 single-episode estimates of the gradient for a fixed corridor policy \(p\). Left: weight \(G_t\). Right: weight \(G_t - b\), with \(b\) the average return \(J(p)\). The purple line is the true gradient.

📊 Interactive: the same gradient, with less noise

What to notice

  • Same centre, narrower spread. At \(p = 0.3\) the true gradient is \(8.48\). The estimates average \(7.16\) without a baseline and \(7.73\) with one (both are within sampling noise of the truth), but the spread drops from \(36.0\) to \(21.0\), 42% less.
  • Positive gradient means "increase \(p\)" (at \(p = 0.3\) we are left of the optimum). Move the slider past 0.59 and the true gradient turns negative.
  • Now scroll back to the learning curves in Step 5 and look at the green curve. At \(\alpha = 2^{-8}\) the baseline version has no stuck runs (average \(-12.3\) over the last 100 episodes, against \(-53.0\) for plain REINFORCE), and at \(2^{-7}\) only 1 of 50 runs gets stuck instead of 32. Less noise lets you take bigger steps safely.
  • The baseline is not magic: at very small step sizes it doesn't help here (at \(2^{-13}\) it even starts a little slower, because our learned baseline begins at 0 and has to catch up).

From baselines to advantages

With \(b(s) = V^\pi(s)\), the weight \(G_t - V^\pi(s_t)\) is a sample estimate of the advantage

\[A^\pi(s, a) = Q^\pi(s, a) - V^\pi(s),\]

how much better action \(a\) was than the policy's average behaviour in state \(s\). If we also use the learned \(V\) to estimate the return itself (instead of waiting for the episode to end), we get actor-critic methods, the topic of the next lesson.

docs.title: Step 7 — The price: on-policy and sample-hungry
docs.text:
The policy gradient is an expectation over episodes played by the current policy. As soon as we update \(\theta\), the old episodes come from a different policy and no longer give a correct estimate. So REINFORCE is on-policy: it uses each episode for one update and throws it away. Compare DQN, which stores experience in a replay buffer and learns from each transition many times.

Together with the high variance, that makes vanilla REINFORCE sample-hungry: it often needs many thousands of episodes. Most of what comes next is about fixing this:

  • Actor-critic (A2C) learns a value function to cut the variance further and updates during the episode.
  • PPO reuses each batch of episodes for several careful updates, keeping the new policy close to the old one.
  • SAC brings back a replay buffer for continuous control.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Here is REINFORCE, with and without a learned baseline, on CartPole: push a cart left or right to keep a pole upright, +1 for every step it stays up, at most 500 steps. The environment is written out in plain Python (it's the standard CartPole physics), so you only need PyTorch.

import math, random
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn


class CartPole:
    """The classic pole-balancing task: +1 per step, at most 500 steps."""

    def reset(self):
        self.s = np.random.uniform(-0.05, 0.05, size=4)   # cart pos, cart vel, pole angle, pole ang. vel
        self.t = 0
        return self.s.astype(np.float32)

    def step(self, action):                               # action 0 = push left, 1 = push right
        x, x_dot, th, th_dot = self.s
        force = 10.0 if action == 1 else -10.0
        cos, sin = math.cos(th), math.sin(th)
        temp = (force + 0.05 * th_dot**2 * sin) / 1.1
        th_acc = (9.8 * sin - cos * temp) / (0.5 * (4 / 3 - 0.1 * cos**2 / 1.1))
        x_acc = temp - 0.05 * th_acc * cos / 1.1
        self.s = np.array([x + 0.02 * x_dot, x_dot + 0.02 * x_acc,
                           th + 0.02 * th_dot, th_dot + 0.02 * th_acc])
        self.t += 1
        fell = abs(self.s[0]) > 2.4 or abs(self.s[2]) > 0.2095
        return self.s.astype(np.float32), 1.0, fell or self.t >= 500


def returns_to_go(rewards, gamma):
    G, out = 0.0, []
    for r in reversed(rewards):
        G = r + gamma * G
        out.append(G)
    return torch.tensor(out[::-1])


def train(use_baseline, seed, episodes=600, gamma=0.99):
    random.seed(seed); np.random.seed(seed); torch.manual_seed(seed)
    env = CartPole()
    policy = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 64), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(64, 2))   # state -> action preferences
    value = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 64), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(64, 1))    # baseline b(s) = V(s)
    opt_pi = torch.optim.Adam(policy.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    opt_v = torch.optim.Adam(value.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    history = []
    for ep in range(episodes):
        # 1. play one episode with the current policy
        states, actions, rewards = [], [], []
        s, done = env.reset(), False
        while not done:
            with torch.no_grad():
                probs = torch.softmax(policy(torch.from_numpy(s)), dim=-1)
            a = torch.multinomial(probs, 1).item()
            states.append(s); actions.append(a)
            s, r, done = env.step(a)
            rewards.append(r)
        history.append(sum(rewards))

        # 2. the return G_t from every time step
        S = torch.from_numpy(np.array(states))
        A = torch.tensor(actions)
        G = returns_to_go(rewards, gamma)

        # 3. weight for each log-probability: G_t, or G_t - b(s_t)
        if use_baseline:
            V = value(S).squeeze(-1)
            weight = G - V.detach()
            opt_v.zero_grad(); ((G - V) ** 2).mean().backward(); opt_v.step()
        else:
            weight = G

        # 4. gradient ASCENT on  sum_t weight_t * log pi(a_t | s_t)
        log_probs = torch.log_softmax(policy(S), dim=-1)[torch.arange(len(A)), A]
        loss = -(weight * log_probs).sum()              # minus sign: optimisers minimise
        opt_pi.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt_pi.step()
    return history


torch.set_num_threads(1)
for use_baseline in [False, True]:
    history = train(use_baseline, seed=0)
    print(f"baseline={use_baseline!s:5}  average return: first 100 episodes {np.mean(history[:100]):5.1f}, "
          f"last 100 episodes {np.mean(history[-100:]):5.1f}")

baseline=False  average return: first 100 episodes  38.4, last 100 episodes 348.1
baseline=True   average return: first 100 episodes  35.2, last 100 episodes 483.4

Both versions learn to balance the pole (a random policy lasts only 22 steps on average), and both runs together take about 35 seconds on one CPU core. One seed can be lucky, so we also trained each version with 10 different seeds. Averaged over the last 100 episodes, plain REINFORCE reached 376.8 (worst seed 163.1) and REINFORCE with a baseline 439.4 (worst seed 347.0). The baseline won on 8 of the 10 seeds.

Notes on the code

  • V.detach(): the baseline only scales the policy update. Without detach(), the policy loss would also try to change the value network.
  • The "loss" is not a measure of how good the policy is: its value can go up while the policy improves. Only its gradient means something.
  • Real implementations add a few tricks: normalising the weights in each batch, batching several episodes per update, and an entropy bonus that keeps the policy from becoming deterministic too early.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"The PyTorch loss in REINFORCE is a loss like in supervised learning.\"

It is a trick to get the right gradient out of autograd. Its value depends on the sampled episode and the size of the returns, and it doesn't go down steadily as the agent improves. Track the average return instead.

\"Subtracting a baseline changes what the algorithm learns.\"

It doesn't: the baseline term averages to exactly zero (Step 6), so the expected update is the same. It only reduces the noise. That is why any reasonable baseline is allowed, even a bad one.

\"If every reward is positive, every action gets reinforced, so the agent can't learn.\"

Every sampled action is pushed up, but better actions are pushed up more, so on average the policy still improves. It is just very noisy and can lock onto a worse action, as in run 2 of the bandit widget. A baseline fixes that.

\"Stochastic policies are only for exploration; the best policy is always deterministic.\"

That is true in a fully observed MDP, but not when the agent can't see everything (the short corridor) or in games against opponents (rock–paper–scissors). Policy-gradient methods can represent and find the best random policy.

\"Policy gradient finds the best policy.\"

It is gradient ascent, so it finds a local optimum of \(J(\theta)\). With neural networks, \(J\) has many hills, and an unlucky run can settle on a mediocre one.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. A softmax policy has π = (0.2, 0.5, 0.3). You sample the second action and the return is G = +2. With α = 0.1, how do the three preferences change?

$\Delta h = \alpha\, G\, (\mathbb{1}[a=b] - \pi(b)) = 0.1 \cdot 2 \cdot (-0.2,\, 0.5,\, -0.3) = $ (−0.04, +0.10, −0.06). The sampled action goes up, the other two go down.

2. Why can't you just take the gradient of the return through the environment, as you would through a loss function?

The return depends on what the environment does after each action, and we don't have a differentiable formula for that (it may be a physics engine, a game or the real world). The policy gradient theorem avoids this: after taking the log, the environment's transition probabilities drop out, and only \( abla_ heta \ln \pi_ heta(a_t \mid s_t)\) remains, which we can differentiate.

3. Show that subtracting a baseline b(s) doesn't change the expected update.

\(\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi}[b(s) abla_ heta \ln \pi_ heta(a\mid s)] = b(s)\sum_a \pi_ heta(a\mid s) rac{ abla_ heta \pi_ heta(a\mid s)}{\pi_ heta(a\mid s)} = b(s)\, abla_ heta \sum_a \pi_ heta(a \mid s) = b(s)\, abla_ heta 1 = 0\). It works because \(b\) doesn't depend on the action. A "baseline" that depends on the action taken would bias the update.

4. Why can't REINFORCE learn from a replay buffer of old episodes, like DQN does?

The policy gradient is an average over episodes played by the current policy \(\pi_ heta\). Old episodes were played by older policies, so they over-represent actions the current policy no longer likes, and the estimate is wrong. REINFORCE is on-policy. (PPO and other methods correct for this with importance weights, within limits.)

5. A Gaussian policy for a continuous action has mean μ = 0.5 and σ = 0.2. It samples a = 0.8, and the outcome is better than expected. Which way does the update move μ?

For a Gaussian, \( rac{\partial \ln \pi(a)}{\partial \mu} = rac{a - \mu}{\sigma^2} = rac{0.3}{0.04} = 7.5\) (autograd agrees). The weight \(G_t - b\) is positive, so μ moves up, towards 0.8: the policy shifts towards the action that worked well.

  • Richard Sutton et al., Policy Gradient Methods for Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation (NeurIPS 1999). The policy gradient theorem.

docs.title: Q-Learning and SARSA
docs.text:
TL;DR

With no model of the world, an agent can still learn to act well. It learns action values \(Q(s,a)\) from its own experience, one step at a time, and acts by picking the action with the biggest \(Q\). SARSA updates \(Q\) towards the value of the action it will actually take next (on-policy). Q-learning updates towards the value of the best next action, whatever it actually does (off-policy). On the cliff world from lesson 1 this small difference matters: Q-learning learns the short route along the cliff edge but keeps falling off while it explores; SARSA learns a safer detour and collects more reward while learning.

Level: beginner–intermediate · Prerequisites: What is RL? and Monte Carlo & TD learning (the TD update)

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
Until now our agents have either been told their policy (lesson 1) or evaluated a fixed one. This lesson is the payoff: an agent that starts knowing nothing about the cliff world, not where the goal is and not where the cliff is, and finds a good route by itself, only by trying.

  • Q-learning (Watkins, 1989) is one of the most famous algorithms in RL. Put a neural network in place of the table and you get Deep Q-Networks, the method that learned to play Atari games from pixels (next lesson).
  • The difference between on-policy and off-policy learning that you meet here comes back everywhere: PPO (used to fine-tune chatbots) is on-policy, DQN and SAC are off-policy. Knowing which one you have tells you whether you can reuse old data, and how your agent behaves while it learns.

docs.title: Step 1 — From V to Q: without a model, learn action values
docs.text:
The previous lesson learned the value \(V(s)\) of each state from experience with TD learning. That tells you how good it is to be somewhere. But to act, you need to compare actions. With \(V\) alone, choosing an action means looking one step ahead:

\[ \pi(s) = \arg\max_a \; \sum_{s'} p(s' \mid s, a)\,\big[\, r + \gamma V(s') \,\big] \]

That needs \(p(s' \mid s, a)\): a model of where each action leads. A model-free agent doesn't have one. The fix is to learn the action value \(Q(s,a)\) directly, "how good is it to take action \(a\) in state \(s\), and carry on from there". Then acting needs no model at all:

\[ \pi(s) = \arg\max_a Q(s, a) \]

The price is four numbers per cell instead of one. The board below shows the optimal action values \(Q^*(s,a)\) of the cliff world, as four triangles per cell.

No discount in this lesson

We use \(\gamma = 1\) here, as Sutton & Barto do for their cliff-walking example. Every episode ends at the goal or the cliff, so the sums stay finite, and \(Q\) is then simply the expected total reward from that point. That makes the numbers easy to read: the 7-step route along the edge is worth \(6 \times (-1) + 10 = +4\).

🔢 Interactive: four numbers per cell, Q*(s, a)

What to notice

  • At the start cell, \(Q^*(s, \uparrow) = 4\) (the edge route) and \(Q^*(s, \rightarrow) = -20\) (straight into the cliff). The best action is just the biggest number.
  • Just above the cliff at row 2, col 1, the four values are \(\uparrow 4\), \(\rightarrow 6\), \(\downarrow -20\), \(\leftarrow 4\). The greedy policy hugs the edge, because with a perfect, non-exploring agent the edge is safe.
  • \(V^*(s)\) is just the largest of the four: \(V^*(s) = \max_a Q^*(s,a)\).
  • Raise the slip chance: the values near the cliff drop, and from slip 0.1 on the arrows lead away from the edge (the optimal route becomes the 11-step detour). \(Q^*\) already includes the risks of the environment. Remember this; it will matter in Step 5.

docs.title: Step 2 — SARSA: learn from the move you actually make next
docs.text:
The TD update from the previous lesson nudged \(V(s)\) towards a one-step target, \(r + \gamma V(s')\). Do exactly the same with \(Q\). After taking action \(a\) in state \(s\), getting reward \(r\) and landing in \(s'\), the agent picks its next action \(a'\) with its usual ε-greedy policy, and uses \(Q(s', a')\) as its guess of the future:

\[ Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha \,\big[\, \underbrace{r + \gamma\, Q(s', a')}_{\text{TD target}} - Q(s,a) \,\big] \]

The bracket is the TD error \(\delta_t\); \(\alpha\) is the step size. Then the agent really does take \(a'\), and the loop repeats. The update uses five things, \((s, a, r, s', a')\), which is where the name comes from: State, Action, Reward, State, Action.

What to notice

  • SARSA is the TD update from the previous lesson, with \(Q(s,a)\) in place of \(V(s)\). Nothing else is new.
  • The target uses \(a'\), the action the agent really takes next, including random exploratory moves. So SARSA learns the value of the policy it is actually following, exploration and all. That is what on-policy means.
  • At a terminal state (goal or cliff) there is no future, so the target is just \(r\).

docs.title: Step 3 — Q-learning: learn about the best move, whatever you do next
docs.text:
Q-learning changes one thing. Instead of the action the agent will take next, it uses the best action in \(s'\):

\[ Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha \,\big[\, r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s,a) \,\big] \]

The agent still behaves ε-greedily, so it keeps exploring. But its target always assumes "from the next state on, I will play greedily". So Q-learning learns \(Q^*\), the values of the greedy policy, even though it never follows that policy exactly. Learning about one policy (greedy) while following another (ε-greedy) is called off-policy learning.

A worked example shows the difference. Suppose the agent stands just above the cliff (row 2, col 1), steps right, gets \(r = -1\) and lands on (row 2, col 2). Say its \(Q\) already equals the \(Q^*\) values from Step 1, where \(Q^*(s', \cdot)\) is \(\uparrow 6\), \(\rightarrow 7\), \(\downarrow -20\), \(\leftarrow 5\). With \(\gamma = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 0.3\):

Method Next action used in the target Target Q-learning the best one, \(\rightarrow\) (whatever the agent does next) \(-1 + 7 = 6\) SARSA, if \(a' = \rightarrow\) (greedy) \(\rightarrow\) \(-1 + 7 = 6\) SARSA, if \(a' = \downarrow\) (random move into the cliff) \(\downarrow\) \(-1 - 20 = -21\) SARSA, averaged over ε-greedy \(a'\) \(3.75\)

Q-learning's target ignores the agent's own clumsiness. SARSA's target includes it: on average, standing next to the cliff is worth less to an agent that sometimes steps off at random. Over many updates, SARSA's values for the edge cells end up lower, and that is what pushes it away from the edge.

What to notice

  • The two updates differ in one term: \(Q(s', a')\) versus \(\max_{a'} Q(s', a')\).
  • With \(\varepsilon = 0\) they are identical, because then \(a'\) is the greedy action.
  • Neither needs a model: both learn from single transitions \((s, a, r, s')\) as they happen.

docs.title: Step 4 — Watch them learn the cliff
docs.text:
Here is lesson 1's cliff world again, but now nobody tells the agent anything. All \(Q\) values start at 0. Press Train and watch an agent learn by trial and error. Then switch the algorithm and compare.

🧗 Interactive: SARSA and Q-learning learn the cliff world

What to notice

  1. The first episodes are chaos. The agent wanders, bumps into walls and falls off the cliff. Each fall turns the triangle pointing at the cliff red, so the cliff is learned one fall at a time.
  2. Q-learning settles on the edge route. With the defaults (α = 0.2, ε = 0.3), give it a few hundred episodes: the green dashed line runs along row 2, right next to the cliff. That is the optimal route (7 steps, +4).
  3. SARSA settles on a detour. Reset with SARSA: its dashed line usually goes up to the top row, the long way round (11 steps, 0). Its values next to the cliff stay redder, because they include its own random steps into the cliff.
  4. Training versus testing. Press Run greedy policy (ε = 0) after training both. Q-learning's route now scores +4, SARSA's only 0. But while training, the readout's "fell off the cliff" count is much higher for Q-learning. Which one is "better" depends on whether you care about the reward collected while learning.
  5. Try slip = 0.2. Now even a greedy agent can slide off the edge, so Q-learning's \(Q^*\) also learns to keep away. Q-learning accounts for the environment's randomness, just not for its own exploration.

docs.title: Step 5 — Who collects more reward while learning?
docs.text:
One run of one agent is noisy. To compare fairly, the widget below trains 200 SARSA agents and 200 Q-learning agents (each with its own random seed) for 500 episodes and plots the average total reward per episode as they learn. This is the classic cliff-walking experiment from Sutton & Barto's textbook, on our smaller map.

📈 Interactive: reward per episode while learning (200 runs each)

What to notice

  • With \(\varepsilon = 0.3\), SARSA's curve ends above Q-learning's. In our Python check (200 runs, α = 0.2, ε = 0.3, γ = 1, 500 episodes) the average reward per episode over the last 100 episodes was −6.80 for SARSA and −8.63 for Q-learning. In those episodes 39% of Q-learning's episodes ended in the cliff, against 14% for SARSA (SARSA still falls sometimes: the start cell itself is next to the cliff). Your widget numbers will differ slightly, since it runs its own seeds.
  • Yet Q-learning learned the better policy. All 200 Q-learning agents ended with the 7-step edge route (+4 when run greedily). 196 of the 200 SARSA agents ended with the 11-step detour (0 when run greedily).
  • Now press ε = 0.1. On this small map the result flips: Q-learning −0.05, SARSA −2.35. Our cliff is only 4 cells long, so with 10% random moves Q-learning falls in only about 1 episode in 8 (12.5%), and the short edge route pays even while exploring. Working out the exact average for a fixed route (a policy evaluation, as in the dynamic programming lesson) gives −0.12 for the ε-greedy edge route and −1.97 for the detour at ε = 0.1, but −8.76 and −7.46 at ε = 0.3. The two cross near ε = 0.2. Sutton & Barto's original map has a 10-cell cliff, which is why their famous figure shows SARSA winning already at ε = 0.1.
  • SARSA at ε = 0.1 is also a lesson in noise: the edge is the better ε-greedy route there, but one unlucky fall makes a big update with α = 0.2, and 112 of the 200 SARSA agents still ended on the detour.

docs.title: Step 6 — On-policy versus off-policy
docs.text:
Every RL agent has two roles for a policy:

  • The behaviour policy is the one that actually picks the actions and generates the experience (here: ε-greedy).
  • The target policy is the one whose values the agent is learning (the one the TD target "assumes" for the future).

On-policy methods like SARSA use the same policy for both. Off-policy methods like Q-learning learn about one policy (greedy) from data generated by another (ε-greedy).

Why would you want off-policy learning? Because the data can come from anywhere: an exploring agent, an old version of the agent, a human demonstrator. That is what lets DQN reuse old experience from a replay buffer (next lesson). On-policy methods have to learn from data that their current policy generated.

Two loose ends:

  • Expected SARSA replaces the sampled \(Q(s', a')\) with its average over the policy: \(r + \gamma \sum_{a'} \pi(a' \mid s')\, Q(s', a')\). It learns the same thing as SARSA but with less noise per update, since it doesn't depend on which \(a'\) happened to be drawn. (That is the 3.75 in the table of Step 3.) In our check, with ε = 0.3, α = 0.1 and 3000 episodes, all 20 Expected SARSA runs ended on the same 11-step detour as SARSA. With a greedy \(\pi\) in the sum, Expected SARSA is Q-learning.
  • If ε shrinks to zero, they meet. SARSA's caution only exists because of exploration. Let ε decay over time and SARSA's target becomes Q-learning's. In our check (ε = 0.3/(1 + episode/20), α = 0.2, 2000 episodes), all 100 Q-learning runs and 86 of 100 SARSA runs ended with the edge route. (The rest of SARSA's runs had stopped exploring before they had re-checked the edge: decaying ε too fast has its own cost.)

What to notice

  • "On-policy" and "off-policy" are about which policy the target describes, not about how the agent behaves. Both of our agents behave identically.
  • Neither is simply better. Off-policy finds the optimal greedy policy and can reuse any data. On-policy optimises the reward you actually get while acting the way you act, which matters when mistakes during learning are costly (a real robot near a real cliff).

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Both algorithms in plain Python, on lesson 1's cliff world. The only difference between them is one line, the target:

import random
from collections import Counter

MAP = ["......",
       "..#...",
       "......",
       "SCCCCG"]
MOVES = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]          # up, right, down, left


class CliffWorld:
    """Lesson 1's grid world: −1 per step, +10 at the goal, −20 for the cliff."""

    def __init__(self, slip=0.0, seed=0):
        self.slip, self.rng = slip, random.Random(seed)

    def reset(self):
        self.pos = (3, 0)
        return self.pos

    def step(self, a):
        if self.rng.random() < self.slip:              # slide sideways
            a = (a + self.rng.choice([1, 3])) % 4
        r, c = self.pos[0] + MOVES[a][0], self.pos[1] + MOVES[a][1]
        if 0 <= r < 4 and 0 <= c < 6 and MAP[r][c] != "#":
            self.pos = (r, c)
        tile = MAP[self.pos[0]][self.pos[1]]
        if tile == "G":
            return self.pos, +10, True
        if tile == "C":
            return self.pos, -20, True
        return self.pos, -1, False


def epsilon_greedy(Q, s, eps, rng):
    if rng.random() < eps:
        return rng.randrange(4)                        # explore
    best = max(Q[s])
    return rng.choice([a for a in range(4) if Q[s][a] == best])   # exploit (break ties randomly)


def train(algo, episodes=500, alpha=0.2, eps=0.3, gamma=1.0, seed=0):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    env = CliffWorld(seed=seed)
    Q = {(r, c): [0.0] * 4 for r in range(4) for c in range(6)}
    rewards = []                                       # total reward of every training episode
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s = env.reset()
        a = epsilon_greedy(Q, s, eps, rng)
        total, done = 0, False
        while not done:
            s2, r, done = env.step(a)
            total += r
            a2 = epsilon_greedy(Q, s2, eps, rng)       # the action we will really take next
            if done:
                target = r                             # no future after the goal or the cliff
            elif algo == "sarsa":
                target = r + gamma * Q[s2][a2]         # on-policy: value of the action we WILL take
            else:
                target = r + gamma * max(Q[s2])        # off-policy: value of the BEST action
            Q[s][a] += alpha * (target - Q[s][a])      # TD update
            s, a = s2, a2
        rewards.append(total)
    return Q, rewards


def greedy_route(Q):
    """Follow the learned greedy policy (ε = 0) from the start, without slipping."""
    env, s, done, total, path = CliffWorld(), None, False, 0, []
    s = env.reset()
    while not done and len(path) < 50:
        s, r, done = env.step(Q[s].index(max(Q[s])))
        total += r
        path.append(s)
    return f"{len(path)} steps, return {total:+d}"


for eps in [0.3, 0.1]:
    print(f"ε = {eps}")
    for algo in ["sarsa", "q-learning"]:
        last100, routes = [], Counter()
        for seed in range(200):
            Q, rewards = train(algo, eps=eps, seed=seed)
            last100.append(sum(rewards[-100:]) / 100)
            routes[greedy_route(Q)] += 1
        print(f"  {algo:10s}  reward per episode (last 100) = {sum(last100) / 200:6.2f}"
              f"   greedy route: {routes.most_common(1)[0][0]} in {routes.most_common(1)[0][1]}/200 runs")

ε = 0.3
  sarsa       reward per episode (last 100) =  -6.80   greedy route: 11 steps, return +0 in 196/200 runs
  q-learning  reward per episode (last 100) =  -8.63   greedy route: 7 steps, return +4 in 200/200 runs
ε = 0.1
  sarsa       reward per episode (last 100) =  -2.35   greedy route: 11 steps, return +0 in 112/200 runs
  q-learning  reward per episode (last 100) =  -0.05   greedy route: 7 steps, return +4 in 200/200 runs

(It takes about 20 seconds in plain Python.) The table Q has \(4 \times 6 \times 4 = 96\) entries. That is fine here, but a game screen has far too many states for a table. Replacing the table with a neural network that outputs \(Q(s, \cdot)\) is the idea behind Deep Q-Networks, the next lesson.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"Q-learning is better than SARSA because it finds the optimal policy.\"

Q-learning finds the optimal greedy policy, the best one if you stop exploring. If the agent keeps exploring (as many real systems do while they learn), SARSA can collect more reward, as the ε = 0.3 curves show. "Better" depends on whether you score the learned policy or the learning itself.

\"SARSA avoids the cliff because it knows the cliff is dangerous.\"

Both algorithms learn that the cliff is bad: both have \(Q(s, \downarrow) \approx -20\) next to it. SARSA avoids the edge because its values include its own future random moves. Set ε to 0 and that reason disappears.

\"Off-policy means the agent doesn't need to explore.\"

Q-learning still needs exploration to see the states and actions it learns about. Off-policy only means the target assumes a different policy (greedy) from the one that behaves (ε-greedy). No exploration, no data about the alternatives.

\"SARSA learns the optimal policy, just more slowly.\"

With a fixed ε, SARSA learns the best ε-greedy policy, which is not the optimal policy when exploration is risky. It only reaches the optimal policy if ε decays towards zero over time.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. Why do model-free agents learn Q(s, a) instead of V(s)?

To act with \(V\) you have to look one step ahead: "which action leads to the best next state?" That needs a model \(p(s' \mid s, a)\). With \(Q\) you just pick \(\arg\max_a Q(s,a)\), no model required.

2. Write down the SARSA and Q-learning updates. Which single term differs?

SARSA: \(Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha[r + \gamma Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)]\), where \(a'\) is the next action the agent really takes. Q-learning: the same, with \(\max_{a'} Q(s',a')\) in place of \(Q(s',a')\).

3. An agent is next to the cliff. Its next action a′ happens to be a random step into the cliff, with Q(s′, a′) = −20, while max Q(s′, ·) = 7. With r = −1 and γ = 1, what are the SARSA and Q-learning targets?

SARSA: \(-1 + (-20) = -21\). Q-learning: \(-1 + 7 = 6\). SARSA "feels" its own random mistake; Q-learning assumes it will act greedily next.

4. In the learning-curves widget at ε = 0.3, Q-learning earns less reward per episode than SARSA, yet its greedy route scores +4 against SARSA's 0. How can both be true?

The curves measure reward while exploring (ε = 0.3). Q-learning's route runs along the cliff edge, where random moves often fall off (39% of its late training episodes ended in the cliff in our Python check). Its greedy route is optimal once exploration stops. SARSA's detour is worse without exploration, but safer with it.

5. Is Q-learning on-policy or off-policy? What practical advantage does that give?

Off-policy: it learns the values of the greedy policy while following an ε-greedy one. Because the target doesn't depend on how the data was generated, it can learn from old experience, other agents or demonstrations. DQN uses this to learn from a replay buffer of past transitions.

docs.text:

  • Christopher Watkins & Peter Dayan, Q-learning, Machine Learning 8, 1992. The convergence proof for Q-learning.
  • Gavin Rummery & Mahesan Niranjan, On-line Q-learning using connectionist systems, Cambridge tech. report, 1994. The paper that introduced SARSA (under another name).
  • Harm van Seijen et al., A theoretical and empirical analysis of Expected Sarsa, IEEE ADPRL 2009.
  • David Silver, UCL Course on RL, Lecture 5: Model-Free Control.

docs.title: What is Reinforcement Learning?
docs.text:
TL;DR

In reinforcement learning (RL), an agent learns by trial and error. It looks at the state of its world, takes an action, and gets back a reward: a number saying how good that was. Nobody tells it the right answer. Its goal is to find a policy (a strategy) that collects as much reward as possible over the long run, not just right now.

Level: beginner · Prerequisites: none. Knowing what a sum (\(\sum\)) is helps for the math.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
Some of the most striking results in AI came from reinforcement learning:

  • Games: AlphaGo beat the world champion at Go (2016), and Atari-playing agents learned dozens of games from raw pixels.
  • Robotics and control: robot hands that learn to manipulate objects, and controllers that cool data centres or shape the plasma in fusion reactors.
  • Chatbots: ChatGPT, Claude and other assistants are fine-tuned with RL from human feedback (RLHF). The "reward" is a score for how helpful and safe a reply is.

The common thread: there is no dataset of correct answers, only a way to tell whether things went well. RL is the toolbox for learning in that situation.

docs.title: Step 1 — Learning from consequences, not from answers
docs.text:
Think about how you teach a dog to sit. You can't show it a thousand labelled examples of "correct sitting". Instead, it tries things, and when it happens to sit, it gets a treat. Over time it learns that sitting (when you say "sit") leads to treats.

That is reinforcement learning. Compare it with the other two main kinds of machine learning:

Supervised learning Unsupervised learning Reinforcement learning What you get inputs with correct labels inputs only a reward after each action The question it answers "What is the right output?" "What structure is in this data?" "What should I do?" Feedback is… immediate and exact none delayed, noisy, just a score Example classify an X-ray group customers play a game, steer a robot

Two things make RL harder than supervised learning:

  1. The reward doesn't say what the right action was. A score of −1 tells you that you did badly, not what you should have done instead.
  2. Rewards can be delayed. In chess the only real reward is winning or losing at the very end. Which of your 40 moves deserves the credit? This is called the credit assignment problem.

docs.title: Step 2 — The loop: agent and environment
docs.text:
Every RL problem has the same two players:

  • The agent: the learner and decision-maker (the dog, the game player, the robot's controller).
  • The environment: everything outside the agent (the room, the game, the physical world).

They interact in a loop, one time step at a time:

  1. The agent sees the current state \(s_t\) (where am I? what does the board look like?).
  2. It picks an action \(a_t\) (move left, push the button, say this word).
  3. The environment responds with a new state \(s_{t+1}\) and a reward \(r_{t+1}\).
  4. Repeat.

One run from a starting state to an ending (terminal) state is called an episode, for example one game of chess or one attempt to cross a room.

Try it: you are the agent. Get the orange dot to the goal. Each step costs −1 (so dawdling is bad), reaching the goal gives +10, and stepping into the cliff gives −20 and ends the episode. Then turn on the slippery floor and play a few more episodes.

🎮 Interactive: be the agent

What to notice

  • The shortest route (up one, right along the cliff edge, down) needs 7 steps, for a total reward of \(6 \times (-1) + 10 = +4\). The route along the top row needs 11 steps, for a total of 0.
  • With the slippery floor on, the same action in the same state can lead to different results. Environments are often random like this, and a good agent has to plan for it. Does walking along the cliff edge still feel like a good idea?
  • You could see the whole map. A real RL agent starts with no idea where the goal or the cliff is. It has to discover them by trying, falling off the cliff many times along the way.

State, action, reward in the wild

Problem State Actions Reward This grid world which cell you are in up, right, down, left −1 per step, +10 goal, −20 cliff Atari game the screen pixels joystick moves change in game score Robot arm joint angles, camera image motor torques +1 when the object is grasped Chatbot (RLHF) the conversation so far the next word a score for the finished reply

docs.title: Step 3 — What does "best" mean? The return and discounting
docs.text:
The agent's goal is not to get the biggest reward on the next step. It is to get the most reward in total, from now until the end. This total is called the return, written \(G_t\):

\[ G_t = r_{t+1} + r_{t+2} + r_{t+3} + \dots \]

In practice we almost always add a discount factor \(\gamma\) (Greek gamma, a number between 0 and 1), which makes rewards in the future count for less:

\[ G_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma\, r_{t+2} + \gamma^2\, r_{t+3} + \dots = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k\, r_{t+k+1} \]

A reward that arrives \(k\) steps from now is multiplied by \(\gamma^k\). With \(\gamma = 0.9\), a reward 10 steps away is worth only \(0.9^{10} \approx 0.35\) of its face value.

Why discount at all?

  • A bird in the hand. The future is uncertain, so sooner is safer.
  • It keeps the maths finite. If an episode could go on forever, an undiscounted sum could be infinite.
  • It is a dial for patience. \(\gamma\) near 0 → a short-sighted agent that only cares about the next reward. \(\gamma\) near 1 → a far-sighted agent that will accept pain now for a bigger payoff later.

Try it: which would the agent rather have: +4 right now, or +10 six steps later? Drag \(\gamma\) and watch the answer flip.

⏳ Interactive: what is a future reward worth today?

What to notice

  • At \(\gamma = 0\) only the very first reward counts, so the agent always grabs A.
  • Around \(\gamma \approx 0.86\) the two options are worth the same (\(10 \cdot \gamma^6 = 4\)).
  • At \(\gamma = 0.99\) the agent is patient: B is worth almost its full 10.
  • Choosing \(\gamma\) changes what "best behaviour" means. Typical values in practice are 0.9 to 0.999.

docs.title: Step 4 — The agent's strategy: the policy
docs.text:
How does the agent decide what to do? It follows a policy, written \(\pi\) (Greek pi). A policy is simply a rule that says which action to take in each state.

  • A deterministic policy picks one action per state: \(a = \pi(s)\). In our grid world, that is one arrow per cell.
  • A stochastic policy gives a probability for each action: \(\pi(a \mid s)\), "the chance of taking action \(a\) in state \(s\)". The random policy below (✱) is the extreme case: every direction has probability \(\tfrac{1}{4}\).

Learning, in RL, means improving the policy. The goal is to find an optimal policy \(\pi^*\): one that gets the highest expected return from every state.

In simple problems a policy can be a lookup table (one arrow per cell). In hard problems like Atari or robotics it is a neural network: it takes the state as input and outputs action probabilities. That is where deep learning and RL meet (deep reinforcement learning).

docs.title: Step 5 — How good is a state? The value function
docs.text:
To improve a policy we need to measure how good it is. The value of a state, under a policy \(\pi\), is the return you can expect if you start there and follow \(\pi\) from then on:

\[ V^{\pi}(s) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\, G_t \mid s_t = s \,\right] \]

"Expected" means averaged over all the random things that can happen: the random choices of a stochastic policy, and the random slips of the environment. You can estimate it by playing many episodes from \(s\) and averaging their returns.

Try it: the board below shows a policy (the arrows) and, in each cell, the value \(V^\pi(s)\) for that policy. Green cells are good places to be, red cells are bad. Click cells to change arrows, or pick a preset.

🧭 Interactive: a policy and its value

What to notice

  1. Values summarise the future. Cells close to the goal are greener, because you can expect a good return from there. With the Random policy almost every cell is deep red: wandering at random usually ends in the cliff (from the start cell, \(V \approx -19.9\)).
  2. Values are an average over real experience. Press Run 1000 episodes. The average return of 1000 played episodes lands very close to \(V(\text{start})\). That is literally what the value means.
  3. The best policy depends on the environment. With slip chance 0, Edge of the cliff is better than Safe detour (\(V = 2.05\) vs \(-2.04\)). Raise the slip chance to 0.2 and the order flips (\(-9.08\) vs \(-6.97\)): on a slippery floor the risky shortcut falls off the cliff too often.
  4. It also depends on \(\gamma\). With slip 0, lower \(\gamma\) to 0.5: the two policies become almost equally good (\(-1.81\) vs \(-1.99\)), because a short-sighted agent barely cares about the +10 at the end.
  5. One bad arrow ripples backwards. Choose Safe detour and click the top-right cell once, so it points left. The agent now bounces between two cells forever, and every cell that leads there turns red.

Two kinds of value

\(V^\pi(s)\) answers "how good is it to be in state \(s\)?" A close relative, the action-value \(Q^\pi(s, a)\), answers "how good is it to take action \(a\) in state \(s\), then follow \(\pi\)?" If you know \(Q\), choosing well is easy: in each state, pick the action with the highest \(Q\). That idea is the heart of Q-learning (see Q-learning and SARSA).

docs.title: Step 6 — Explore or exploit?
docs.text:
There is one more challenge that supervised learning never faces. Because the agent learns from its own actions, it must decide between:

  • Exploiting: do what has worked best so far, to collect reward now.
  • Exploring: try something new, which might be worse, but might reveal something better.

Think of choosing a restaurant. Going to your favourite is exploiting. Trying the new place down the street is exploring. Exploit always and you may never find something better; explore always and you eat a lot of bad meals.

An RL agent that only exploits could take the safe route on its first lucky episode and never discover the shorter one. The simplest fix is ε-greedy (epsilon-greedy): most of the time take the best-known action, but with a small probability \(\varepsilon\) (say 10%), take a random one. The Multi-armed bandits lesson explores this trade-off in depth.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
All the RL methods on the roadmap are different answers to one question: how exactly do we do the "Learn" box?

Here is the grid world from this lesson in plain Python. It uses the same reset() / step() interface as most RL libraries:

import random

MAP = ["......",
       "..#...",
       "......",
       "SCCCCG"]
MOVES = {"up": (-1, 0), "right": (0, 1), "down": (1, 0), "left": (0, -1)}


class CliffWorld:
    """−1 per step, +10 at the goal, −20 for falling off the cliff."""

    def __init__(self, slip=0.0):
        self.slip = slip            # chance of sliding sideways instead of moving as intended

    def reset(self):
        self.pos = (3, 0)
        return self.pos             # the first state

    def step(self, action):
        if random.random() < self.slip:                     # slippery floor: slide left or right
            sideways = {"up": ["left", "right"], "down": ["left", "right"],
                        "left": ["up", "down"], "right": ["up", "down"]}
            action = random.choice(sideways[action])
        dr, dc = MOVES[action]
        r, c = self.pos[0] + dr, self.pos[1] + dc
        if 0 <= r < 4 and 0 <= c < 6 and MAP[r][c] != "#":  # walls and edges: stay put
            self.pos = (r, c)
        tile = MAP[self.pos[0]][self.pos[1]]
        if tile == "G":
            return self.pos, +10, True                      # next state, reward, episode over?
        if tile == "C":
            return self.pos, -20, True
        return self.pos, -1, False


def run_episode(env, policy, gamma=0.95, max_steps=100):
    state = env.reset()
    G, discount = 0.0, 1.0
    for t in range(max_steps):
        action = policy(state)                     # 1. agent picks an action
        state, reward, done = env.step(action)     # 2. environment responds
        G += discount * reward                     # 3. add up the discounted reward
        discount *= gamma
        if done:
            break
    return G


def random_policy(state):
    return random.choice(list(MOVES))


def edge_policy(state):                            # hug the cliff: up once, then right, then down
    r, c = state
    if r == 3:
        return "up"
    if r < 2:
        return "down" if c != 2 else "right"     # (0, 2) sits above the wall
    return "down" if c == 5 else "right"


for slip in [0.0, 0.2]:
    env = CliffWorld(slip)
    for name, policy in [("random", random_policy), ("edge", edge_policy)]:
        returns = [run_episode(env, policy) for _ in range(10_000)]
        print(f"slip={slip}  {name:6s}  average return = {sum(returns) / len(returns):6.2f}")

slip=0.0  random  average return = -19.87
slip=0.0  edge    average return =   2.05
slip=0.2  random  average return = -19.87
slip=0.2  edge    average return =  -9.10

These averages match the values \(V(\text{start})\) shown in the policy widget. Notice that nothing here learns yet: the policies are written by hand. Making the agent find a good policy by itself is what the next lessons are about.

For real projects, the standard library of environments is Gymnasium (pip install gymnasium). The loop looks exactly the same:

import gymnasium as gym

env = gym.make("FrozenLake-v1", is_slippery=True)   # a slippery grid world, much like ours
state, info = env.reset(seed=0)
total = 0.0
done = False
while not done:
    action = env.action_space.sample()               # a random policy
    state, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(action)
    total += reward
    done = terminated or truncated
print("return:", total)

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"The agent tries to maximise the next reward.\"

It tries to maximise the return: the (discounted) sum of all future rewards. Often the best action has a bad immediate reward, like sacrificing a piece in chess or taking the long way round the cliff.

\"The reward tells the agent what it should have done.\"

A reward is just a score for what did happen. It never says what the right action was. That is the key difference from supervised learning, and the reason RL needs so much trial and error.

\"Reward and value are the same thing.\"

The reward is the immediate signal from the environment, one step at a time. The value is the agent's prediction of the total future reward from a state. A cell next to the cliff gives the same −1 reward as any other cell, but under a risky policy its value is much lower.

\"If I give rewards for the right things, the agent will do what I want.\"

Agents are very good at finding loopholes. A famous example is a boat-racing agent that learned to spin in circles collecting bonus points instead of finishing the race. Designing rewards that really capture what you want (reward design) is one of the hardest parts of applied RL.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. Name the agent, a state, an action and the reward for a self-driving car learning to park.

Agent: the car's controller. State: camera and sensor readings, the car's position and speed. Actions: steering angle, accelerate, brake. Reward: for example +100 for parking correctly, −100 for a collision, and a small −1 per second to encourage speed.

2. An agent receives rewards 0, 0, 0, +8 on its next four steps, then the episode ends. What is its return with γ = 0.5?

$G = 0 + 0.5 \cdot 0 + 0.5^2 \cdot 0 + 0.5^3 \cdot 8 = 0.125 \cdot 8 = $ 1.

3. What happens to an agent's behaviour if you set γ = 0?

It becomes completely short-sighted (myopic): only the very next reward matters, so it ignores any long-term consequence of its actions.

4. In the policy widget, why does the cliff-edge policy get worse as the slip chance grows, while it is the best with no slip?

With no slip, the edge path is the shortest, so it pays the fewest −1 step costs. With slip, every step along the edge risks sliding into the cliff (−20). Averaged over many episodes, those falls cost more than the extra steps of the safe detour. The value captures this average, which is why the best policy depends on the environment's randomness.

5. What is the difference between exploration and exploitation, and why does an RL agent need both?

Exploitation means choosing the action currently believed to be best; exploration means trying other actions to learn more. Without exploration the agent may never discover a better strategy; without exploitation it never cashes in on what it has learned.

docs.text:
