docs.title: RL from Human Feedback (RLHF) and DPO
docs.text:
TL;DR

A pre-trained language model predicts text; it does not try to be helpful. RLHF fixes that in three stages: fine-tune on good examples (SFT), train a reward model from human comparisons ("reply A is better than reply B"), then use RL (usually PPO) to make the model produce replies the reward model likes, while a KL penalty keeps it close to where it started. DPO reaches the same goal with a single supervised-style loss on the comparisons: no reward model and no RL loop.

Level: advanced · Prerequisites: Policy gradients, Actor-critic (PPO). Knowing what a language model does ("predict the next token") helps.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
This is where the whole RL series pays off. In the first lesson the chatbot row of the table said: state = the conversation so far, action = the next word, reward = a score for the finished reply. This lesson fills in that row.

  • It is how chat assistants are aligned. OpenAI's InstructGPT paper (Ouyang et al., 2022) showed that labellers preferred replies from a 1.3-billion-parameter model fine-tuned with RLHF over replies from the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 it started from. The same recipe, or a close relative, is used to fine-tune most chat assistants.
  • It turns "be helpful" into something you can optimise. Nobody can write a formula for a good answer. But people can easily say which of two answers is better. RLHF learns a reward from those judgements.
  • It shows RL's classic failure modes in a modern setting. Reward hacking, distribution shift and the need for a "leash" on the policy all show up, and the fixes reuse ideas from PPO and from the value-function lessons.

docs.title: Step 1 — The problem: a text predictor is not an assistant
docs.text:
A pre-trained language model has read a huge amount of text and learned one thing: given some text, predict the next token (a word or a piece of a word). Ask it a question and it continues the text in whatever way is most typical of the internet. That might be an answer. It might also be three more questions, a forum argument, or a confident wrong answer.

Prompt: "Why is the sky blue? Explain for a 10-year-old." What a pre-trained model might write "Why is grass green? Why is the sea salty? 50 science questions kids ask…" (it continues the list it thinks it is reading) What we want "Sunlight is made of all colours. Air bounces blue light around much more than red, so blue comes at you from every part of the sky."

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the obvious first fix: collect prompts with good human-written answers and train the model to imitate them (ordinary next-token cross-entropy). It helps a lot. But it has limits:

  1. Writing ideal answers is slow and expensive, and the model can only be as good as the demonstrations.
  2. Imitation never says what is bad. The model sees good answers, not "this answer is wrong", "this one is rude", "this one is long-winded".
  3. "Helpful, honest, harmless" is hard to write as a reward function. You can't code def reward(answer): ... for helpfulness.

The key observation behind RLHF (Christiano et al., 2017) is that comparing is much easier than writing or scoring. Show a person two replies and ask "which is better?". They can answer in seconds, and they don't need to agree on an absolute scale. Those comparisons are the training signal.

docs.title: Step 2 — A language model is a policy
docs.text:
To use RL, we need the familiar pieces from lesson 1: states, actions, a policy and a reward. A language model already is a policy. Generating a reply token by token is an episode:

The probability of a whole reply \(y = (y_1, \dots, y_T)\) is the product of the token probabilities, so its log-probability is a sum:

\[ \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x) = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \log \pi_\theta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t}) \]

That is exactly the \(\log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\) term from the policy gradients lesson, summed over the episode. So REINFORCE, actor-critic and PPO all apply without change. The hard part is the reward.

What to notice

  • The "environment" is trivial: appending a token is deterministic, and nothing pushes back. All the difficulty sits in the reward, which is given only once per reply.
  • Because the reward is per reply, it is common to treat the whole reply as one big action. That simpler view (a "contextual bandit", like the bandits lesson with a prompt as context) is the one the rest of this lesson uses, and it is the view DPO is built on.

docs.title: Step 3 — The RLHF recipe in three stages
docs.text:
The pipeline popularised by InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022), building on Christiano et al. (2017) and Stiennon et al. (2020), has three stages. Click through it:

What to notice

  • Humans appear only once, as labellers of comparisons. Everything after that is automatic: the reward model stands in for the humans during RL, so the policy can be scored millions of times.
  • The SFT model plays two roles in stage 3: it is the starting point of the policy and the reference \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) that the KL penalty measures distance from.

docs.title: Step 4 — Learning a reward from comparisons (Bradley–Terry)
docs.text:
The labellers give us triples \((x, y_w, y_l)\): a prompt, the winning (preferred) reply and the losing one. We want a reward model \(r_\phi(x, y)\) that outputs one number per reply. How do we turn "A beat B" into a training signal for numbers?

The Bradley–Terry model (from 1952, originally for ranking chess players and sports teams) says: the probability that A beats B depends only on the difference of their scores, squashed through the sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\):

\[ P(y_w \succ y_l \mid x) = \sigma\big(r_\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l)\big) \]

Training the reward model is then ordinary maximum likelihood, i.e. logistic regression on the score difference:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{RM}}(\phi) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x, y_w, y_l)}\Big[\log \sigma\big(r_\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l)\big)\Big] \]

Try it: set the reward model's two scores and see what it predicts and how much loss it pays for each possible human choice.

⚖️ Interactive: Bradley–Terry preference probability and loss

What to notice

  • Equal scores mean a coin flip: \(\Delta = 0\) gives \(P = 0.5\) and loss \(\log 2 \approx 0.693\) either way. That is where training starts.
  • Getting it right pays little, getting it wrong costs a lot. At \(\Delta = 2\) the model says \(P = 0.881\); if humans chose A the loss is only 0.127, but if they chose B it is 2.127. At \(\Delta = 4\) the loss for a correct prediction is down to 0.018, so confident, correct pairs stop contributing much.
  • Add +1 to both: nothing changes. Rewards are only defined up to a constant. A reward model's absolute numbers mean nothing; only differences between replies to the same prompt do. (This shift-freedom is exactly what makes DPO possible in Step 6.)
  • Humans disagree and are noisy, so a perfect reward model would not hit 100% accuracy. In the code below, the true hidden preference itself only predicts 84.8% of held-out human choices.

In practice the reward model is a copy of the SFT model with the next-token output layer swapped for a single scalar output. In the toy version below, each "reply" is just three features (helpful, correct, length) and the reward model is linear. The hidden human taste ignores length:

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
X = torch.randn(500, 3)                     # 500 responses, features: helpful, correct, length
w_true = torch.tensor([1.5, 2.0, 0.0])      # the hidden "human taste": length doesn't matter
r_true = X @ w_true

# 5000 comparisons: the labeller prefers a over b with probability sigmoid(r_a - r_b)
a, b = torch.randint(0, 500, (5000,)), torch.randint(0, 500, (5000,))
a_wins = torch.rand(5000) < torch.sigmoid(r_true[a] - r_true[b])
chosen, rejected = torch.where(a_wins, a, b), torch.where(a_wins, b, a)
train, test = slice(0, 4000), slice(4000, 5000)


def reward_model_loss(r_chosen, r_rejected):
    """Bradley-Terry: -log P(chosen beats rejected) = -log sigmoid(r_w - r_l)."""
    return -F.logsigmoid(r_chosen - r_rejected).mean()


reward_model = torch.nn.Linear(3, 1, bias=False)   # in real RLHF: a transformer with a scalar head
opt = torch.optim.Adam(reward_model.parameters(), lr=0.05)
for step in range(301):
    loss = reward_model_loss(reward_model(X[chosen[train]]).squeeze(-1),
                             reward_model(X[rejected[train]]).squeeze(-1))
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    if step % 100 == 0:
        print(f"step {step:3d}  loss {loss.item():.3f}")

with torch.no_grad():
    r = reward_model(X).squeeze(-1)
    acc = (r[chosen[test]] > r[rejected[test]]).float().mean().item()
    acc_true = (r_true[chosen[test]] > r_true[rejected[test]]).float().mean().item()
print("learned weights:", [round(v, 2) for v in reward_model.weight[0].tolist()])
print(f"held-out accuracy: reward model {acc:.3f}, true reward {acc_true:.3f}")

step   0  loss 0.774
step 100  loss 0.334
step 200  loss 0.334
step 300  loss 0.334
learned weights: [1.41, 1.86, 0.05]
held-out accuracy: reward model 0.850, true reward 0.848

From nothing but "A beat B" labels, the reward model recovered the hidden taste (\([1.41, 1.86, 0.05]\) vs the true \([1.5, 2.0, 0.0]\)) and predicts held-out human choices as well as the true reward does. With a real network and real text, it is never this clean: the reward model sees a limited set of comparisons and has to generalise to replies unlike any it was trained on. That is the weak spot Step 5 deals with.

docs.title: Step 5 — RL fine-tuning with a KL leash
docs.text:
Now the RL stage. The policy \(\pi_\theta\) (initialised from the SFT model) writes replies, the reward model scores them, and we maximise

\[ J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D},\; y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)}\big[\, r_\phi(x, y) \,\big] \;-\; \beta\, \mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)\,\big\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)\big) \]

The first term is "get a high score". The second is a leash: the KL divergence \(\mathrm{KL}(\pi \| \pi_{\text{ref}}) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi}\big[\log \tfrac{\pi(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)}\big]\) measures how far the policy has drifted from the SFT model, and \(\beta\) sets how strongly drifting is punished.

The optimiser is usually PPO from the actor-critic lesson. In InstructGPT-style implementations the KL term is folded into the reward, \(r_\phi(x, y) - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)}\), often spread over tokens as a per-token penalty, and a value head (the critic) estimates advantages. So during training four networks are in play: the policy, the frozen reference, the frozen reward model and the critic.

Why the leash? The reward model is only a proxy for what people want. It was trained on replies from the SFT model, so it is only trustworthy near the SFT model's replies. A policy that is pushed hard to maximise the proxy will find the places where the proxy is wrong: replies the reward model over-rates. This is reward hacking or reward over-optimisation, an instance of Goodhart's law ("when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"). Gao et al. (2022) measured it directly: as RL pushes the policy further from its start, the learned reward keeps rising while the true quality first rises and then falls.

The KL-regularised objective has a beautiful exact solution. For one prompt, the best possible policy is

\[ \pi^*(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)\,\exp\!\Big(\frac{r(x, y)}{\beta}\Big), \qquad Z(x) = \sum_{y} \pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)\exp\!\Big(\frac{r(x, y)}{\beta}\Big) \]

Reweight the reference model by the exponentiated reward. (Why: a few lines of algebra show \(\mathbb{E}_\pi[r] - \beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi \| \pi_{\text{ref}}) = \beta \log Z(x) - \beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi \| \pi^*)\). The first term doesn't depend on \(\pi\), and a KL is zero only when the two distributions are equal, so \(\pi = \pi^*\) is the maximum.) We can't compute \(Z(x)\) for a real model, since it sums over every possible reply. That is why RLHF needs RL to approximate \(\pi^*\). But in a toy with five candidate replies we can compute it exactly.

Try it: the prompt is "Why is the sky blue?", asked by a 10-year-old. The SFT model \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) spreads its probability over five replies: A a simple correct answer, B a correct but technical one, C a wrong one ("it reflects the ocean"), D a refusal, and E gushing flattery ("What a WONDERFUL question!!!") with no real answer. The reward model got E badly wrong: it scores it 3.0, the highest of all, while its true quality is −0.5. Lower \(\beta\) (loosen the leash) and watch.

🪢 Interactive: the KL-regularised optimum and reward hacking

What to notice

  • Large \(\beta\) = tight leash. At \(\beta = 10\), \(\pi^*\) is almost \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) (KL 0.012) and the true quality barely moves from the starting model's −0.275 to −0.112.
  • Moderate \(\beta\) helps for real. At \(\beta = 1\) the policy shifts mass from C and D to A (0.391), and the true quality rises to 0.715. Scanning \(\beta\), true quality peaks at 0.717 around \(\beta \approx 1.05\).
  • Small \(\beta\) = reward hacking. At \(\beta = 0.25\) the policy puts 0.947 of its mass on the flattery reply E. The reward-model score climbs to 2.945, but true quality falls to −0.368, worse than the model we started with. As \(\beta \to 0\) the policy collapses onto E entirely (score 3.0, quality −0.5). The purple and green curves on the right are Goodhart's law in one picture.
  • Tick "fix the reward model's mistake on E": now the two curves move together, and loosening the leash keeps helping (true quality 1.976 at \(\beta = 0.25\), nearly all mass on A). The KL penalty is insurance against the reward model's errors, which in real life you can't see.
  • Notice \(\pi^*\) can only move mass between replies that \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) already gives some probability to: a reply with \(\pi_{\text{ref}} = 0\) stays at 0. RLHF sharpens and re-ranks what the SFT model can already say. It doesn't teach it things it could never produce.

docs.title: Step 6 — DPO: skip the reward model and the RL loop
docs.text:
RLHF with PPO works, but it is heavy: two training stages, four networks in memory, sampling replies inside the training loop, and PPO's many hyperparameters. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO; Rafailov et al., 2023) asks: since we know the exact form of the optimal policy, can we skip straight to it?

The trick is to read the closed form from Step 5 backwards. Take logs and solve for the reward:

\[ r(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x) \]

Any policy implies a reward: \(\beta\) times its log-ratio to the reference, plus a term that depends only on the prompt. Now plug this into the Bradley–Terry model from Step 4. Bradley–Terry only uses differences of rewards for the same prompt, so the troublesome \(\beta \log Z(x)\) cancels:

\[ P(y_w \succ y_l \mid x) = \sigma\Big(\beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w \mid x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l \mid x)}\Big) \]

Replace \(\pi^*\) by our trainable policy \(\pi_\theta\) and fit it to the human comparisons by maximum likelihood, exactly as we fitted the reward model:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(\theta) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x, y_w, y_l)}\Big[\log \sigma\Big(\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w \mid x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l \mid x)}\Big)\Big] \]

That's it: the reward model loss with the reward replaced by \(\beta \log \pi_\theta / \pi_{\text{ref}}\). The policy is the reward model ("your language model is secretly a reward model" is the paper's subtitle). Training needs only the log-probabilities of the two fixed replies under \(\pi_\theta\) and \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\): no sampling, no critic, no reward model. Its gradient pushes \(\log \pi_\theta(y_w)\) up and \(\log \pi_\theta(y_l)\) down, weighted by \(\sigma(\hat r_l - \hat r_w)\), i.e. by how badly the implicit rewards \(\hat r = \beta \log \pi_\theta / \pi_{\text{ref}}\) currently rank the pair.

Try it: the same five replies and the same \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) as above. The training data are 200 human comparisons (20 for each pair of replies), drawn from the hidden true quality. Each click runs plain gradient descent (learning rate 1) on the DPO loss.

🎯 Interactive: DPO on five candidate replies

What to notice

  • Step 0: the policy equals \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\), every implicit reward is 0 and the loss is \(\log 2 = 0.693\), just like an untrained reward model.
  • With \(\beta = 1\): after 10 steps A has grown from 0.15 to 0.377 and C has shrunk from 0.30 to 0.126. After 200 steps the policy is \([0.65, 0.268, 0.028, 0.039, 0.015]\) and the loss has levelled off at 0.388.
  • It lands on the green ticks. Fit a Bradley–Terry reward model \(\hat r\) to the same 200 comparisons and compute \(\pi_{\text{ref}} \exp(\hat r/\beta)/Z\): you get \([0.651, 0.267, 0.028, 0.039, 0.015]\), the same policy. DPO and "reward model + exact KL-regularised RL" reach the same answer on this toy, which is the claim of the DPO paper.
  • \(\beta\) is still the leash. \(\beta = 0.5\) ends further from \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) (A at 0.884, KL 1.485, true quality 1.877); \(\beta = 2\) stays closer (A at 0.405, KL 0.295, true quality 0.773).
  • The flattery reply E never gets a chance here: humans compared it directly and it lost most of its comparisons, and there is no separate reward model to fool. That doesn't make DPO immune to over-optimisation, though; with few or one-sided comparisons it can also drift far from \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) in ways the data don't justify.

docs.title: Step 7 — RLHF with PPO vs DPO, and what came next
docs.text:
RLHF with PPO DPO What is trained a reward model, then the policy (plus a critic) the policy only Networks in memory during training policy, reference, reward model, critic policy, reference Data used while training the policy fresh replies sampled from the current policy (on-policy) a fixed dataset of (prompt, winner, loser) Loss PPO's clipped policy-gradient objective on \(r - \beta\,\mathrm{KL}\) a logistic loss on log-probability ratios Strengths can keep exploring and score new replies; a reward model can be reused simple, stable, cheap; ordinary supervised training code Weak spots complex and sensitive to hyperparameters; reward hacking of the reward model can't score replies outside its dataset; depends heavily on the quality and coverage of the comparisons

Neither one is "the winner": both are widely used, and they solve the same objective in theory. Other well-known variations change one ingredient each:

  • Who labels? In RLAIF, an AI model produces the preference labels instead of people. Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022) does this guided by a short written list of principles.
  • Which reward? For maths or code, the reward can come from a checker (is the final answer right? do the tests pass?) instead of a learned model, which removes one source of reward hacking.
  • Which RL algorithm? GRPO (Shao et al., 2024, in the DeepSeekMath paper) drops PPO's critic: it samples a group of replies per prompt and uses the group's average reward as the baseline, the same baseline idea as in REINFORCE.
  • Which preference loss? Many DPO variants (IPO, KTO, ...) change the loss, for example to cope with noisy labels or with single "thumbs up / thumbs down" ratings instead of pairs.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Both routes start from the same human comparisons and the same SFT model, and aim for the same KL-regularised optimum \(\pi^* \propto \pi_{\text{ref}} \exp(r/\beta)\):

Here is DPO on the five-reply toy from the widget, with a compact dpo_loss. In a real model, logp_w would be the sum of token log-probabilities of the winning reply (Step 2), computed by the policy, and ref_logp_w the same under the frozen SFT model:

import itertools
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
names = ["A simple", "B technical", "C wrong", "D refuses", "E flattery"]
ref = torch.tensor([0.15, 0.20, 0.30, 0.30, 0.05])     # π_ref: the SFT model's probabilities
quality = torch.tensor([2.0, 1.0, -1.5, -1.0, -0.5])   # hidden human taste (never shown to DPO)

# 20 human comparisons for every pair of responses
winners, losers = [], []
for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(5), 2):
    for _ in range(20):
        i_wins = torch.rand(()) < torch.sigmoid(quality[i] - quality[j])
        winners.append(i if i_wins else j); losers.append(j if i_wins else i)
W, L = torch.tensor(winners), torch.tensor(losers)


def dpo_loss(logp_w, logp_l, ref_logp_w, ref_logp_l, beta):
    """-log sigmoid( beta * [log π/π_ref (y_w) - log π/π_ref (y_l)] )"""
    h = beta * ((logp_w - ref_logp_w) - (logp_l - ref_logp_l))
    return -F.logsigmoid(h).mean()


beta = 1.0
theta = ref.log().clone().requires_grad_(True)          # the policy's logits; start at π_ref
opt = torch.optim.SGD([theta], lr=1.0)
for step in range(201):
    logp = torch.log_softmax(theta, dim=0)
    loss = dpo_loss(logp[W], logp[L], ref.log()[W], ref.log()[L], beta)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    if step in (0, 10, 50, 200):
        print(f"step {step:3d}  loss {loss.item():.3f}  π = {[round(p, 3) for p in logp.exp().tolist()]}")

step   0  loss 0.693  π = [0.15, 0.2, 0.3, 0.3, 0.05]
step  10  loss 0.448  π = [0.377, 0.313, 0.126, 0.147, 0.038]
step  50  loss 0.390  π = [0.592, 0.293, 0.041, 0.054, 0.019]
step 200  loss 0.388  π = [0.65, 0.268, 0.028, 0.039, 0.015]

For real models, Hugging Face's TRL library implements reward-model training, PPO, DPO and GRPO trainers on top of transformers.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"RLHF teaches the model new knowledge.\"

Mostly it doesn't. The optimal policy \(\pi_{\text{ref}} \exp(r/\beta)/Z\) only reweights replies the starting model could already produce. RLHF changes which of its possible behaviours the model prefers (helpful, honest, on-topic, polite), not what it knows. Knowledge comes from pre-training.

\"The reward model knows what humans want.\"

It is a learned approximation from a limited set of comparisons, and it can be confidently wrong on replies unlike its training data, such as the flattery reply in the widget. Optimise it too hard and you get reward hacking. That's why there is a KL penalty, and why teams keep collecting fresh comparisons.

\"DPO isn't really RL, so it has nothing to do with this course.\"

DPO is trained like supervised learning, but it solves the same KL-regularised RL objective as RLHF; its loss is derived from that objective's exact solution. On the toy above it reaches the same policy as "reward model + optimal RL". It is RL's answer, computed in closed form.

\"A smaller β is always better because the model improves more.\"

A smaller \(\beta\) lets the policy move further from \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\), and the proxy reward always goes up. Whether the true quality goes up depends on whether the reward (or the preference data) is right in the region the policy moves into. In the KL widget, true quality peaks at a moderate \(\beta\) and then falls.

\"Rewards from the reward model are on a meaningful absolute scale.\"

Bradley–Terry only constrains differences: adding a constant to every score changes nothing. A reward of 3.2 means nothing alone; it only means something compared with other replies to the same prompt.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. In the RL view of a language model, what are the state, the action, the episode and the reward?

State: the prompt plus all tokens generated so far. Action: the next token (from the whole vocabulary). Episode: generating one complete reply. Reward: in RLHF, a single score from the reward model for the finished reply (plus a KL penalty), so rewards are sparse and delayed.

2. The reward model gives reply A a score of 3 and reply B a score of 1. What probability does Bradley–Terry give to humans preferring A, and what is the loss if they actually preferred B?

\(\Delta = 3 - 1 = 2\), so \(P(A \succ B) = \sigma(2) = 0.881\). If humans chose B, the loss is \(-\log \sigma(-2) = 2.127\): a confident wrong prediction is punished heavily.

3. What would happen in RLHF if you set β = 0?

Nothing would stop the policy from drifting as far as it likes to maximise the reward model's score. It would find replies the reward model over-rates (reward hacking) and could collapse onto a few of them, losing fluency and diversity. In the KL widget, very small \(\beta\) puts essentially all mass on the flattery reply E, with true quality −0.5, worse than the starting model.

4. Why does the partition function Z(x) disappear in the DPO loss, and why does that matter?

DPO writes the reward as \(\beta \log \frac{\pi(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x)\). Bradley–Terry uses only the difference of two rewards for the same prompt, so the \(\beta \log Z(x)\) terms cancel. That matters because \(Z(x)\) is a sum over every possible reply and can't be computed; without the cancellation the DPO loss would be intractable.

5. Give one advantage of RLHF with PPO over DPO, and one advantage of DPO over RLHF with PPO.

PPO: it is on-policy, so it scores fresh replies from the current model and can improve beyond the replies in a fixed dataset; the reward model can also be reused. DPO: it is much simpler and cheaper, with no reward model, no critic and no sampling during training, and it trains stably with ordinary supervised code.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Paul Christiano et al., Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences (2017). The original idea: learn a reward from comparisons of short clips, then run RL on it.
  • Nisan Stiennon et al., Learning to Summarize from Human Feedback (2020). The reward model + PPO + KL recipe applied to language.
  • Long Ouyang et al., Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback (2022). InstructGPT: SFT → reward model → PPO.
  • Rafael Rafailov et al., Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model (2023). The DPO derivation in full.
  • Leo Gao, John Schulman & Jacob Hilton, Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization (2022). Goodhart's law measured.
  • Yuntao Bai et al., Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback (2022). AI-generated preference labels guided by written principles.
  • Nathan Lambert, Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (free online book). A thorough, practical overview.

docs.title: The Tsetlin Automaton: A Memory That Learns
docs.text:
TL;DR

A Tsetlin automaton is a learner whose entire memory is one integer: a position on a short ladder. Good news (a reward) pushes it deeper into what it is doing; bad news (a penalty) pushes it toward the middle, and crossing the middle means changing its mind. Tsetlin invented it in the 1960s to play bandit problems. A Tsetlin machine gives every literal of every rule one of these memories: the position goes up (memorize) or down (forget) at random, depending on the training examples. Because each update is a small random step, the position does a random walk, and we can compute exactly where it spends its time. A literal that is True often enough for its class ends up Memorized, and the Forget Value sets what "often enough" means. A deeper memory turns this into a sharper, more decisive yes-or-no.

Level: beginner–intermediate · Prerequisites: What is a Tsetlin machine? (literals and rules) and Multi-armed bandits (arms, rewards, ε-greedy). The math needs only fractions and powers.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
• It is the only moving part. A Tsetlin machine is built from thousands of these tiny memories, one per literal per rule. Every rule it learns is just a list of which memories are in their upper half. Understand one memory and you understand what a whole Tsetlin machine is made of.
  • You can predict the result exactly. For a neural network, "what will this weight end up as?" rarely has a clean answer. For one literal of a Tsetlin machine, it has a short formula (Granmo, An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines, Ch. 2, §2.1). You will derive it, check it by simulation, and see why the Forget Value and the memory depth do what they do.
  • It is extremely cheap. A memory that is one small integer, updated by adding or subtracting 1, is ideal for low-power chips. That is a large part of why Tsetlin machines are interesting for hardware, including medical devices that run on a battery.

docs.title: Step 1 — Tsetlin's idea: a memory that is a single integer
docs.text:
Michael Lvovitch Tsetlin (1924–1966) was a Soviet mathematician and physicist. Around 1961 he asked a simple question: how can a very small machine learn to act well in a random environment, when it doesn't know the rules of that environment and can't store much? His answer, now called the Tsetlin automaton, keeps track of all its experience with one integer. The Tsetlin machine is named after him (Granmo, Ch. 1, "Tsetlin Machine Origins").

The setting is exactly the two-armed bandit from the RL series: two actions (arms), each giving a reward with some unknown probability and a penalty otherwise. The automaton has \(2N\) states in a row:

  • the left \(N\) states mean "play arm A", the right \(N\) states mean "play arm B";
  • states far from the centre are deep (confident), states next to the centre are shallow (about to change its mind).

The learning rule is just two sentences:

  1. Reward: move one step deeper into the current half (or stay put if already at the deepest state).
  2. Penalty: move one step toward the centre. If you were already next to the centre, you cross over, so the next pull uses the other arm.

Compare this with the bandit agents you already know. ε-greedy keeps an average reward and a count for every arm and does arithmetic with them. The Tsetlin automaton keeps no estimate of anything. Its position is a kind of running "confidence score", and the depth \(N\) decides how many penalties in a row it takes to talk it out of its current choice.

What to notice

  • Win-stay, lose-shift, with inertia. With \(N = 1\) the rule is "keep the arm after a reward, switch after a penalty". Larger \(N\) adds inertia: a deep automaton shrugs off a few unlucky penalties.
  • It never stops moving. Even on the better arm, penalties keep coming now and then, so the state keeps wandering. Learning is a balance between being pushed out and pulled in, not a final answer.

docs.title: Step 2 — Watch it play a two-armed bandit
docs.text:
Arm A pays a reward with probability 0.4, arm B with probability 0.7, and the automaton starts in the shallowest state of arm A (the worse arm). Next to it, on the same two arms, an ε-greedy agent from the bandits lesson (\(\varepsilon = 0.1\), sample averages) plays its own game. Press +1000 pulls right after the page loads to get the run quoted below.

🎰 Interactive: a Tsetlin automaton plays a two-armed bandit

What to notice

  • It finds the better arm with one integer. In the first run (run #1, \(N = 3\)), after 1000 pulls the automaton had played arm B on 92.7% of pulls and the ε-greedy agent on 81.3%. That run is a lucky one for the automaton. Averaged over 500 runs (in Python), the automaton reaches 88.8% over the first 1000 pulls and ε-greedy 93.4%. So with \(N = 3\) the automaton is slightly worse than ε-greedy on average, with far less memory. With \(N = 5\) it reaches 96.7% and overtakes.
  • Depth is the dial. The green dashed line is the exact long-run share (computed in Step 5's way). For these arms it is 66.7% with \(N = 1\), 80.0% with \(N = 2\), 89.3% with \(N = 3\), 97.5% with \(N = 5\) and 99.96% with \(N = 10\). Slide \(N\) and watch the dot settle deeper.
  • It keeps changing its mind, a little. In run #1 the automaton switched arms 45 times in 1000 pulls. Each switch is a short excursion to arm A that ends after a penalty or two.
  • Now press "Swap the arms", then +1000 pulls again. The world changes: arm A becomes the good one. In run #1, over those 1000 pulls the automaton spent 87.6% of pulls on the new best arm, the ε-greedy agent only 5.2% (the readout's last-100 shares end at 94% and 7%). Its sample averages are built from hundreds of old rewards, so they take a very long time to move. The automaton only needs a short run of penalties to cross the centre. That is what Granmo means by an algorithm that can "change its mind".

When does the automaton fail?

A penalty pushes inward and a reward pushes outward, so the automaton can only settle on an arm if that arm gives more rewards than penalties, i.e. pays with probability above 0.5. With arms paying 0.2 and 0.4, both push the automaton toward the centre more often than away from it. Then even 20 states per arm give only 75.0% on the better arm, and more states don't help. The same "which push is stronger?" question decides what a Tsetlin machine's memory learns, as Steps 4–7 show.

docs.title: Step 3 — From actions to memory: one integer per literal
docs.text:
A Tsetlin machine reuses the automaton, with new names. Each literal in each rule (lesson 1) gets its own little ladder of memory positions:

Tsetlin automaton The book's literal memory \(2N\) states memory positions \(1, 2, \dots, D\) (the book's Chapter 1 uses \(D = 10\)) the two actions Forgotten (lower half, positions \(1 \dots D/2\)) or Memorized (upper half) deepest state of each action position 1 = Maximally Forgotten, position \(D\) = Maximally Memorized reward / penalty feedback that pushes the literal up (memorize) or down (forget)

A rule's condition is the AND of its Memorized literals. The book calls the number of positions \(D\) the memory depth; in research papers you'll read "a Tsetlin automaton with \(2N\) states", so \(D = 2N\), and the two actions are called include and exclude. A new rule starts with every literal just below the line (position \(D/2\), "about to be memorized but still Forgotten").

Two details matter for everything that follows:

  • Updates are random. Before moving a literal up, the machine draws a random number between 0 and 1 and skips the move if it is above the Memorize Value. Moving down is skipped if the number is above the Forget Value. Randomness stops a coincidence from locking the rule in, and it keeps rules exploring (Granmo, Ch. 1, §1.3).
  • Which way to push. For one literal and a training example of the rule's own class \(Y\), the rule is simple: if the literal is True, push it up (memorize); if it is False, push it down (forget). Lesson 3 explains the full feedback rules, which also handle the whole rule and the other classes.

What to notice

  • "Memorized" is a region, not a single value. A literal at position 6 and one at position 10 are both in the rule. The deeper one would need many more forgetting steps to leave.
  • Memorize and Forget Value are two speed dials. The book's Chapter 1 examples use pairs that add to 1, like Memorize 0.1 and Forget 0.9. From Chapter 2 on, the book (like the research papers) uses Memorize Value 1 and Forget Value \(1/s\), where \(s\) is called the specificity. This lesson uses that version.

docs.title: Step 4 — One literal, one class: a random walk
docs.text:
Take the simplest case. A rule for class \(Y\) sees only examples of \(Y\), and one of its literals, \(L\), is True in a fraction \(p = P(L \mid Y)\) of them. Each example then moves the literal:

  • up one position with probability \(p\) (literal True; Memorize Value 1, so the move always happens), unless already at the top;
  • down one position with probability \((1-p)\cdot\frac{1}{s}\) (literal False, and the random draw allows the forget step), unless already at the bottom;
  • otherwise it stays where it is.

The examples come in random order, so the position wanders up and down: a random walk. Its next position depends only on where it is now and on the next random example. Mathematicians call such a process a Markov chain (the same "Markov" as in MDPs).

🧠 Interactive: one literal's memory, example by example

What to notice

  • The bars settle onto the orange ticks. With the defaults (\(p = 0.3\), \(s = 3\), depth 10), press +10,000 examples once: the literal has spent 75.9% of its time Memorized, against an exact long-run value of 77.8%. A million examples in Python give 77.7%. The orange ticks are that exact answer, derived in the next step.
  • It never stops wandering. Press Play and watch the triangle. Even when it is usually Memorized, a run of False examples can push it below the line for a while.
  • Find the tipping point. Slide \(p\) down to 0.25 with \(s = 3\): the bars spread out evenly over all positions. Just above 0.25, the literal leans toward Memorized; just below, toward Forgotten. The readout's ratio ρ crosses 1 exactly there.

docs.title: Step 5 — The exact learning outcome
docs.text:
Run the walk for a long time and record the share of time it spends at each position. That share settles down to a fixed distribution, the stationary distribution \(\pi_1, \dots, \pi_D\). The book finds it by solving \(\pi = \pi \mathbf{M}\), where \(\mathbf{M}\) is the matrix of transition probabilities (or by multiplying a starting distribution by \(\mathbf{M}^{10000}\)). For a walk that only moves one step at a time there is a shortcut:

In the long run, the walk crosses each gap upward exactly as often as downward. (It can't go up across the gap between positions \(i\) and \(i+1\) twice without coming back down in between.)

The rate of upward crossings is "time at \(i\)" × "probability of moving up", and the rate of downward crossings is "time at \(i+1\)" × "probability of moving down". So

\[ \pi_i \cdot p \;=\; \pi_{i+1} \cdot \frac{1-p}{s} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{\pi_{i+1}}{\pi_i} \;=\; \rho \;=\; \frac{s\,p}{1-p}. \]

Every step up the ladder multiplies the time spent there by the same ratio \(\rho\). So \(\pi_i \propto \rho^{\,i-1}\): a geometric staircase, rising if \(\rho > 1\) and falling if \(\rho < 1\). Add up the upper half (with \(D = 2n\) positions) and almost everything cancels:

\[ P(\text{Memorized}) \;=\; \frac{\rho^{\,n}}{1+\rho^{\,n}}. \]

Read off what it says:

  • The tipping point is \(\rho = 1\), i.e. \(p = p^* = \dfrac{1}{s+1}\). A literal that is True in more than a fraction \(\frac{1}{s+1}\) of its class's examples is more likely Memorized than not. With \(s = 3\) that is \(p^* = 0.25\), which is why the widget balanced there.
  • The Forget Value sets the tipping point. A large \(s\) (small Forget Value \(1/s\)) means slow forgetting, so even rarer literals stay: with \(s = 15\), \(p^* = 0.0625\). A small \(s\) keeps only very common literals. The book puts it as "the Forget Value allows you to control the frequency of the patterns learnt" (Ch. 2, §2.1).
  • The defaults again: \(p = 0.3\), \(s = 3\) gives \(\rho = 1.286\), and with depth 10 (\(n = 5\)), $P(\text{Memorized}) = 1.286^5/(1 + 1.286^5) = $ 0.778, the orange ticks above.

Chapter 1's Memorize Value + Forget Value = 1

With a general Memorize Value \(m\) and Forget Value \(f\), the ratio is \(\rho = \frac{m\,p}{f\,(1-p)}\). If \(m + f = 1\), then \(\rho = 1\) exactly when \(p = f\): a literal survives if it is True in more than a fraction "Forget Value" of the class's examples. Take the three cars of the book's vehicle table (Granmo, Ch. 1, Table 1.1): Four Wheels is True for all three, Yellow for two, Blue for one. With depth 10 and Memorize 0.5 / Forget 0.5, Yellow (2/3 > 0.5) is Memorized with probability 0.970 and Blue (1/3) only 0.030. With Chapter 1's Memorize 0.1 / Forget 0.9, even Yellow drops to 0.001, and only literals that hold for every car, like Four Wheels, stay. (This treats each literal on its own. In a real rule the literals interact, which is the subject of lesson 3.)

What to notice

  • The answer is a probability, not a verdict. The Tsetlin machine never "decides once and for all". The book: "the outcome of Tsetlin machine learning is not a single solution", it is a distribution over solutions that the machine keeps visiting.
  • The start doesn't matter. The stationary distribution is the same wherever the literal starts. That is why the book says the initialization "does not affect the end result" (Ch. 1, §1.3).

docs.title: Step 6 — Deeper memory, sharper decisions
docs.text:
The formula \(\rho^n/(1+\rho^n)\) has a familiar shape. Write it as \(1/(1+\rho^{-n})\) = \(\sigma(n \ln\rho)\), where \(\sigma\) is the logistic sigmoid. The depth \(n\) multiplies the "evidence" \(\ln\rho\) before the sigmoid. Doubling the depth makes the switch from Forgotten to Memorized twice as steep.

📈 Interactive: deeper memory sharpens the decision

What to notice

  • Every curve passes through 0.5 at \(p^*\). Depth doesn't move the tipping point; only \(s\) does.
  • Depth decides how decisive the literal is. With \(s = 3\), take \(p = 0.3\), just above \(p^* = 0.25\): depths 2, 4, 8 and 20 give $P(\text{Memorized}) = $ 0.563, 0.623, 0.732, 0.925. At \(p = 0.2\), just below: 0.429, 0.360, 0.240, 0.053. A shallow memory hedges; a deep one commits.
  • Depth 2 is a coin flip with a bias. With one Forgotten and one Memorized position, the curve is very flat: the literal flips between in and out of the rule all the time.
  • The price of depth is speed. Back in the bandit widget, a deep automaton needs more penalties to cross the centre. Averaged over 500 runs, in the first 100 pulls after the arms swap, the automaton played the new best arm 82.3% of the time with \(N = 3\) but only 20.5% with \(N = 20\).

docs.title: Step 7 — The other class joins: the book's complete single-literal chain
docs.text:
A real rule also sees examples of other classes, written \(\bar{Y}\) ("not \(Y\)"). The book (Ch. 2, §2.1) builds the full chain from the four kinds of example a single literal can meet. With Memorize Value 1 and Forget Value \(1/s\):

Example What happens to the literal Feedback (lesson 3) class \(Y\), literal True: \((L, Y)\) one step up Recognize class \(Y\), literal False: \((\lnot L, Y)\) one step down, with probability \(1/s\) Erase other class, literal False: \((\lnot L, \bar{Y})\) one step up, but only while Forgotten Reject other class, literal True: \((L, \bar{Y})\) nothing none

The third row is new. If the literal is Forgotten, the rule ignores it, and the rule wrongly fires for an example of another class. Memorizing a literal that is False for that example would make the rule reject it. Once the literal is Memorized, the job is done and Reject Feedback stops pushing. Multiply each kind of move by how often its example occurs and you get three numbers per example:

\[ \begin{aligned} a &= P(L \mid Y)\,P(Y) + P(\lnot L \mid \bar{Y})\,P(\bar{Y}) && \text{(up, while Forgotten)}\\ r &= P(L \mid Y)\,P(Y) && \text{(up, while Memorized)}\\ e &= \tfrac{1}{s}\,P(\lnot L \mid Y)\,P(Y) && \text{(down, anywhere above 1)} \end{aligned} \]

The same balance argument as in Step 5 works, with ratio \(a/e\) for the steps inside the Forgotten half (and across the line) and \(r/e\) inside the Memorized half. For depth 4 it gives

\[ \pi_1 : \pi_2 : \pi_3 : \pi_4 \;=\; e^3 \;:\; a\,e^2 \;:\; a^2 e \;:\; a^2 r , \]

which is the book's Table 2.1 after multiplying everything by \(s^3/P(Y)\). Larger depths just add more factors of \(a/e\) and \(r/e\). The four scenarios of the book make the factors concrete. We computed each one exactly and by simulating a million examples (code below):

Book scenario Settings Exact \(\pi_1 \dots \pi_D\) \(P(\text{Memorized})\) Book says 1. Infrequent literal, fast forgetting \(s = 1\), \(P(Y) = 0.9\), \(P(L \mid Y) = 0.1\), \(P(\lnot L \mid \bar{Y}) = 0.9\), depth 4 0.783, 0.174, 0.039, 0.004 0.043 0.04 2. Same literal, slow forgetting as 1, but \(s = 15\) 0.029, 0.098, 0.327, 0.545 0.872 0.87 3. Discriminative literal \(s = 15\), \(P(Y) = 0.82\), \(P(L \mid Y) = 0.99\), \(P(\lnot L \mid \bar{Y}) = 0.5\), depth 4 0.000, 0.000, 0.001, 0.999 \(1 - 4.1 \times 10^{-7}\) 0.9999 4. Deeper memory as 3, but depth 8 almost all at 8 \(1 - 1.9 \times 10^{-13}\) ≈ 1.0 🧪 Interactive: the complete single-literal chain, with the book's scenarios

What to notice

  • Scenario 1 vs 2: the Forget Value decides. In scenario 1 the literal is True for only 10% of class \(Y\) and carries no information about the class (the book checks with Bayes' rule that \(P(Y \mid L) = 0.9 = P(Y)\)). With fast forgetting (\(s = 1\)) it is almost always Forgotten. Slow the forgetting to \(s = 15\) and the same literal is kept 87% of the time: it is now above the frequency threshold the Forget Value sets. The widget starts in scenario 2; its first 10,000 examples spend 87.9% of the time Memorized.
  • Scenario 3: discriminative literals are kept firmly. A literal that is True for 99% of class \(Y\) and False for half the other class gets pushed up by both Recognize and Reject. It is Memorized all but \(4 \times 10^{-7}\) of the time.
  • Scenario 4: depth again. Going from 4 to 8 positions shrinks the chance of being Forgotten from \(4.1 \times 10^{-7}\) to \(1.9 \times 10^{-13}\). Each extra position multiplies the odds by another factor \(a/e\) or \(r/e\): "increasing the number of Literal Automaton states improves learning accuracy exponentially" (Ch. 2, §2.1).

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Knob What it does Effect on one literal \(p = P(L \mid Y)\) how often the literal is True in its class more often → pushed up more often Forget Value \(1/s\) how often a forget step is carried out sets the tipping point \(p^* = 1/(s+1)\) (only class \(Y\)) memory depth \(D\) number of memory positions same tipping point, but a sharper, more decisive outcome; slower to change its mind other class: \(P(\lnot L \mid \bar{Y})\) how often the literal rules out other classes extra push up while Forgotten (Reject): discriminative literals are kept

Here is the whole analysis in numpy: the exact stationary distribution from the "balanced flow across each gap" rule, and a simulation to check it, on the book's four scenarios.

import numpy as np


def literal_chain(p_Y, p_L_Y, p_notL_notY, s, depth):
    """Up/down probabilities of one literal's memory position (positions 1..depth)."""
    a = p_L_Y * p_Y + p_notL_notY * (1 - p_Y)    # up while forgotten: Recognize + Reject
    r = p_L_Y * p_Y                              # up while memorized: Recognize only
    e = (1 - p_L_Y) * p_Y / s                    # down: Erase with Forget Value 1/s
    up = [a if i <= depth // 2 else r for i in range(1, depth)]   # from position i to i+1
    return up, e


def stationary(p_Y, p_L_Y, p_notL_notY, s, depth):
    """Exact long-run distribution: flow up across each gap = flow down across it."""
    up, e = literal_chain(p_Y, p_L_Y, p_notL_notY, s, depth)
    w = np.cumprod([1.0] + [u / e for u in up])
    return w / w.sum()


def simulate(p_Y, p_L_Y, p_notL_notY, s, depth, steps=1_000_000, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    pos, time_at = depth // 2, np.zeros(depth)
    for u1, u2, u3 in rng.random((steps, 3)):
        if u1 < p_Y:                                         # an example of class Y
            if u2 < p_L_Y:
                pos = min(depth, pos + 1)                    # literal True: memorize
            elif u3 < 1 / s:
                pos = max(1, pos - 1)                        # literal False: forget, with prob 1/s
        elif u2 < p_notL_notY and pos <= depth // 2:         # other class, literal False
            pos += 1                                         # memorize, but only while forgotten
        time_at[pos - 1] += 1
    return time_at / steps


scenarios = {"1": (0.9, 0.1, 0.9, 1, 4), "2": (0.9, 0.1, 0.9, 15, 4),
             "3": (0.82, 0.99, 0.5, 15, 4), "4": (0.82, 0.99, 0.5, 15, 8)}
for name, args in scenarios.items():
    exact, sim = stationary(*args), simulate(*args)
    half = args[-1] // 2
    print(f"scenario {name}: P(memorized) exact {exact[half:].sum():.4f}, simulated {sim[half:].sum():.4f}")
print("scenario 2, exact per position:", np.round(stationary(*scenarios["2"]), 3))

scenario 1: P(memorized) exact 0.0430, simulated 0.0426
scenario 2: P(memorized) exact 0.8724, simulated 0.8719
scenario 3: P(memorized) exact 1.0000, simulated 1.0000
scenario 4: P(memorized) exact 1.0000, simulated 1.0000
scenario 2, exact per position: [0.029 0.098 0.327 0.545]

The exact values match the book's figures (0.04, 0.87, 0.9999 and ≈ 1.0) and the simulation agrees to within a few thousandths. We also checked the exact answer against the book's own method, \(\pi \mathbf{M}^{10000}\), and against its Table 2.1.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"A Memorized literal stays memorized.\"

The position keeps moving forever. In scenario 2 the literal is Memorized 87.2% of the time, so 12.8% of the time it is out of the rule. Learning gives a distribution, and the rule you read off at any moment is one sample from it. Deeper memory makes the sample far more reliable.

\"Deeper memory is simply better.\"

Deeper memory makes the long-run outcome sharper, but it also makes the automaton slower to change its mind. After the arms swapped, an automaton with 20 states per arm played the new best arm only 20.5% of the time in the next 100 pulls, against 82.3% with 3 states (500 runs each). Depth trades decisiveness against adaptivity.

\"The automaton estimates how good each action is.\"

It stores no estimate, average or count, only its position. The position is not a probability either: two automata at the same position can face very different environments. Only the long-run distribution of the position tells you about the environment.

\"A literal is memorized if it is True for most examples of the class.\"

The tipping point is \(p^* = 1/(s+1)\), set by the Forget Value, not 50%. With \(s = 15\) a literal that is True for only 7% of the class can still be Memorized more often than not. Choosing \(s\) is choosing how frequent a pattern must be to enter a rule.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. A Tsetlin automaton with N = 1 (one state per arm) plays arms paying 0.4 and 0.7. What share of pulls goes to the better arm in the long run?

With \(N = 1\) it is win-stay, lose-shift: it leaves an arm after every penalty. It leaves arm A with probability 0.6 and arm B with probability 0.3, so it stays on B twice as long: share on B $= \frac{0.6}{0.6 + 0.3} = $ 66.7%, the value the widget shows for \(N = 1\).

2. Only class-Y examples, s = 4, and the literal is True in 25% of them. Is it more likely Memorized or Forgotten? What is P(Memorized) with depth 4?

The tipping point is \(p^* = 1/(4+1) = 0.2\), and \(0.25 > 0.2\), so Memorized is more likely. \(\rho = \frac{4 \times 0.25}{0.75} = 1.333\), depth 4 means \(n = 2\): $P = \frac{1.333^2}{1 + 1.333^2} = \frac{1.778}{2.778} = $ 0.64.

3. You want rules to keep literals that are True in at least 10% of a class's examples. Which s (and Forget Value) should you choose?

Set the tipping point \(\frac{1}{s+1} = 0.1\), so \(s = 9\) and the Forget Value is \(1/9 \approx 0.111\). (This uses the single-literal picture; in a real rule, literals interact, as lesson 3 shows.)

4. Why does Reject Feedback push the literal up only while it is Forgotten?

Reject Feedback is there to stop the rule from firing on another class. If the literal is already Memorized and False for that example, the rule's AND is already False: the rule doesn't fire, and there is nothing to fix. Only a Forgotten literal that is False for the other class could still help, by joining the rule.

5. In the bandit widget, swapping the arms barely bothers the automaton but ruins ε-greedy. Why?

ε-greedy's sample average for the old best arm is built from hundreds of rewards, and each new reward moves it by only 1/n. It takes a very long time to fall below the other arm's estimate (which is rarely updated, since that arm is mostly explored at random). The automaton has no such long memory: a few penalties in a row move it across the centre. In run #1 that meant 87.6% vs 5.2% on the new best arm over the next 1000 pulls.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Ole-Christoffer Granmo, An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines (free online). Ch. 1, §1.3 (graded memory, Memorize and Forget Value, randomized updates; the "Tsetlin Machine Origins" box) and Ch. 2, §2.1 (the single-literal Markov chain, Table 2.1 and the four scenarios). This lesson's figures are redrawn from these sections.
  • Ole-Christoffer Granmo, The Tsetlin Machine: A Game Theoretic Bandit Driven Approach to Optimal Pattern Recognition with Propositional Logic (2018). The original Tsetlin machine paper, in research-paper terms (Type I/II feedback, include/exclude, specificity \(s\)).
  • M. L. Tsetlin, Automaton Theory and Modeling of Biological Systems (Academic Press, 1973). English translation of Tsetlin's work on automata in random environments.
  • Kumpati Narendra & Mandayam Thathachar, Learning Automata: An Introduction (1989). The textbook treatment of the Tsetlin automaton and its relatives, including when they are guaranteed to find the better action.
