docs.title: Many Rules Voting: Classification with a Tsetlin Machine
docs.text:
TL;DR

One AND-rule can describe only one kind of patient. A Tsetlin machine therefore uses a whole team of rules: some vote for a class, some vote against it. Each rule whose condition is True casts one vote, and the vote sum \(v\) (votes for minus votes against) decides the class. During training, a single number, the Voting Margin \(T\), decides how much feedback each example hands out: examples the team already gets right by a margin of \(T\) votes give no feedback at all, and examples it gets wrong give a lot. That simple rule makes the rules spread out over different sub-patterns instead of all learning the same one. This lesson builds the complete machine, extends it to many classes, and runs it end to end on the breast-cancer recurrence data, with an honest look at the accuracy.

Level: beginner–intermediate · Prerequisites: Recognize, Erase & Reject feedback (how a single rule learns). Fractions and a sum are all the math you need.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
In the last lesson a single rule learned a single pattern, such as "if Deg-malig 3 and not Menopause lt40 then Recurrence". Real classes are rarely that tidy:

  • Patients recur for different reasons. In the breast-cancer data, some recurrences come with a highly malignant tumour, others with many affected lymph nodes, and a rule demanding both misses everyone who has only one of them.
  • Evidence should add up. A clinician weighs several findings, some pointing towards recurrence and some away from it. A sum of votes does the same thing, and you can still read every vote as a plain rule.
  • This is the whole machine. Everything from the earlier lessons (literals, the graded memory, the three kinds of feedback) comes together here. After this lesson you can write a working Tsetlin machine in about 70 lines of numpy and read what it learned.

The ideas follow Granmo, An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines, Ch. 1, §1.5–1.7, and Ch. 2, §2.3. The visuals and code are redrawn and rewritten for this site.

docs.title: Step 1 — One rule is not enough
docs.text:
A rule in a Tsetlin machine is an AND of literals: every memorized literal must be True for the rule to fire. That makes each rule a description of one kind of object. But a class often contains several kinds.

Look at the 85 patients with a recurrence in the UCI breast-cancer data (286 patients in total; we count "3 or more involved lymph nodes" as not Inv-nodes 0-2):

Recurrence patients (85) how many Deg-malig 3 and 3+ involved nodes 27 Deg-malig 3 only 18 3+ involved nodes only 12 neither 28

And how often patients with each profile recur, out of everyone with that profile:

Profile recurred Deg-malig 3 and 3+ nodes 27 of 37 (73%) Deg-malig 3 only 18 of 48 (38%) 3+ nodes only 12 of 36 (33%) neither 28 of 165 (17%)

There are (at least) two recurrence profiles: a highly malignant tumour, and spread to the lymph nodes. The single rule "Deg-malig 3 AND not Inv-nodes 0-2" only catches the 27 patients who have both. To also catch the 18 + 12 who have just one of them, you need an OR: "Deg-malig 3" or "not Inv-nodes 0-2". An AND-rule cannot express an OR, but two rules can: one for each profile.

This is the general recipe. Any yes/no pattern can be written as an OR of AND-rules (logicians call it disjunctive normal form), so a team of AND-rules can describe any class, as long as the team is big enough and its members learn different things. Making them learn different things is the main topic of this lesson.

What to notice

  • One AND-rule = one sub-pattern (one "profile"). Several sub-patterns need several rules.
  • None of the profiles is certain: even the strongest one recurs in only 73% of cases, and 28 of the 85 recurrences fit neither profile. Keep this in mind when we measure accuracy in Step 6.

docs.title: Step 2 — Rules vote: the vote sum v
docs.text:
A Tsetlin machine for two classes has two groups of rules:

  • rules that vote for the class (here: Recurrence),
  • rules that vote against it (they vote for No recurrence).

To classify a patient, every rule checks its condition on the patient's literals. Each rule whose condition is True casts one vote. Then

\[ v \;=\; \underbrace{\#\{\text{rules for Recurrence that fire}\}}_{\text{votes for}} \;-\; \underbrace{\#\{\text{rules against that fire}\}}_{\text{votes against}} \]

and the machine predicts Recurrence if \(v > 0\) and No recurrence otherwise. A tie (\(v = 0\)) has to go one way or the other; here it goes to the more common class, No recurrence (the book's notebook sends ties to the first class instead, and the convolutional lesson follows the notebook). (In the research papers the two groups are the positive and negative polarity clauses \(C^+_j\) and \(C^-_j\), and \(v = \sum_j C^+_j - \sum_j C^-_j\).) An empty rule, one with no literals memorized, stays silent when classifying.

The book's first example uses the six patients from the earlier lessons and three rules: R1 and R2 are the same rule, "Deg-malig 3 and not Menopause lt40", voting for Recurrence, and R3, "Inv-nodes 0-2", votes against. Pick the book's patients in the widget below:

🗳️ Interactive: rules vote on a patient

What to notice

  • Patient #1 (ge40, 3-5 nodes, Deg-malig 3): R1 and R2 fire, R3 does not, so \(v = +2\) → Recurrence. Correct.
  • Patient #5 (premeno, 0-2 nodes, Deg-malig 3) fires all three rules: R3 votes against because of the 0-2 nodes. The duplicate R1 + R2 still win, \(v = 2 - 1 = +1\). A lone rule would have been out-voted to a tie. Duplicated rules act as a weight.
  • The vote sums for the six patients are \(+2, -1, +2, -1, +1, -1\): all six correct.
  • Switch to "learned from 200 patients" to see the 20 rules the machine learns in Step 6, written in plain English. Hover a rule to see its raw literals.

This is what the book means by unifying rule-based and summation-based decisions: each vote is a readable rule, like a branch of a decision tree, and the decision is a sum, like logistic regression with all weights equal to 1.

docs.title: Step 3 — The Voting Margin T: how much feedback does an example get?
docs.text:
Training has to decide, for every example, which rules learn from it. A naive answer is "all of them, every time". Then every rule for Recurrence sees the same stream of examples and the same feedback, and they all drift towards the same, most frequent pattern. You get ten copies of one rule.

The Tsetlin machine instead asks: how far is this example from being safely classified? You choose a Voting Margin \(T\), a whole number of votes. For a training example:

  1. Compute the vote sum from the example's own point of view: votes for its true class minus votes for the other class. (Empty rules count as True during training, so a fresh machine has something to work on.)
  2. Clip it to the range \([-T, T]\).
  3. Give each rule, independently, feedback with probability
\[ p \;=\; \frac{T - v}{2T}. \]

The book's example uses \(T = 2\), so \(p = (2 - v)/4\):

vote sum \(v\) (own class − other) \(-2\) or less \(-1\) \(0\) \(+1\) \(+2\) or more feedback probability \(p\) 1 0.75 0.5 0.25 0

If the team already wins by \(T\) votes, nobody learns from this example: the job is done, and those rules are free to work on other examples. If the team is losing badly, every rule gets feedback.

The kind of feedback is the same as in the previous lesson. A rule of the example's own class gets Recognize Feedback if it fired and Erase Feedback if it did not. A rule of the other class gets Reject Feedback if it fired (it voted wrongly) and nothing otherwise.

🎚️ Interactive: how the Voting Margin hands out feedback

What to notice

  • Two mirror-image lines. The chart's \(v\) counts votes for Recurrence. For a patient with recurrence that is "own minus other"; for a patient without, it is the reverse. So the two kinds of patients want \(v\) pushed in opposite directions.
  • Outside the purple band nothing changes. Once \(v \ge T\) for a recurrence patient (or \(v \le -T\) for a non-recurrence patient), the probability is 0. Raising \(T\) widens the band: the team must win by more votes before it stops learning.
  • The book's prioritisation example (\(T = 2\), rules "Deg-malig 3 and not lt40" and "Deg-malig 3" for, "Inv-nodes 0-2" against): patients #1 and #3 reach \(v = +2\) and give no feedback; #4, #5 and #6 are one vote short and give feedback a quarter of the time; patient #2 (no recurrence, but both rules for Recurrence fire) ends in a tie, \(v = 0\), and gives feedback half of the time. The examples that need it most get the most attention.

docs.title: Step 4 — The complete learning algorithm
docs.text:
Put the pieces together and you have the whole training procedure. Every rule starts empty, with all its literals at the top of the Forgotten half of its memory. Then, for each training example in turn:

That is the entire algorithm. There is no gradient, no loss function and no global optimiser. Each rule only ever sees its own condition, the example, and one coin flip. The coordination between rules comes entirely from the shared vote sum inside \(p\).

Why it coordinates the rules (the book's argument)

  • Reject Feedback is targeted. Only rules that fired and voted for the wrong class receive it. Rules that voted correctly are shielded.
  • Useful rules learn fastest. A rule that matches many examples of its class and never votes wrongly gets the most Recognize Feedback and no Reject Feedback, so its literals sink deepest into memory.
  • Satisfied examples stop pulling. Once a sub-pattern is covered by enough votes, its examples hand out no more feedback. The remaining feedback comes from examples that are not yet covered, so idle or weak rules drift towards those. The book calls this a resource-allocation effect.

docs.title: Step 5 — Why the margin matters: two rules, one OR pattern
docs.text:
Chapter 2 of the book makes this precise with the smallest interesting case. The class is \(Y = x_1 \text{ OR } x_2\) (with 10% of the labels flipped as noise). There are two rules, both voting for \(Y\), and each rule can memorize \(x_1\), \(x_2\), both, or neither. Of the 16 possible pairs of rules, only two solve the problem: one rule "if \(x_1\) then Y" and the other "if \(x_2\) then Y".

A tempting wrong answer is "if \(x_1\) AND \(x_2\) then Y": it is very precise when it fires, but it misses every example where only one of them is True. Two copies of it are a sub-optimal configuration (a local optimum): no single rule can improve things by changing alone.

In this game there are no rules voting against \(Y\), so \(v\) is just the number of firing rules. With margin \(T\), a \(Y\) example gives each rule feedback with probability \((T - v)/T\), and a not-\(Y\) example with probability \(v/T\) (with \(v\) capped at \(T\)). With \(T = 2\): a \(Y\) example with one rule firing gives feedback half of the time; with both firing, never.

🤝 Interactive: two rules learning x1 OR x2

What to notice

  • Without a margin (every rule gets feedback every time), fast-forward to 200,000 steps: the pair spends 60.7% of the time as two copies of "x1 AND x2", and only 7.1% in the correct OR solution. Both rules chase the same, most precise pattern.
  • With \(T = 2\) the picture flips: 81.4% of the time in the OR solution, and only 0.3% as two AND-copies. As soon as one rule covers \(x_1\), examples it handles no longer push the other rule, which is left to pick up \(x_2\).
  • \(T\) must fit the team. With \(T = 1\) (one vote is "enough") the second rule rarely gets feedback and only 28.6% of the time is spent in the solution. With \(T = 3\) or \(T = 4\) the team can never reach the margin (two rules give at most two votes), so feedback never fully stops: 26.4% and 18.1%, and with \(T = 4\) the two AND-copies are back at 25.4%.
  • These are time shares from one seeded run (seed 42, Forget Value \(1/s\) with \(s = 4\), Memorize Value 1.0, memory depth 4), computed in Python and reproduced exactly by the widget. The book computes the exact long-run probabilities with a Markov chain instead and finds the same story: without the margin the AND-copies are the most likely outcome; with \(T = 2\) any configuration involving them has essentially zero probability.

The lesson generalises: the Voting Margin should be roughly the number of votes you expect a well-covered example to collect. Too small, and rules stop learning before every sub-pattern has a rule. Too large, and feedback never switches off, so rules keep crowding onto the most common pattern.

docs.title: Step 6 — The full run: breast-cancer recurrence
docs.text:
Now the real thing. The data is the public UCI Breast Cancer dataset (University Medical Centre, Ljubljana, donated by M. Zwitter and M. Soklic): 286 patients, 85 of whom (29.7%) had a recurrence. Like the book's chapter, we use three properties, Menopause, Inv-nodes and Deg-malig, and Booleanize them with one feature per value: 3 + 7 + 3 = 13 Boolean features, so 26 literals.

The setup, fixed in advance:

  • shuffle the patients with seed 1; 200 for training, 86 for testing (23 of the test patients had a recurrence);
  • 10 rules for and 10 rules against Recurrence, Voting Margin \(T = 10\);
  • Forget Value \(1/s\) with \(s = 3\) (so Memorize Value \(2/3\));
  • memory depth 200 (positions 1–200; Memorized above 100). The book's toy examples use depth 10; a deeper memory makes the rules steadier on noisy data;
  • 60 epochs; a tie (\(v = 0\)) is predicted as No recurrence.

The widget trains exactly this machine in your browser. Change the knobs and it retrains in a second or two.

🏋️ Interactive: train a Tsetlin machine on breast-cancer data

What to notice

  • With the defaults the machine ends at 75.0% training and 74.4% test accuracy (64 of 86 test patients right). That sounds fine until you see the dashed line: always answering "no recurrence" scores 73.3% on the same test set. The machine is one patient better than the trivial answer.
  • It catches some recurrences. It flags 15 test patients, 8 of them correctly, so it finds 8 of the 23 recurrences, with 7 false alarms among the 63 others. The trivial answer finds none.
  • The test curve jumps around. Between epochs 11 and 60 the test accuracy moves between 68.6% and 76.7%. With 86 test patients, one patient is 1.2 percentage points, so a single lucky or unlucky epoch says little.
  • The rules for Recurrence spread out. Look at the learned rules: one broad rule, "Inv-nodes is not 0-2", matches 29 recurrence and 26 non-recurrence training patients; the rest specialise on small groups (6-8, 12-14, 15-17 or 24-26 nodes, or Menopause lt40). That is the resource allocation of Step 4 at work: once the common cases are covered, idle rules move to patients nobody has covered yet. On noisy data that also means chasing rare individuals: four identical rules memorized "Inv-nodes 24-26", which matches a single training patient.
  • Try \(T = 1\) or \(T = 2\), or 1 rule per class. With one rule per class and \(T = 1\) the machine never predicts Recurrence on this split. Change the seed to get a different train/test split and watch the accuracy move by several points.

docs.title: How good is that, honestly?
docs.text:
One split is not enough to judge a model on 86 test patients. So we repeated the run on 10 different random splits (seeds 1–10, same settings) and compared with simple baselines on the same splits and the same 13 features:

Method (10 random 200/86 splits) test accuracy, mean ± sd Always "no recurrence" 70.7% ± 3.1 The book's single rule "Deg-malig 3 and not Menopause lt40" 71.2% ± 3.8 Tsetlin machine (10 + 10 rules, \(T = 10\), \(s = 3\)) 71.3% ± 3.7 (range 64.0–75.6%) Logistic regression (scikit-learn defaults) 72.7% ± 3.5 Decision tree, depth 3 72.9% ± 3.7

All of these are within about one standard deviation of each other and of the trivial baseline. Using all nine properties of the dataset instead of three gave the same Tsetlin-machine accuracy (71.3% ± 2.9). Sweeping the margin over the same 10 splits: \(T = 1\) and \(T = 2\) were worse (69.1% each, with larger spread), and \(T = 5\), 10, 20, 50 and 10000 all landed between 70.8% and 72.4%.

What this tells you about the data, not just the model

These three properties (and even all nine) simply do not contain enough information to predict recurrence well: remember from Step 1 that 28 of the 85 recurrences fit neither risk profile. No method in the table escapes that. What the Tsetlin machine adds is not accuracy but transparency: every vote it casts is a rule you can read and check against clinical knowledge. With a test set of 86 patients, a difference of a few points between methods, or between one split and another, is noise. Lesson 1 of this series reports 76.7% against a 70.9% baseline on a different split (seed 42) with a different set of 11 features; our 10-split range of 64.0–75.6% shows how much a single split can move.

docs.title: Step 7 — Reading the model as plain English
docs.text:
A learned rule is a list of memorized literals, for example (from the default run above):

NOT Inv-nodes 6-8 AND NOT Inv-nodes 24-26 AND NOT Deg-malig 3 → against Recurrence

Literals that mention the same property can be merged, the way the book simplifies "Deg-malig 3 and not Deg-malig 1 and not Deg-malig 2" to "Deg-malig 3":

IF Inv-nodes is not 6-8 or 24-26 AND Deg-malig is not 3 then vote against Recurrence.

This rule matches 108 of the 138 non-recurrence training patients and 25 of the 62 recurrence patients. The widgets in Step 2 and Step 6 do this merging automatically. A few habits make a learned model easy to read:

  • Count duplicates. Rules that say the same thing are one rule with a bigger weight: +4 means four votes. (Two rules can list slightly different literals and still be equivalent, such as "Deg-malig 2" and "Deg-malig 2 AND NOT Deg-malig 1"; the widgets merge them.)
  • Check each rule's coverage, the number of training patients of each class it matches. A rule matching 1 patient is an anecdote, not a pattern.
  • Spot rules that can never fire. Reject Feedback sometimes leaves a rule demanding two values of the same property at once ("Inv-nodes 9-11 AND Inv-nodes 12-14"). It is harmless dead weight.
  • Read the vote for one patient. In the Step 2 widget, pick book patient #5 with the learned rules: no rule fires on either side, \(v = 0\), so it is predicted as No recurrence even though it recurred. You can see exactly why the model got it wrong: no learned rule describes "premeno, 0-2 nodes, Deg-malig 3".

Interpretable is not the same as correct

Readable rules let you audit a model: you can see that four rules memorized a single patient with 24-26 nodes, and decide that this is overfitting. They do not make the model right. The breast-cancer machine above is honest about its uncertainty only because you can look inside it.

docs.title: Step 8 — More than two classes
docs.text:
So far one team of rules decided between two classes. For \(m\) classes (say Car, Plane and Boat), the standard Tsetlin machine (Granmo, 2018) gives every class its own team, each with rules voting for and against that class. Each team computes its own vote sum \(v_i\), and the class with the highest vote sum wins.

Training each example updates two teams: its own team, exactly as in Step 4 with the example counted as "own class", and one other team chosen at random, with the example counted as "other class" for that team. Updating just one other team, rather than all of them, keeps the cost the same however many classes there are. The two-class machine of this lesson is the special case with a single team: rules for Recurrence and rules against it.

What to notice

  • Each team is a two-class Tsetlin machine of its own: "this class" against "everything else".
  • The output is still readable: for any prediction you can list the firing rules in the winning team and in its closest rival.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Here is the complete two-class machine in numpy, about 70 lines, trained on the same three properties. It follows the algorithm of Step 4 line by line, but vectorised over rules and literals. It uses numpy's random numbers and its own train/test shuffle, so its numbers differ a little from the widget's.

from collections import Counter

import numpy as np

# ---- 1. Booleanize: one feature per value of Menopause, Inv-nodes and Deg-malig (UCI Breast Cancer data)
VALUES = {"menopause": (1, ["lt40", "ge40", "premeno"]),             # (column after the label, values)
          "inv-nodes": (3, ["0-2", "3-5", "6-8", "9-11", "12-14", "15-17", "24-26"]),
          "deg-malig": (5, ["1", "2", "3"])}
rows = [line.strip().split(",") for line in open("data/breast-cancer.data") if line.strip()]
X = np.array([[r[c + 1] == v for c, vals in VALUES.values() for v in vals] for r in rows], dtype=np.int8)
y = np.array([r[0] == "recurrence-events" for r in rows], dtype=np.int8)
names = [f"{p} {v}" for p, (c, vals) in VALUES.items() for v in vals]


class TsetlinMachine:
    """Two classes. memory[c, j, k] = position (1 … depth) of literal k in rule j of class c."""

    def __init__(self, n_features, rules_per_class=10, T=10, s=3.0, depth=200, seed=1):
        self.T, self.s, self.depth, self.half = T, s, depth, depth // 2
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.memory = np.full((2, rules_per_class, 2 * n_features), depth // 2)  # top of Forgotten

    def fires(self, lits, training=False):
        """Which rules fire? A rule fires when every memorized literal is True."""
        memorized = self.memory > self.half                        # (2, rules, literals)
        ok = ~np.any(memorized & (lits == 0), axis=2)
        if not training:
            ok &= memorized.any(axis=2)                            # empty rules stay silent when classifying
        return ok

    def predict(self, x):
        f = self.fires(np.concatenate([x, 1 - x]))
        return int(f[1].sum() - f[0].sum() > 0)                    # vote sum v > 0 → class 1

    def update(self, x, y):
        lits = np.concatenate([x, 1 - x])                          # literals: x_k, then NOT x_k
        f = self.fires(lits, training=True)
        v = f[y].sum() - f[1 - y].sum()                            # votes for own class − votes against
        v = np.clip(v, -self.T, self.T)
        p = (self.T - v) / (2 * self.T)                            # Voting Margin: feedback probability
        _, n_rules, n_lits = self.memory.shape
        chosen = self.rng.random((2, n_rules)) <= p                # which rules get feedback this time
        u = self.rng.random((n_rules, n_lits))
        own, other = self.memory[y], self.memory[1 - y]            # views: changes go into self.memory

        # Recognize Feedback (own-class rules that fire): memorize True literals, forget False ones
        rec = (chosen[y] & f[y])[:, None]
        own += rec & (lits == 1) & (u <= (self.s - 1) / self.s) & (own < self.depth)
        own -= rec & (lits == 0) & (u <= 1 / self.s) & (own > 1)
        # Erase Feedback (own-class rules that don't fire): forget every literal
        era = (chosen[y] & ~f[y])[:, None]
        own -= era & (u <= 1 / self.s) & (own > 1)
        # Reject Feedback (other-class rules that fire): memorize Forgotten False literals
        rej = (chosen[1 - y] & f[1 - y])[:, None]
        other += rej & (lits == 0) & (other <= self.half)

    def fit(self, X, y, epochs):
        for _ in range(epochs):
            for i in self.rng.permutation(len(X)):
                self.update(X[i], y[i])
        return self

    def rules(self, c, names):
        lits = names + ["NOT " + n for n in names]
        return [" AND ".join(l for l, m in zip(lits, rule) if m > self.half) or "(empty)" for rule in self.memory[c]]


order = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(len(X))              # 200 patients to train on, 86 to test
train, test = order[:200], order[200:]
tm = TsetlinMachine(X.shape[1], rules_per_class=10, T=10, s=3.0, depth=200, seed=1).fit(X[train], y[train], epochs=60)
acc = lambda idx: np.mean([tm.predict(X[i]) == y[i] for i in idx])
print(f"train accuracy {acc(train):.3f} · test accuracy {acc(test):.3f} · always 'no recurrence' on test {1 - y[test].mean():.3f}")
for c, label in ((1, "Recurrence"), (0, "No recurrence")):
    for rule, count in Counter(tm.rules(c, names)).most_common(2):
        print(f"{count} × IF {rule} THEN {label}")

train accuracy 0.775 · test accuracy 0.744 · always 'no recurrence' on test 0.698
5 × IF inv-nodes 24-26 THEN Recurrence
2 × IF inv-nodes 9-11 THEN Recurrence
3 × IF inv-nodes 0-2 AND NOT menopause lt40 AND NOT inv-nodes 3-5 AND NOT inv-nodes 6-8 AND NOT inv-nodes 9-11 AND NOT inv-nodes 12-14 AND NOT inv-nodes 15-17 AND NOT inv-nodes 24-26 AND NOT deg-malig 3 THEN No recurrence
1 × IF inv-nodes 0-2 AND NOT menopause lt40 AND NOT inv-nodes 6-8 AND NOT inv-nodes 9-11 AND NOT inv-nodes 12-14 AND NOT deg-malig 1 AND NOT deg-malig 2 THEN No recurrence

Download breast-cancer.data from the UCI repository first. On this split the machine beats the trivial answer by more (74.4% vs 69.8%), and again five rules spent themselves on the only patient in the whole dataset with 24-26 nodes. The first No-recurrence rule simplifies to "Inv-nodes 0-2 and Menopause is not lt40 and Deg-malig is 1 or 2".

Piece What it does Book term (research term) Rule AND of memorized literals; votes when True rule (clause \(C_j\)) Rules for / against +1 / −1 votes for the class (positive / negative polarity clauses) Vote sum \(v\) votes for − votes against; the sign is the prediction vote sum (\(\sum C^+_j - \sum C^-_j\)) Voting Margin \(T\) feedback probability \((T - v)/2T\) during training Voting Margin (threshold / target \(T\)) Recognize, Erase, Reject how a picked rule changes its memory (Type Ia, Type Ib, Type II feedback) One team per class multi-class: the highest vote sum wins (multi-class Tsetlin machine)

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"The Voting Margin is a decision threshold.\"

No. Classification only looks at the sign of \(v\). The Voting Margin \(T\) is used only during training, to decide how likely each rule is to get feedback. A trained machine never looks at \(T\).

\"More feedback is better, so always give every rule feedback.\"

In the OR game, feedback on every step left the two rules as copies of "x1 AND x2" for 60.7% of the time, and in the correct OR solution only 7.1% of the time. With \(T = 2\) the solution held 81.4% of the time. Switching feedback off for examples that are already safe is what lets rules specialise.

\"Rules know about each other.\"

They don't. Each rule only sees its own condition, the example and one random number. The only shared quantity is the vote sum \(v\), which sets the feedback probability for everyone. Coordination emerges from that single number.

\"74% test accuracy means the model works.\"

On this dataset, answering "no recurrence" for everyone already scores 70.7% on average over 10 splits, and the Tsetlin machine averaged 71.3%. Always compare with the trivial baseline, use more than one split, and look at what the model gets right (here: 8 of 23 recurrences on the default split).

\"Duplicate rules are wasted.\"

Partly true and partly not. Duplicates act as weights: in the book's example, the duplicated R1 + R2 out-vote R3 for patient #5. But four copies of a rule that matches a single patient is wasted capacity, and a sign of overfitting.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. With T = 2, three rules for Recurrence fire and one rule against fires on a patient with recurrence. What is the feedback probability?

Own class minus other: \(v = 3 - 1 = 2\), which is already at the margin. $p = (2 - 2)/4 = $ 0: no rule learns from this patient.

2. Same rules, but the patient did NOT have a recurrence. What happens?

From the patient's point of view \(v = 1 - 3 = -2\), so $p = (2 - (-2))/4 = $ 1: every rule is picked. The rules against Recurrence get Recognize (the one that fired) or Erase (the others). The three rules for Recurrence that fired voted wrongly and get Reject Feedback, which pushes a False literal of this patient into each of them.

3. Why does a Tsetlin machine predict with the sign of v, but train with (T − v)/2T?

Prediction only needs to know which side wins. Training also wants a safety margin: an example won by a single vote is fragile, so it keeps asking for feedback until it wins by \(T\) votes. And examples won by \(T\) votes or more stop asking, which frees the rules to cover other sub-patterns.

4. You have 4 rules for a class whose examples come in 4 clearly different sub-patterns. Is T = 1 or T = 20 the better choice?

Neither. With \(T = 1\) one firing rule is enough, so a second sub-pattern covered by the "wrong" rule stops the learning early, and there is little pressure to fill every niche. With \(T = 20\) the margin can never be reached (4 rules give at most 4 votes), so feedback never switches off and the rules crowd onto the most frequent sub-pattern. A margin around the number of votes a well-covered example can collect (here a few) works best, as the OR game showed with \(T = 2\) for two rules.

5. The learned model predicts 'No recurrence' for book patient #5 (premeno, 0-2 nodes, Deg-malig 3), who did recur. How would you find out why?

Read the votes. In the Step 2 widget with the learned rules, no rule fires on either side, so \(v = 0\) and the tie goes to No recurrence. No learned rule describes this profile, and the data explains why: Deg-malig 3 without lymph-node spread recurred in only 38% of patients. A black-box model would give you the same wrong answer without the explanation.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Ole-Christoffer Granmo, An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines (free online), Ch. 1, §1.5–1.7 (voting, the Voting Margin and the complete algorithm) and Ch. 2, §2.3 (rule interaction and the OR example with its Markov-chain analysis). This lesson follows those sections.
  • Ole-Christoffer Granmo, The Tsetlin Machine – A Game Theoretic Bandit Driven Approach to Optimal Pattern Recognition with Propositional Logic (2018). The original paper, including the multi-class machine and the clause/threshold terminology.
  • M. Zwitter and M. Soklic, Breast Cancer dataset, UCI Machine Learning Repository. The data used in Step 6.
  • The Tsetlin automaton and Recognize, Erase & Reject feedback: the memory and the feedback this lesson builds on.

docs.title: Confidence, Trustworthiness and Composites
docs.text:
TL;DR

A Tsetlin machine (TM) can tell you how sure it is, for free: the confidence of a prediction is the size of the vote sum, \(|v|\). Many rules agreeing gives a large \(|v|\); few rules, or rules that disagree, give a \(|v|\) near zero. A TM is trustworthy when its confidence matches its performance: the cases it is sure about should be the ones it gets right. You check this on held-out data by answering only the cases above a confidence threshold and measuring accuracy on them, which gives a coverage/accuracy trade-off (answer fewer patients, make fewer mistakes, refer the rest to a human). Vote sums are a ranking, not probabilities, so check how they line up with real outcomes before reading too much into them. Finally, several specialised TMs can form a TM composite: each one normalises its vote sum by its own range, and the normalised sums are added. On a breast-cancer dataset, three specialists that each see one group of measurements reach 88.0%, 90.7% and 82.6% accuracy alone, and 96.1% together.

Level: intermediate · Prerequisites: Classification by voting (rules voting for and against a class, the vote sum \(v\), the Voting Margin \(T\)). Convolutional Tsetlin machines helps for the image examples, but isn't needed.

This lesson follows Chapter 7 of Ole-Christoffer Granmo's free book An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines, redrawn and retold in this site's style. The patient experiments are our own runs, made for this lesson.

docs.title: Why should I care?
docs.text:
Think about your family doctor (the chapter opens with this example). Nobody expects them to know every corner of medicine. You trust them because of one skill: they know when they don't know, and then they refer you to a specialist.

A model that helps with clinical decisions needs the same skill, and medical AI is full of situations where it matters:

  • Triage. A screening model could handle the clear-cut cases and send the doubtful ones to a radiologist or pathologist. That only works if "doubtful" is something the model can measure.
  • Safety. A confident wrong answer is the most dangerous kind. You want to know how often the model is confident and wrong before anyone relies on it.
  • Combining sources. Hospitals hold different patient populations; one patient has blood tests, images and clinical notes. Models trained on each source could work as a team, if their opinions can be put on the same scale.

Tsetlin machines are a good fit here because the same vote sum that decides the class also measures how sure the machine is, and the rules behind every vote can be read. This lesson shows how to measure confidence, how to check whether it deserves trust, and how to build TM composites.

docs.title: Step 1 — Confidence is the size of the vote sum
docs.text:
Recall from Classification by voting how a two-class TM decides: every rule whose condition is true casts a vote, votes for the class count \(+1\), votes against it count \(-1\), and the vote sum \(v\) decides (class if \(v \ge 0\)). The chapter's key observation is that \(v\) carries more information than its sign:

  • Many rules agree on "yes" → a large positive \(v\). The machine is confident in the class.
  • Many rules agree on "no" → a large negative \(v\). The machine is confident in the other class.
  • Few rules vote, or they disagree → \(v\) near zero. There is no clear consensus: the machine is uncertain.

So the chapter defines confidence as the size of the vote sum, ignoring its sign:

\[ \text{confidence} = |v| \]

The chapter illustrates this with a small, invented example: predicting which of six students pass a course from three habits (did they follow the lectures, read the textbook, do the assignments?), using three rules. Click the buttons to answer only the students whose confidence reaches a threshold.

🎓 Interactive: confidence for six students (the book's Table 7.1)

What to notice

  • Students #1 and #3 match R1 and R2 and nothing votes against them: \(v = +2\), the most confident Pass.
  • Student #2 is the interesting one. R2 (Textbook) votes Pass, R3 (no Assignments) votes Fail, so \(v = 0\): a tie. The machine still has to pick something (\(v \ge 0\) gives Pass), and it is wrong. It is also the least confident student.
  • Ranking by confidence: #1 and #3 (\(|v| = 2\)), then #4, #5, #6 (\(|v| = 1\)), then #2 (\(|v| = 0\)). Answer everyone and accuracy is 5 of 6 (83%). Answer only \(|v| \ge 1\) and it is 5 of 5 (100%). The one mistake was the case the machine was least sure about.

How big is "big"? The Voting Margin \(T\) gives the natural scale. During learning, a TM clips \(v\) at \(\pm T\) and stops giving feedback for an example once its vote sum reaches \(T\) in the right direction: \(T\) is how sure training asks the machine to be. So \(|v| \ge T\) means "as sure as training ever pushed it", and \(|v|/T\) is a handy 0-to-1 reading of confidence. (Vote sums can go beyond \(T\) when more rules happen to agree; they are simply not pushed further.)

More than two classes

A multi-class TM keeps one vote sum per class and predicts the class with the largest sum. The chapter takes that largest sum as the confidence:

\[ \text{multi-class confidence} = \max_{\text{classes}} v_{\text{class}} \]

A common alternative in other models, not used in the chapter, is the gap between the largest and second-largest sums, which also catches the case where two classes are both strongly supported.

docs.title: Step 2 — Trustworthiness: confidence must match performance
docs.text:
Confidence on its own proves nothing. A person can be very confident and still wrong, and someone too timid to act also does badly. Confidence is only useful when it matches ability. The chapter sums this up in a 2 × 2 table:

Low performance High performance High confidence 🚩 Overconfident ✅ Justifiably confident Low confidence ✅ Justifiably uncertain 🐢 Underconfident

For a classifier, you test this by comparing predictions with the true labels at each confidence level, exactly as in the student widget: if accuracy rises as you keep only the more confident cases, then confidence is faithful to performance, and the machine is trustworthy in this sense. If accuracy is flat (or even falls), its confidence tells you nothing.

The chapter also reports this test for a much larger problem: a multi-class TM that sorts colour images into 100 classes, using Boolean features made by thresholding each pixel's colour against its neighbours. Ranking 10,000 test images by multi-class confidence (from about −2,500 to 10,000), accuracy climbs from about 34% for the least confident images to 100% for the most confident ones (Granmo, Ch. 7, Fig. 7.3; we did not rerun this). The machine was unsure about images made mostly of colour texture, such as a pink flower, and sure about large, distinct objects such as a tank or the Eiffel Tower.

What to notice

  • Trustworthiness here is a property you measure on data the machine has not seen, not something you assume.
  • The test does not need the confidence to be a probability. It only asks: are the more confident cases more often right?

docs.title: Step 3 — Confidence on real patients
docs.text:
Now the real test, on two breast-cancer datasets. For each, we trained our own TM (numpy, written for this lesson following the book's algorithm; 20 rules, Voting Margin \(T = 10\), Memorize Value \(2/3\), Forget Value \(1/3\), 40 passes over the data). To make the test honest, we used 5-fold cross-validation: the patients are split into five groups, and each group's vote sums come from a machine trained on the other four. Every vote sum below is for a patient the machine had never seen.

  1. Diagnosis (Wisconsin). The public Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer data (also bundled with scikit-learn): 569 patients, 212 malignant and 357 benign. Each has 30 measurements of the cell nuclei in a digitised image of a fine-needle aspirate (10 properties such as radius, texture and concavity, each as a mean, a standard error and a "worst" value). We Booleanize each measurement with 4 thresholds ("mean radius > 11.39?", and so on, at the 20th, 40th, 60th and 80th percentiles of the training patients), giving 120 Boolean features.
  2. Recurrence (the book's data). The public UCI Breast Cancer data from the Institute of Oncology in Ljubljana, which Chapter 1 of the book uses: 286 patients, 85 of whom had a recurrence, with 9 properties (age, menopause, tumour size, involved nodes, malignancy grade and so on), one Boolean feature per value: 41 features.

Slide the threshold to answer only patients with \(|v|\) at or above it. The rest are referred.

🎚️ Interactive: answer only the confident cases

What to notice

  • Diagnosis: confidence is very informative. Answering everyone, the machine is right 92.3% of the time (44 errors in 569). At \(|v| \ge 2\) it answers 473 patients (83.1%) with 99.2% accuracy (4 errors). The 96 referred patients hold 40 of the 44 errors.
  • The silent cases. 42 patients (7.4%) got \(v = 0\): either no rule fired, or the votes for and against cancelled out. They are classed malignant by the \(v \ge 0\) rule, but 25 of them are benign: a machine with nothing to say should not be trusted to say it.
  • Confident is not the same as infallible. At \(|v| \ge 10\) (the full Voting Margin) it still makes 1 error in 64 patients: a malignant case that got the most confident possible benign vote, \(v = -10\).
  • Recurrence: switch datasets. Here the TM's overall accuracy is 72.4%, barely above the 70.3% you get by always saying "no recurrence". Accuracy does rise with confidence (84.1% at \(|v| \ge 6\)), but look at the dashed line: all 69 of those patients are predicted "no recurrence", and always guessing "no recurrence" in that same group also gives 84.1%. The rising curve here only shows the machine finding the patients whose recurrence was least likely to begin with; within that group its confidence adds nothing beyond the class balance.

That last point is a general lesson, not a quirk of Tsetlin machines. Always compare against the simplest baseline, in the same subgroup. An accuracy-vs-confidence curve that rises can still describe a model that has learned little.

docs.title: Step 4 — Knowing when to refer: a triage rule
docs.text:
A confidence threshold turns a classifier into a triage tool: answer when sure, refer when not. Because a TM is built from readable rules, it can hand the human more than "I don't know". It can show which rules fired on each side, so the clinician sees what the conflict was.

What does "the rules that fired" look like? Here are some rules our size specialist (Step 8) learned, from one of the five training runs. Each is an AND of thresholded measurements:

  • if worst radius > 20.35 then malignant
  • if mean radius > 17.16 then malignant
  • if area SE > 57.94 then malignant (SE = standard error)
  • if worst perimeter ≤ 91.31 then benign
  • if worst perimeter ≤ 91.31 and mean perimeter ≤ 91.35 then benign

(A few of its other rules are long chains of thresholds that a person would want to simplify, and one rule appears twice, just like the duplicated rules in the book's Chapter 1 example.) This is what the chapter means by trustworthiness in a wider sense: an answer you can check (why) together with an honest signal of doubt (how sure).

Before anything like this touches patients

These are teaching experiments, not a validated clinical tool. A real triage threshold has to be chosen on a separate validation set and then checked on fresh data from the setting where it will be used. The Wisconsin data come from one centre, decades ago; a new scanner, lab or patient population can shift every number above. Errors also have different costs: missing a cancer is not the same as a false alarm, so a real system might demand more confidence before saying "benign" than before saying "malignant" (our own suggestion, not from the book).

docs.title: Step 5 — An honest look at calibration
docs.text:
It is tempting to read \(|v|/T\) as a probability: "\(v = 8\) with \(T = 10\) means 80% sure". That is not what the vote sum is. The TM never learns probabilities; it learns rules and pushes vote sums towards \(\pm T\). Whether a vote sum corresponds to 60% or 99% of patients actually being positive is an empirical question, and the answer differs between machines and datasets.

The standard way to look is a reliability diagram (as in Guo et al., 2017). Group the held-out patients by their vote sum and, for each group, plot the share that truly had the positive class. Here are both of our machines.

📊 Interactive: what does each vote sum really mean?

What to notice

  • Diagnosis: the scale saturates fast. Every one of the 11 patients with \(v = +2\) was malignant, as were all 115 with \(v \ge 8\). A vote sum of +2 is "only" 20% of the margin, yet it already behaves like near-certainty. Reading \(|v|/T\) as a probability would badly understate this machine's confidence.
  • The middle is where the doubt lives. \(v = 0\): 17 of 42 malignant (40%). \(v = +1\): 9 of 18 (50%), even though the machine says "malignant" for all of them. \(v = -1\): 6 of 36 (17%).
  • Small groups, wide error bars. 11 out of 11 sounds conclusive, but the 95% interval for \(v = +2\) runs from 74% to 100%. With a few hundred patients, a per-vote-sum table is a rough sketch.
  • Recurrence: nothing is certain. The positive vote sums never pass +4, and their recurrence shares bounce around (8 of 11 at \(v = +2\), 6 of 11 at \(v = +3\)). Even \(v = -5\) still had 11 recurrences among 29 patients (38%). This machine's ranking is weak, and the picture shows it immediately.

If you need actual probabilities (for a risk score, or to combine with costs), you can learn a mapping from vote sum to probability on validation data, for example by binning as above or by fitting a logistic curve to \(v\) (Platt scaling). That mapping is only as good as the data it was fitted on, and it has to be re-checked when the patient population changes.

docs.title: Step 6 — Different machines, different skills
docs.text:
The second half of the chapter is about teamwork. Just as a house needs carpenters, plumbers and electricians, a hard problem may need several Tsetlin machines with different skills. The chapter names two ways TMs end up with different skills:

  • Different populations. Two hospitals train their own recurrence TMs. Different demographics, treatments and equipment give each machine its own perspective.
  • Different modalities. One TM reads blood tests, another mammograms, a third the doctor's notes. Each sees something the others miss.

A TM composite lets such machines work together. Each machine runs on its own, completely unchanged, but instead of announcing a class it reports its vote sum. Because the only thing exchanged is a vote sum, any kind of TM (plain, convolutional, trained on any data) can join a composite: the chapter calls this plug-and-play. The research paper behind the chapter calls them TMComposites.

The chapter's toy example reuses the recurrence rules from Chapter 1, split into two machines:

  • Recurrence TM, trained only on recurrence patients: R1 and R2, both "if Deg-malig 3 and NOT Menopause lt40 then Recurrence".
  • Non-Recurrence TM, trained only on non-recurrence patients: R3, "if Inv-nodes 0-2 then Non-Recurrence".

Step through the composite for patient #1 of the book's Table 1.9 (Menopause ge40, Inv-nodes 3-5, Deg-malig 3; she did have a recurrence).

Doing the same for all six patients of the book's Table 1.9 (our calculation):

Patient Recurrence TM \(v\) → ÷ 2 Non-Recurrence TM \(v\) → ÷ 1 Composite Prediction Truth #1 +2 → +1 0 → 0 +1 Recurrence Recurrence #2 0 → 0 1 → 1 −1 No recurrence No recurrence #3 +2 → +1 0 → 0 +1 Recurrence Recurrence #4 0 → 0 1 → 1 −1 No recurrence No recurrence #5 +2 → +1 1 → 1 0 Recurrence Recurrence #6 0 → 0 1 → 1 −1 No recurrence No recurrence

A note on signs

The chapter writes the composite as the sum of the two normalised vote sums and predicts Recurrence when it is \(\ge 0\). For that to work, the Non-Recurrence machine's votes must count as negative (they are votes against Recurrence), just like rules voting against a class in a single TM. With more than two classes this question disappears: each machine reports one sum per class, the sums are added class by class, and the largest wins.

docs.title: Step 7 — Normalisation: one scale for every machine
docs.text:
Why divide at all? Because members of a composite can be built very differently: different data, different numbers of rules, different Voting Margins. A machine with 40 rules can produce vote sums of ±20; one with 10 rules rarely goes past ±5. Added raw, the big machine would drown out the small one, whatever their actual skill.

The chapter's fix is simple. Each machine finds the highest and lowest vote sum it produces on the (training) data, and divides by the difference:

\[ \text{normalised vote sum} = \frac{v}{\;v_{\text{highest}} - v_{\text{lowest}}\;} \]

The composite then adds the normalised sums and decides as usual:

\[ v_{\text{composite}} = \sum_{\text{machines } m} \frac{v_m}{\;v_{m,\text{highest}} - v_{m,\text{lowest}}\;}, \qquad \text{class if } v_{\text{composite}} \ge 0 \]

After normalisation, every machine's opinion lives on a range of width 1. A machine that is confident relative to its own range counts for more than one that is lukewarm, regardless of size. That is how the composite "leans on the confident ones".

What to notice

  • The factor is a property of the machine, computed once from data, not of the patient.
  • Use the training data (or a validation set) for the range, never the patients you test on.
  • Normalising by the range is the chapter's choice. It is simple and needs no labels, but it is sensitive to a single extreme vote sum; other scalings are possible.

docs.title: Step 8 — Build a composite
docs.text:
Back to the Wisconsin data. Instead of one machine that sees all 30 measurements, we trained three specialists, each seeing only one group of measurements, and gave them deliberately different sizes:

Specialist Sees (mean, SE and worst of …) Boolean features Rules \(T\) Normalisation factor (per fold) Accuracy alone Size TM radius, perimeter, area 36 10 4 7 to 10 88.0% Shape TM compactness, concavity, concave points 36 40 20 40 90.7% Texture TM texture, smoothness, symmetry, fractal dimension 48 20 10 18 to 20 82.6%

All other settings are as in Step 3, with the same 5-fold cross-validation and seed. Tick specialists on and off, switch normalisation off, and browse the patients on whom the specialists disagree.

🧩 Interactive: three specialists, one composite

What to notice

  • The team beats every member. Alone, the specialists reach 88.0%, 90.7% and 82.6%. The normalised composite of all three reaches 96.1% (22 errors in 569). The specialists disagree on 183 patients; the composite gets 164 of those right.
  • Normalisation matters here. Switch it off: the raw sum drops to 94.2%, because the 40-rule shape machine shouts loudest. The first patient shown (patient 11, malignant) is a case in point: size +2/8 = +0.25, shape −14/40 = −0.35, texture +3/19 = +0.16. Normalised, the sum is +0.06 → malignant ✓. Raw, it is 2 − 14 + 3 = −9 → benign ✗.
  • But it is not magic. Among the 183 disagreement cases, normalising fixed 14 and broke 3. For the shape + texture pair it even does worse than the raw sum (90.0% vs 91.7%). Normalising makes the scales comparable; it cannot know which machine is right.
  • Fair comparison. One TM on all 30 measurements with 20 rules reaches 92.3%; with 70 rules (as many as the three specialists together) it reaches 96.1%, the same as the composite. The composite's advantage is not raw accuracy: it is that separately trained machines can be combined without retraining, which is exactly the situation of different hospitals or different modalities.
  • The composite has a confidence too: \(|v_{\text{composite}}|\). Answering only \(|v_{\text{composite}}| \ge 0.25\) covers 90.7% of patients at 98.6% accuracy, and \(\ge 0.5\) covers 76.1% at 99.3%.

We repeated the whole experiment with two other random splits (seeds 2 and 3). The normalised composite reached 94.9% and 96.1%, the raw sum 93.5% and 94.2%, and no single specialist went above 90.7%. So the ranking held, though the exact numbers move by a percentage point or so.

The chapter's image composite

The chapter's larger example (Fig. 7.6) combines four multi-class TMs for colour images, each with a different view of the same picture: one on a histogram of gradients, one on colour thresholding with 10 × 10 convolution filters, and two on colour thermometers with 3 × 3 and 4 × 4 convolution filters (see Convolutional Tsetlin machines). Each normalises its class sums, the sums are added class by class, and the composite predicts the class with the largest total (argmax). The book develops image understanding in a later chapter.

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
Here is the whole composite experiment in numpy, the Tsetlin machine included. It reproduces the numbers in Step 8 and runs in about half a minute.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer


class TsetlinMachine:
    """Two-class TM: the first half of the rules vote for class 1, the rest for class 0."""

    def __init__(self, n_features, n_rules, T, s=3.0, depth=200, seed=0):
        self.T, self.s, self.N = T, s, depth // 2                       # positions 1..depth; memorized above N
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.memory = np.full((n_rules, 2 * n_features), self.N)     # every literal starts barely forgotten
        self.sign = np.where(np.arange(n_rules) < n_rules // 2, 1, -1)

    def vote(self, X):                                                  # vote sum v for every row of X
        lit, mem = np.hstack([X, 1 - X]), self.memory > self.N
        fired = ((1 - lit) @ mem.T == 0) & mem.any(axis=1)              # all memorized literals true, rule not empty
        return fired.astype(int) @ self.sign

    def fit(self, X, y, epochs=40):
        for _ in range(epochs):
            for i in self.rng.permutation(len(y)):
                lit = np.concatenate([X[i], 1 - X[i]])
                out = ~np.any((self.memory > self.N) & (lit == 0), axis=1)
                v = int(out @ self.sign) * (1 if y[i] == 1 else -1)       # votes for the object's own class
                p = (self.T - np.clip(v, -self.T, self.T)) / (2 * self.T)   # far from the margin: more feedback
                chosen = self.rng.random(len(out)) < p
                own = self.sign == (1 if y[i] == 1 else -1)
                for j in np.where(chosen & own)[0]:                     # Recognize / Erase feedback
                    r = self.rng.random(lit.size)
                    if out[j]:
                        self.memory[j] += (lit == 1) & (r < (self.s - 1) / self.s)
                        self.memory[j] -= (lit == 0) & (r < 1 / self.s)
                    else:
                        self.memory[j] -= r < 1 / self.s
                    np.clip(self.memory[j], 1, 2 * self.N, out=self.memory[j])
                for j in np.where(chosen & ~own & out)[0]:              # Reject feedback
                    self.memory[j] += (lit == 0) & (self.memory[j] <= self.N)
        return self


def thermometer(train, test, q=4):                                      # "x > threshold" bits, 4 per measurement
    cuts = np.quantile(train, np.arange(1, q + 1) / (q + 1), axis=0)
    bits = lambda A: np.concatenate([(A > c).astype(np.int8) for c in cuts], axis=1)
    return bits(train), bits(test)


data = load_breast_cancer()
X, y, names = data.data, (data.target == 0).astype(int), list(data.feature_names)   # y = 1: malignant
cols = lambda *kinds: [i for k in kinds for i, n in enumerate(names) if k in n]
views = {"size": (cols("radius", "perimeter", "area"), 10, 4),                        # (columns, rules, T)
         "shape": (cols("compactness", "concavity", "concave points"), 40, 20),
         "texture": (cols("texture", "smoothness", "symmetry", "fractal"), 20, 10)}

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)                                          # stratified 5-fold split
fold = np.zeros(len(y), int)
for c in (0, 1):
    idx = rng.permutation(np.where(y == c)[0])
    fold[idx] = np.arange(len(idx)) % 5

normalised, raw = {}, {}
for name, (columns, rules, T) in views.items():
    raw[name], normalised[name] = np.zeros(len(y)), np.zeros(len(y))
    for k in range(5):                                                  # every vote comes from a TM that never saw the patient
        tr, te = thermometer(X[fold != k][:, columns], X[fold == k][:, columns])
        tm = TsetlinMachine(tr.shape[1], rules, T, seed=100 + k).fit(tr, y[fold != k])
        seen = tm.vote(tr)
        raw[name][fold == k] = tm.vote(te)
        normalised[name][fold == k] = tm.vote(te) / (seen.max() - seen.min())   # Eq. 7.3
    print(f"{name:8s} alone: accuracy {np.mean((raw[name] >= 0) == y):.1%}")

composite = normalised["size"] + normalised["shape"] + normalised["texture"]
print(f"composite, raw sums:        {np.mean((sum(raw.values()) >= 0) == y):.1%}")
print(f"composite, normalised sums: {np.mean((composite >= 0) == y):.1%}")
for threshold in (0.25, 0.5):                                           # confidence = |composite vote sum|
    keep = np.abs(composite) >= threshold
    print(f"|composite| >= {threshold}: answer {keep.mean():.1%} of patients, "
          f"accuracy {np.mean((composite[keep] >= 0) == y[keep]):.1%}, refer {np.sum(~keep)}")

size     alone: accuracy 88.0%
shape    alone: accuracy 90.7%
texture  alone: accuracy 82.6%
composite, raw sums:        94.2%
composite, normalised sums: 96.1%
|composite| >= 0.25: answer 90.7% of patients, accuracy 98.6%, refer 53
|composite| >= 0.5: answer 76.1% of patients, accuracy 99.3%, refer 136

Each literal's memory here has a depth of 200 positions (1 to 200, memorized above 100), rules start with every literal at position 100, just below the memorized half, and s = 3 gives Memorize Value 2/3 and Forget Value 1/3, as in Recognize, Erase & Reject feedback. The feedback probability \((T - v)/(2T)\) is the book's \((2 - v)/4\) with a general Voting Margin.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
\"A confident Tsetlin machine is a correct one.\"

Confidence makes errors rarer, not impossible. Our diagnosis TM gave one malignant patient the most confident possible benign vote (\(v = -10\)). Always report how many confident errors remain, not just the accuracy.

\"If accuracy rises with confidence, the model is useful.\"

Check the baseline in the same subgroup. On the recurrence data, accuracy rose to 84.1% at \(|v| \ge 6\), but every one of those 69 patients was predicted "no recurrence", and simply always saying "no recurrence" scores 84.1% there too.

\"\(v = 8\) with \(T = 10\) means an 80% chance.\"

Vote sums are a ranking, not probabilities. On the diagnosis data, all 11 patients with \(v = +2\) (only 20% of the margin) were malignant, while \(v = +1\) was a coin flip (9 of 18). To get probabilities, fit a mapping on validation data, and re-check it whenever the setting changes.

\"A composite wins because it has more rules.\"

A single TM with the same total of 70 rules matched our composite (96.1% each). The point of a composite is that machines trained separately, on different data, sizes and margins, can be combined plug-and-play, and each stays small and readable.

\"Normalisation always improves the composite.\"

It makes the machines' scales comparable, which helped the full trio (96.1% vs 94.2% raw). But for the shape + texture pair, the raw sum did better (91.7% vs 90.0%). Normalisation decides how loud each machine is, not which one is right.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. One TM gives patient A the vote sum \(v = -3\) and patient B \(v = +1\). Which prediction is more confident, and what does each predict?

Confidence is \(|v|\): patient A has confidence 3, patient B has 1, so A's prediction is more confident. A is predicted as the other class (negative sum); B is predicted as the class (\(v \ge 0\)), but only weakly: few rules or disagreeing rules.

2. A multi-class TM gives vote sums Car = 4, Plane = 9, Boat = −2. What does it predict, and with what confidence (the chapter's definition)?

It predicts the class with the largest sum, Plane, and the chapter's multi-class confidence is that largest sum, 9. (The gap to the runner-up, 9 − 4 = 5, is another useful measure, though not the chapter's.)

3. Machine A's training vote sums range from −5 to +4; machine B's from −20 to +20. For a patient, A votes +3 and B votes −12. What does the composite predict, with and without normalisation?

Normalised: A gives \(3 / (4 - (-5)) = 3/9 \approx +0.33\), B gives \(-12 / 40 = -0.30\). The sum is about +0.03 ≥ 0: the positive class, although only just (very low composite confidence). Raw: \(3 - 12 = -9\), the negative class. Without normalisation, B wins simply because it has more rules.

4. On our diagnosis run, answering only \(|v| \ge 2\) kept 473 of 569 patients at 99.2% accuracy. What is the price, and how would you choose the threshold for real use?

The price is 96 referred patients (16.9%) that a human must handle; in exchange, 40 of the 44 errors land in that referred group instead of being reported confidently. A real threshold is chosen on a separate validation set, weighing the cost of a missed cancer, a false alarm and a referral, and then checked on fresh data from the clinic where it will be used, not on the test data quoted here.

5. Why must the confidence check use patients the machine has not seen?

On its training patients a TM has been pushed to reach the Voting Margin, so its vote sums there are large and mostly right: confidence would look perfectly trustworthy. Only held-out patients (here via 5-fold cross-validation) show how confidence behaves on new cases, which is the only situation that matters in practice.

docs.text:

  • Ole-Christoffer Granmo, TMComposites: Plug-and-Play Collaboration Between Specialized Tsetlin Machines (2023). The research paper behind the composites.

  • Data: W. N. Street, W. H. Wolberg & O. L. Mangasarian (1993), the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer data; M. Zwitter & M. Soklic, the UCI Breast Cancer (recurrence) data, University Medical Centre, Institute of Oncology, Ljubljana.
